findings.title: test_release_clears_assignee asserts an invariant the read-time gate alone satisfies
findings.explanation: After calling close_claim + update_state(RELEASED), the test asserts row.assignee_hf_id is None to claim the 'ReciterRow invariant holds'. But _assemble (repo_state.py:60) only fills assignee_* when state == UNDER_REVIEW. So row.assignee_hf_id is None purely because the row is now RELEASED — even if close_claim had been a complete no-op, the assertion would still pass. The test does NOT actually verify that close_claim closed the claim. To cover the real invariant, query the claims table (e.g. assert claims.released_at IS NOT NULL or get_open_claim('d1') is None) in addition to the read-row check, or re-transition back to UNDER_REVIEW to prove the open-claim row is gone.
findings.proposed_action: Add an explicit assertion that the open claim was actually closed (e.g. `assert repo_claims.get_open_claim('d1') is None`) before/instead of relying on the assembled ReciterRow.
findings.verifier_notes: The test calls close_claim() but only verifies that row.assignee_hf_id is None after state changes to RELEASED. This assertion passes regardless of whether close_claim actually executed because _assemble (repo_state.py:60) only populates assignee_* when BOTH state == UNDER_REVIEW AND claim IS NOT NULL. With state=RELEASED, gate #2 prevents population even if released_at was never set. The SQL LEFT JOIN gate (repo_state.py:72 with c.released_at IS NULL) provides a second independent gate that also results in None. The test should query repo_claims.get_open_claim('d1') to verify gate #1 actually worked (claim was truly closed).

findings.title: test_repo_transitions defines its own _seed_user instead of using _helpers.seed_user
findings.explanation: The dominant pattern across inspector/tests/db/ is to import `seed_user`/`seed_delivery` from `._helpers` (used by test_repo_state, test_repo_requests_activity, test_review_followups). test_repo_transitions instead defines a private `_seed_user` at module top that does the same INSERT OR IGNORE — pure duplication.
findings.proposed_action: Delete the local `_seed_user` in test_repo_transitions.py and `from ._helpers import seed_user` like the rest of the package.
findings.verifier_notes: test_repo_transitions.py defines _seed_user (line 16) with identical implementation to seed_user in _helpers.py (line 8). All calls in test_repo_transitions use default arguments only, matching the helper exactly. The pattern is violated here — other test files (test_repo_state, test_repo_requests_activity, test_review_followups) consistently import seed_user from _helpers instead. This is straightforward duplication with no documented isolation or special-case reason.

findings.title: test_for_slug_timeline inlines the vocab+delivery FK chain instead of using _helpers.seed_delivery
findings.explanation: test_for_slug_timeline duplicates _helpers._seed_vocab + the deliveries INSERT inline (11 lines) with the comment 'seed a delivery so the slug FK holds'. _helpers.seed_delivery() already does exactly this and is used elsewhere. The inline copy hardcodes the same vocab slugs ('hafs','mur','src','ch') the helper inserts.
findings.proposed_action: Replace the inline INSERT block with `seed_delivery('d1')` imported from `._helpers`.
findings.verifier_notes: The test_for_slug_timeline function at inspector/tests/db/test_repo_transitions.py:87-110 inlines the exact same FK chain setup (reciters → riwayahs/styles/sources/channels → deliveries) that seed_delivery() in _helpers.py:24-32 provides. The helper is actively used in 13+ other tests (test_repo_state.py, test_repo_requests_activity.py, test_review_followups.py, etc.) but NOT imported or used here. The test doesn't verify added_by_hf_id ('u1' vs 'sys'), so the difference is immaterial to test correctness. This is a valid DRY violation: the inline block duplicates 11 lines of hardcoded vocab slugs and delivery insert logic. The inline code works, but refactoring to seed_delivery('d1') would eliminate duplication per project conventions (DRY in best-practices.md).

findings.title: _actor() helper is re-defined verbatim across db tests; should be conftest-promoted
findings.explanation: Every test module that needs an Actor defines its own `_actor(hf='u1', login='alice', role=...)` factory — same constructor call, only the default role varies. This is the textbook fixture-promotion target: a `make_actor` factory fixture in `tests/db/conftest.py` (or `tests/conftest.py` for the wider duplication) would eliminate 6+ near-identical copies.
findings.proposed_action: Promote `_actor` to a conftest fixture (factory pattern, parameterized role/hf/login) and import it where needed.
findings.verifier_notes: Reduce severity from 'low' to 'informational' or 'style'; scope proposed action to DB tests only (inspector/tests/db/conftest.py) rather than suggesting project-wide promotion; note that services tests have incompatible signatures and should remain separate; update explanation to distinguish between real repetition (DB layer) and intentional variation (services layer with different defaults and mocking needs).

findings.title: Unused `timezone` import in test_repo_state.py
findings.explanation: `from datetime import datetime, timezone` is at the top of the file but `timezone` is never referenced — only `datetime.fromisoformat()` is used inside `_dt()`. Likely a leftover from an earlier draft.
findings.proposed_action: Drop `timezone` from the import.
findings.verifier_notes: The `timezone` import on line 5 of inspector/tests/db/test_repo_state.py is never referenced anywhere in the file. The only datetime construction occurs via _dt() which uses datetime.fromisoformat() to parse ISO strings with embedded timezone info—no timezone object is needed. Related conftest.py code shows the pattern of actual timezone usage (datetime.now(timezone.utc)), which is absent in test_repo_state.py. Import appears leftover from initial scaffolding (commit 9557f66e).

findings.title: repo_state.update_state KeyError on unknown column + empty-fields short-circuit untested
findings.explanation: `update_state` has two important branches: (a) the empty-fields short-circuit at line 153-154 (`if not fields: return`), and (b) the KeyError raise at line 157-158 for any field not in `_WRITABLE`. Neither is exercised — the only update_state call across the entire test tree is `state=... state_since=...` (test_repo_state.py:70). A future refactor changing `_WRITABLE` could silently drop or accept fields without test feedback.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests: (1) `update_state('d1')` no-op returns cleanly without DB writes; (2) `update_state('d1', bogus=1)` raises KeyError with the column name in the message; (3) update of `revision_in_progress`/`last_job_finished_at`/`visibility_reason` round-trips via get_row.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified the two unhappy paths and column round-trips are genuinely untested: (1) Empty fields short-circuit at line 153-154 is not exercised—no test calls update_state() with zero kwargs; (2) KeyError raise at line 157-158 for unknown columns is not exercised—no test passes a bogus field; (3) Multiple writable columns (revision_in_progress, last_job_finished_at, visibility_reason) are updated in production code (state.py:197, 214, 438) but never round-trip tested via update_state + get_row in test_repo_state.py. The only existing test (test_release_clears_assignee:70) only updates state + state_since. Production code at state.py calls update_state with timestamps_job_ids, last_job_finished_at, and dynamic **updates that could include visibility/visibility_reason/revision_in_progress. The gap is real and refactoring _WRITABLE could silently break without test feedback.

findings.title: repo_transitions.feed offset/limit pagination and since() cutoff untested
findings.explanation: test_feed_order_and_event_filter exercises ordering, the events filter, and the empty-allow-list short-circuit, but never `offset=`/`limit=` pagination semantics. `since(cutoff_iso, limit=...)` (used by the activity feeds) has zero test coverage — neither the lexical-ISO ordering claim in its docstring nor the limit truncation is verified.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests: (1) feed(limit=2, offset=1) returns the middle slice in newest-first order; (2) since(cutoff_iso) yields only records with ts >= cutoff and stays newest-first; (3) since with limit truncates correctly.
findings.verifier_notes: The `since()` function (repo_transitions.py:152) is mocked out in all public_activity tests via `_install_audit()` patching `_iter_partitions()`, so it has zero direct test coverage. The `feed()` function (repo_transitions.py:167) is tested in `test_feed_order_and_event_filter()` (test_repo_transitions.py:53) but only with the default offset=0; no tests exercise non-zero offset values or the pagination slicing semantics. The docstring claims in `since()` about lexical-ISO ordering and limit truncation are never verified. The gap is real and the proposed tests (offset slicing, since() with cutoff verification, since() with limit) are appropriate.

findings.title: repo_claims.set_marked_ready submission-column round-trip not tested at repo level
findings.explanation: test_marked_ready_derived_from_claim toggles ready True/False but only asserts the derived `marked_ready` boolean on the assembled ReciterRow. The columns set_marked_ready actually writes (`mark_ready_checklist`, `mark_ready_comment_checks`, `mark_ready_comment_issues`, `mark_ready_bypass_used`) and the unmark-clears-all-five contract documented in the docstring are not asserted at this layer — test_reviews_detail covers the happy submission path via the service layer, but the unmark-resets-all path is not covered anywhere.
findings.proposed_action: Add a repo-level test that sets all five columns via `set_marked_ready(ready=True, checklist_json=..., comment_checks=..., comment_issues=..., bypass_used=True)`, queries the row, and then calls `set_marked_ready(ready=False)` and asserts all five columns are NULL on the open claim.
findings.verifier_notes: The docstring in repo_claims.py:107-120 explicitly documents that set_marked_ready with ready=False "clears all five columns" (marked_ready_at, mark_ready_checklist, mark_ready_comment_checks, mark_ready_comment_issues, mark_ready_bypass_used). Testing shows: (1) test_reviews_detail.py::test_detail_marked_ready_round_trips_submission writes all four submission columns and reads them back but does not test unmarking; (2) test_route_claims.py::test_mark_unmark_round_trip unmarksand asserts the state file's marked_ready boolean is False but never queries the claims table to verify the submission columns are NULL; (3) test_repo_state.py::test_marked_ready_derived_from_claim doesn't write submission columns in the first place. No test exists that writes all five columns and then verifies they all become NULL after unmarking.

findings.title: test_supersede_current_marks_prior_rows asserts n == 0 — name promises the opposite
findings.explanation: The test name says 'supersede_current marks prior rows'. The actual assertion is `assert n == 0` because id1 was already superseded in the pre-insert sweep (`supersede_current(except_id=-1)`). The test never directly verifies the rowcount returned when supersede actually marks a row — `n` from the first sweep (which should be 1, since id1 is non-superseded at that point) is discarded. The docstring acknowledges this. The test therefore validates the safe-path ordering convention but does NOT test what its name claims (the return value when prior rows are actually marked).
findings.proposed_action: Either (a) rename to test_supersede_current_idempotent_when_prior_already_marked, or (b) split into two tests: one asserting the first sweep returns 1 (rows actually marked), and a second asserting subsequent sweeps return 0 (idempotent). Capture and assert the first sweep's rowcount.
findings.verifier_notes: The test name `test_supersede_current_marks_prior_rows` claims to test that supersede_current marks rows and returns the count. However, the actual assertion is `assert n == 0` from the SECOND supersede call (line 73), which tests the idempotent property (no additional rows to mark because id1 was already superseded in the first call on line 69). The first sweep's return value (which should be 1 when actually marking id1) is discarded (line 69, return value not captured). The docstring acknowledges this (lines 74-75: "id1 was superseded in the pre-insert sweep; supersede(except=id2) sweeps nothing more"). The test validates the ordering convention and partial-unique constraint correctly, but the name promises to test the marking behavior (return count when rows are actually marked), which it does not assert. This is a naming clarity issue — the test should either be renamed to reflect what it actually tests (idempotent behavior) or split into two tests: one capturing and asserting the first sweep returns 1, and another asserting idempotence returns 0.

findings.title: _seed_minimal_delivery duplicates seed_delivery / _seed_delivery_chain with bespoke raw SQL
findings.explanation: The release tests inline a third raw-SQL seed helper that overlaps with `_helpers.seed_delivery` and conftest `_seed_delivery_chain`. It differs only in (a) the riwayah/source/channel slugs (`hafs_an_asim` / `everyayah` vs the helpers' `hafs`/`src`/`ch`), (b) extra codec/container/bitrate_mode columns, (c) the `gh_release_eligible=1` flag on `channels`. The release-specific need is real, but a fourth ad-hoc INSERT chain inside a test file (with the same FK chain shape the conftest helper already manages) is convention drift across the db/ tests. Neighbouring tests (`test_repo_state.py`, `test_repo_access.py`) all consume `_helpers.seed_delivery`.
findings.proposed_action: Extend `inspector/tests/db/_helpers.py::seed_delivery` (or add a sibling `seed_release_delivery`) to accept the gh_release_eligible flag + optional codec/container/bitrate, so test_repo_releases.py can `from ._helpers import seed_release_delivery` instead of carrying its own raw-SQL INSERT chain.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding correctly identifies that _seed_minimal_delivery (test_repo_releases.py:22-43) duplicates the FK chain insertion pattern from _seed_delivery_chain (conftest.py:153-169) and seed_delivery (_helpers.py:24-32). The differences are: (a) specific vocab slugs (hafs_an_asim/everyayah vs hafs/src/ch), (b) explicit codec/container/bitrate_mode values (which have schema defaults anyway), (c) gh_release_eligible=1 flag. Crucially, none of the 8 test functions using _seed_minimal_delivery assert on these specific values—they only need valid FK chains. The tests would work identically with the shared helper if it accepted optional parameters. The proposed consolidation is technically sound and would reduce maintenance burden. Severity is appropriate for isolated convention drift in a single test module.

findings.title: _seed_minimal_delivery imports get_conn at function scope
findings.explanation: The file imports `services.db` and `repo_releases` at module level, but `get_conn` is imported inside the helper function. The neighbouring db/ tests (test_repo_access.py, test_repo_state.py, test_review_followups.py, conftest.py) consistently put all `services.db` imports at the module top.
findings.proposed_action: Hoist `from services.db import get_conn` to the module's top-level import block.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is correct: get_conn is imported inside _seed_minimal_delivery at line 28, while neighboring test files (test_repo_access.py, test_repo_state.py, test_review_followups.py) and conftest.py all import from services.db at module level. The entire db/ test suite uses either db.transaction() context managers or db.get_conn() accessed through the module namespace — only test_repo_releases.py uses function-scoped import. This is a genuine inconsistency. The function-scoped import works correctly but is inconsistent with codebase convention. Hoisting to module level would have no functional impact and would improve consistency. The severity (low) and proposed action (hoist the import) are appropriate.

findings.title: Full round-trip parity test exercises only a subset of Delivery fields
findings.explanation: test_full_catalog_roundtrip_parity inserts a Delivery without any of: `recording_year`, `variant_label`, `source_url`, `codec`, `container`, `sample_rate_hz`, `channels`, `bitrate_mode`, `bitrate_kbps_nominal`, `total_duration_sec`. So the byte-for-byte `model_dump(by_alias=True)` parity check doesn't actually exercise the (de)serialization of those fields through `insert_delivery` ↔ `_delivery_from_row`. The edit-helper test sets `recording_year` and `variant_label`, but only as edits (UPDATE round-trip), never as INSERT round-trip. A regression in `_delivery_from_row` field ordering or in `insert_delivery`'s placeholder mapping for these columns wouldn't be caught by parity.
findings.proposed_action: Add a delivery fixture variant to `_catalog()` (or a second test) that populates the full Delivery field set (including the enum `bitrate_mode`, `audio_category` variants) and round-trips it through snapshot.
findings.verifier_notes: The test fixture _catalog() in inspector/tests/db/test_repo_catalog.py:33-38 creates a minimal Delivery without populating optional fields like recording_year, variant_label, source_url, codec, container, sample_rate_hz, channels, bitrate_mode, bitrate_kbps_nominal, total_duration_sec. While these fields are serialized as None/defaults in model_dump(), a field-reordering bug in _delivery_from_row (lines 100-123) wouldn't be caught if two fields of the same type were swapped (e.g., variant_label and source_url, both TEXT). The INSERT statement uses explicit column names so it's safe, and _delivery_from_row uses named access so it's also safe, but the byte-for-byte parity test only exercises these fields with None values. The edit test (lines 75-86) does set recording_year and variant_label, but only as UPDATE round-trip, not INSERT. The gap is real but limited since: (1) both enum variants (AudioCategory, BitrateMode) are tested with defaults, (2) named column access prevents most reordering bugs, (3) edit test exercises some fields. Proposed action of adding a comprehensive INSERT fixture is reasonable but not critical.

findings.title: find_source / add_source / find_channel / add_channel have no direct unit tests
findings.explanation: find_source / add_source / find_channel / add_channel are tested only indirectly via test_intake_ingest. There is no direct unit test in the db/ suite covering: (a) lookup-miss returns None, (b) round-trip of host_patterns / audio_categories JSON serde, (c) gh_release_eligible boolean coercion, (d) Duplicate raised on existing slug. Given the Duplicate contract symmetry with add_reciter / add_delivery (which IS tested in test_review_followups), the omission is conspicuous.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests in test_repo_catalog.py: test_add_source_duplicate_raises, test_add_channel_duplicate_raises, test_find_source_none_for_unknown_slug, test_find_channel_roundtrips_host_patterns_and_gh_eligible.
findings.verifier_notes: Direct code inspection confirms the test gap is real. Coverage reports show lines 302 and 332 (the duplicate checks in add_source and add_channel) are never executed. Test integration path uses idempotent service-layer wrappers that prevent calling the repo layer twice with the same slug. In contrast, test_review_followups.py explicitly tests add_reciter and add_delivery duplicates by calling the repo layer directly twice. The find_source/find_channel None-return paths are indirectly covered by the ingest test, but the JSON serde round-trip (host_patterns, audio_categories), boolean coercion (gh_release_eligible), and duplicate detection paths have no direct unit tests. The omission is real and asymmetric to the add_reciter/add_delivery test pattern established in test_review_followups.py.

findings.title: latest_gh_release_summary has no test coverage
findings.explanation: latest_gh_release_summary feeds the Releases-tab summary card with member_count + total_bytes aggregates via a LEFT JOIN. No test exercises: (a) the LEFT JOIN behavior when a release has zero members (member_count=0, total_bytes=0), (b) the SUM aggregation over zip_bytes, (c) the superseded-row exclusion. Regressions in the JOIN/GROUP BY logic would ship undetected.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests covering: empty release (LEFT JOIN returns row with COUNT=0 and total_bytes=0), multi-member release with summed zip_bytes, and superseded release excluded.
findings.verifier_notes: The function latest_gh_release_summary (repo_releases.py:196-214) contains SQL logic with LEFT JOIN, GROUP BY aggregations, and supersession filtering. No unit test directly exercises this function. Integration tests in test_route_admin_releases.py call the /api/admin/releases/status endpoint that uses this function, but those tests never create any gh_release rows, so the aggregation logic is never actually exercised. The proposed test scenarios (empty release, multi-member release, superseded exclusion) are valid and would catch regressions in the JOIN/GROUP BY logic.

findings.title: edit_reciter / edit_delivery edge cases (unknown slug, empty/non-writable fields) uncovered
findings.explanation: test_edit_reciter_and_delivery exercises the happy path. Not covered: (a) edit_reciter('missing_id', ...) — should return None (find_reciter miss path), (b) edit_reciter with an unknown / non-writable field like 'reciter_id' or 'random_attr' — should silently drop via the `_RECITER_WRITABLE` whitelist filter (security-relevant: a misuse of the kwargs surface), (c) edit with all-None values — should skip the UPDATE entirely (the `if cols:` guard). Same gaps for edit_delivery.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests asserting: edit_reciter on unknown id returns None; edit_delivery rejects writes to reciter_id / arbitrary attrs (compare before/after row); edit with all None kwargs is a no-op.
findings.verifier_notes: The edge cases are indeed not explicitly tested in test_repo_catalog.py (lines 75-87): (a) edit_reciter on missing ID, (b) edit_reciter with non-writable field like 'reciter_id', (c) edit with all-None values. However, the production code in repo_catalog.py (lines 186-207) correctly handles all three cases through guard clauses: (a) find_reciter returns None when ID doesn't exist, (b) the dict comprehension filters non-writable fields via _RECITER_WRITABLE whitelist, (c) the `if cols:` guard prevents empty UPDATE. This is a test coverage gap for defensive paths that are already correct, not a functional bug. The proposed tests are reasonable for documenting this defensive behavior.

findings.title: content_hash constraint test misses null-content_hash + negative-coverage edge
findings.explanation: test_content_hash_constraints covers zip_bytes=0 and coverage_ayahs=7000 (high-bound). Not covered: (a) coverage_ayahs=-1 (low-bound of the [0, 6236] CHECK), (b) the documented nullable `content_hash` path (the signature is `content_hash: str | None` — no test inserts None to confirm the column allows it). Minor.
findings.proposed_action: Add a parametrize over invalid (zip_bytes, coverage_ayahs) pairs covering both bounds, and add a happy-path test with content_hash=None.
findings.verifier_notes: The test test_content_hash_constraints (inspector/tests/db/test_repo_releases.py:185-207) does cover two edge cases: zip_bytes=0 (violates CHECK zip_bytes > 0) and coverage_ayahs=7000 (violates CHECK coverage_ayahs <= 6236). However, it genuinely misses: (1) coverage_ayahs=-1 to test the lower bound CHECK (coverage_ayahs >= 0), and (2) a happy-path test with content_hash=None to validate the nullable column works (as documented in 0014_releases.sql:80 and used in production code cut_release.py via .get("content_hash")). The schema defines three testable behaviors; the test only validates two. The finding is technically correct—these edge cases are not covered.

findings.title: stamp_stale_on_ts_regen test misses the gh_release_recitations branch
findings.explanation: test_stamp_stale_on_ts_regen exercises the `track='hf'` per-recitation row update but never seeds a `gh_releases` + `gh_release_recitations` membership for the same slug. The second UPDATE inside stamp_stale_on_ts_regen (against gh_release_recitations, conditioned on the most-recent non-superseded gh_releases.id) is therefore not exercised — and the asserted `n == 1` only proves the first UPDATE ran. The function's documented contract ('mark that slug's row in the most-recent gh_releases if it was a member') is not validated.
findings.proposed_action: Extend the test: seed a gh_release + gh_release_recitation for the same slug, then assert n == 2 and that the gh_release_recitations row got stale_since stamped while the same slug in an older (superseded) gh_release does NOT get stamped.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified by reading the function definition (inspector/services/db/repo_releases.py:116-143), the test (inspector/tests/db/test_repo_releases.py:98-109), the schema (migration 0014_releases.sql), and the dataset-and-releases.md documentation. The function's docstring explicitly states it should "mark the current hf row for slug AND mark that slug's row in the most-recent gh_releases (if it was a member) as stale" and return the total stamps applied. The function has two UPDATE statements: first against per_recitation_releases (which the test validates), and second against gh_release_recitations (which is never exercised). The test only seeds a delivery and an HF row, but never creates a gh_releases row or gh_release_recitations membership. Therefore, the second UPDATE runs against zero rows and the test's assertion of n==1 only proves the first UPDATE ran. The production code at inspector/services/admin/timestamps_jobs.py:515 and :576 calls this function expecting both parts to work. The test incompletely validates the contract.

findings.title: Caller-must-supersede-before-insert discipline is the load-bearing invariant but is buried in test docstrings
findings.explanation: The partial-unique `ux_per_recitation_current` is the safety net, but the call-site discipline is: callers must call supersede_current(except_id=-1) BEFORE insert_per_recitation_release. Two tests demonstrate it but each in its own way (one calls supersede(except_id=-1) before insert, then supersede(except_id=id2) after; one omits the pre-supersede and expects IntegrityError). A new contributor onboarding to this subsystem has to reverse-engineer the discipline from `except_id=-1`. The repo function docstring mentions 'caller must supersede the prior current row in the same transaction' but doesn't show the `-1` sentinel pattern.
findings.proposed_action: Document the `supersede_current(except_id=-1, ...)` sentinel pattern explicitly in repo_releases.py docstring (or extract a `insert_replacing_current(...)` helper that does both in one call), and reference the pattern in test_supersede_current_marks_prior_rows.
findings.verifier_notes: The `except_id=-1` sentinel pattern for pre-insert supersede is real and load-bearing. Production code uses it correctly (timestamps_jobs.py:506, 570; hf_publish.py:144), enforced by the partial-unique index (migration 0014:41-42). However, the function docstrings at repo_releases.py:44-45 and 61-66 mention "caller must supersede" but do NOT document the `-1` sentinel or the order discipline. A new contributor onboarding to this subsystem must reverse-engineer the pattern from test docstrings (test_supersede_current_marks_prior_rows:60-62) or production code. The discipline is correct and working, but the documentation is incomplete.

findings.title: fresh_pending sets up FilesystemBackend that pending_requests no longer touches
findings.explanation: `fresh_pending` allocates a FilesystemBackend, sets `INSPECTOR_DATA_DIR`/`INSPECTOR_BACKEND`/`INSPECTOR_FILESYSTEM_ROOT`, and stores the backend in the yielded tuple — but post-cutover `services/state/pending_requests.py` does NOT touch the bucket at all (the docstring even says so: 'No-op under the SQLite substrate'). All persistence flows through `repo_requests` → SQLite. The backend is dead weight: every test unpacks it as `svc, _` or `svc, backend` and ignores it. The autouse `_substrate_db` fixture (conftest.py:117) already provides the migrated DB. This is residual scaffolding from the pre-cutover hydrate-from-bucket world.
findings.proposed_action: Simplify `fresh_pending` to a one-liner that imports & yields `services.pending_requests` (no backend, no env vars). Drop the unused `backend` from the yield. Same applies to `fresh_archive` in test_request_archive.py.
findings.verifier_notes: Code inspection confirms that post-cutover pending_requests.py and request_archive.py do not import or use hf_bucket at all. The pending_requests.py docstring explicitly states "No-op under the SQLite substrate". The fresh_pending and fresh_archive fixtures allocate FilesystemBackend, set INSPECTOR_* env vars, and yield the backend, but: (1) neither service module imports these, (2) all tests either ignore the backend with _ or unpack but never reference it, (3) the autouse _substrate_db fixture (conftest.py:117) already provides the initialized SQLite DB. This is residual scaffolding from the pre-cutover bucket-based architecture. The finding is accurate and the proposed simplification is feasible.

findings.title: Unused top-level imports in test_pending_requests.py
findings.explanation: Top-level `from datetime import datetime, timezone` (line 10) is unused — the only places that need `datetime`/`timezone` re-import them inside function scope (lines 52 and 299, aliased as `_dt`/`_tz`). `PendingRequest` is imported at line 16 but never referenced. findings.verifier_notes: All three unused imports verified via grep and code inspection: (1) Line 10's datetime/timezone are never referenced at module scope — the two functions that use these types (lines 52, 299) import them locally with aliases; (2) Line 16's PendingRequest is imported but never used anywhere in the file; (3) Line 116's storage_paths is imported inside test_submit_creates_entry but never referenced in that function. These are straightforward lint artifacts with zero functional impact. The proposed removal is correct.

findings.title: test_pending_requests_schema.py re-imports datetime inside functions despite top-level import

findings.title: seeded_catalog fixture is a no-op wrapper around fresh_pending
findings.explanation: `@pytest.fixture seeded_catalog(fresh_pending, monkeypatch): return fresh_pending` adds zero behaviour — the catalog seeding it claims to provide already happens inside `fresh_pending` via `_seed_test_catalog_db()`. It also takes `monkeypatch` as a parameter and never uses it. The five tests that depend on it could depend on `fresh_pending` directly with no semantic change.
findings.proposed_action: Delete the `seeded_catalog` fixture and have the five `apply_and_archive_completed_*` tests depend on `fresh_pending` directly. Drop the misleading `seeded_catalog` name.
findings.verifier_notes: The seeded_catalog fixture at inspector/tests/services/test_pending_requests.py:170-174 is indeed a no-op wrapper. It accepts fresh_pending and monkeypatch parameters, then returns fresh_pending unchanged (line 174). The monkeypatch parameter is never used within the fixture. The fixture's own docstring confirms the actual catalog seeding happens inside fresh_pending via _seed_test_catalog_db() called at line 42. All five tests using seeded_catalog (test_apply_and_archive_completed_*) could work identically with fresh_pending, as verified by tracing the test implementations and confirming they don't depend on any additional behavior from seeded_catalog. The unused monkeypatch parameter suggests it was copy-pasted from fresh_pending and forgotten.

findings.title: Stale 'Removed test_hydrate_loads_existing_file' tombstone comment violates comments rule
findings.explanation: test_pending_requests.py lines 105-106 carry a tombstone comment for a deleted test (`# (Removed test_hydrate_loads_existing_file: pending.json bucket hydrate no longer exists ...)`), and test_repo_requests_activity.py lines 98-99 reference 'were dropped with the admin notifications rail (migration 0006)'. Both violate `.claude/rules/comments.md` ('no comments mentioning refactors / cleanups — "no longer", "phase", "removed", "deleted", "deprecated", "legacy", "old", "new", "will change/be" etc.').
findings.proposed_action: Delete the two stale tombstone comments. The git log already records why the tests were removed; the test file should not.

(2) For test_repo_requests_activity.py:98-99, either retain the docstring (it explains current functionality) or reword to avoid "dropped"/"migration number" phrasing while preserving the architectural context that helps readers understand what the test validates.

findings.title: test_activity_tombstone lives in test_repo_requests_activity.py but exercises repo_activity only
findings.explanation: The file's module docstring (`repo_requests (payload adapters, pending→archive) + repo_activity sidecars`) explicitly co-locates two unrelated repos. The single `test_activity_tombstone` test has nothing to do with requests — it tests the activity-tombstone sidecar. That single test would be more discoverable as its own `test_repo_activity.py`, and `test_repo_requests_activity.py` could become `test_repo_requests.py`. The combined file is a low-cost convention violation that complicates `pytest -k` runs.
findings.proposed_action: Split into `test_repo_requests.py` (the four request tests) and `test_repo_activity.py` (the tombstone test). Update the docstring accordingly.
findings.verifier_notes: The test file test_repo_requests_activity.py contains 5 tests: 4 that exercise repo_requests exclusively (lines 20-95), and 1 that exercises repo_activity exclusively (lines 97-113: test_activity_tombstone). The modules have zero interaction — test_activity_tombstone calls only repo_activity.delete(), repo_activity.is_deleted(), repo_activity.deleted_set(), and repo_activity.undelete(). The file's docstring ("repo_requests ... + repo_activity sidecars") misleadingly suggests a relationship. In contrast, test_repo_state.py deliberately co-locates repo_state + repo_claims because they are tightly intertwined in nearly every test. This is a low-severity convention violation that complicates pytest -k filtering. Splitting into test_repo_requests.py and test_repo_activity.py is justified and aligns with single-module test-file patterns elsewhere in the codebase.

findings.title: auto_claim round-trip only verified on pending, not on archived rows
findings.explanation: `test_submit_get_pending_roundtrip` asserts `pr.auto_claim is True` on the pending row, but no test verifies `auto_claim` is preserved through `resolve` into the archived shape. `_to_archived` (line 65) does pull `bool(row['auto_claim'])` from the DB column, but the field is stamped at submit time and never re-touched at resolve. A regression that nulled `auto_claim` during the resolve UPDATE would slip through. The schema round-trip test does assert `auto_claim=True` on an `ArchivedRequest` constructed directly (test_pending_requests_schema.py:186), but that's pure pydantic and bypasses the SQL path.
findings.proposed_action: In `test_resolve_to_archive_and_get_for_slug` set `auto_claim=True` on the submit call and assert `archived[0].auto_claim is True` after resolve. Trivial extension of an existing test.
findings.verifier_notes:
The finding is technically correct. The test `test_resolve_to_archive_and_get_for_slug` does not verify that `auto_claim` survives the pending→archived SQL round-trip. The pending-to-pending test asserts `auto_claim=True` (test_repo_requests_activity.py:38), the schema test validates Pydantic construction (test_pending_requests_schema.py:191), and the migration test validates `auto_claim` on pending rows (test_migration.py:140), but no test asserts `auto_claim` on an `ArchivedRequest` retrieved via `get_for_slug()` after `resolve()`. 

However, the actual risk is very low: the `auto_claim` column is never touched by the resolve UPDATE (repo_requests.py:138-151), so the value is guaranteed to survive intact. The code path is structurally sound—`_to_archived` correctly reads `bool(row['auto_claim'])` on line 65. This is a legitimate regression test gap, not a latent bug. The proposed action (adding `auto_claim=True` to the submit and asserting on the archived row) is a trivial, valuable extension of an existing test.

findings.title: resolve_by_id back-fill exception (accepted+null-slug re-resolve) is untested
findings.explanation: `resolve_by_id` has a non-trivial back-fill branch (lines 200-208): an already-`accepted` intake row whose slug is NULL may be re-resolved to `accepted` *just to attach* the minted slug. The docstring is explicit that this is the ingest mint flow. None of the three requests-repo test files exercise it. There are also no tests for the rejection branches: re-resolving a non-accepted terminal row, or one whose slug is already set, should return False. Coverage exists for the happy path in `test_route_intake_ingest.py` but not at the repo level where the branches live.
findings.proposed_action: Add a `test_resolve_by_id_back_fill_attaches_slug` case (submit slugless → resolve accepted → re-resolve accepted with a slug → assert slug stamped) and `test_resolve_by_id_rejects_double_terminal` (re-resolve a returned row, expect False) inside test_repo_requests_activity.py.
findings.verifier_notes: Code inspection and coverage analysis confirm the finding. Lines 200-208 in repo_requests.py (the backfill exception and rejection logic) are not exercised by any repo-level tests. The coverage report explicitly shows "Missing: 197-209" for test_repo_requests_activity.py. Although the backfill IS tested through integration tests (test_ingest_new_combo_mints_seeds_and_backfills), the rejection branches (double terminal, slug already set) have zero test coverage anywhere. The docstring explicitly documents this non-trivial behavior, making unit-level tests appropriate. findings.title: Per-admin view-mark API (mark_viewed/is_viewed/viewed_ids_for_user/count_unviewed_open_for_user) has no repo-level tests
findings.explanation: Four public functions back the Requests-tab unviewed-badge feature: `mark_viewed` (idempotent INSERT OR IGNORE), `is_viewed`, `viewed_ids_for_user`, `count_unviewed_open_for_user`. None of them are tested at the repo level (only an unrelated `reviews_service.mark_viewed` in test_timestamps_jobs.py:259, which is a different feature). The idempotency contract and the `NOT EXISTS` count predicate are exactly the kind of small SQL details that drift silently.
findings.proposed_action: Add a `test_view_marks_idempotent_and_counted` test (mark twice → still one row, then `count_unviewed_open_for_user` reflects only unviewed pendings) to test_repo_requests_activity.py.
findings.verifier_notes: The four view-mark functions (mark_viewed, is_viewed, viewed_ids_for_user, count_unviewed_open_for_user) in inspector/services/db/repo_requests.py:327-361 have NO unit tests in test_repo_requests_activity.py. findings.title: admin_list_rows and counts_by_status untested at repo level
findings.explanation: `admin_list_rows` drives the admin Requests tab (pending oldest-first, terminal newest-first); `counts_by_status` drives the facet chips. The ORDER BY differs by status — a regression flipping pending to DESC would silently put longest-waiting requests at the bottom. No repo-level test pins the ordering invariants.
findings.proposed_action: Add `test_admin_list_rows_orders_pending_oldest_first` (submit two pendings at different submitted_at → list comes back oldest-first) and `test_counts_by_status_facets` (submit+resolve a mix → assert dict shape).
findings.verifier_notes: Severity: lower (low-medium); Integration tests in test_route_requests.py::test_list_requests_maintainer_open_redacts_and_diffs (and owner variant) already exercise admin_list_rows via the /api/admin/requests endpoint. If the ORDER BY was flipped to DESC for pending requests, those tests would fail because they assert on the returned row structure. Proposed action remains valid but should note this existing route-level coverage. Unit-level tests are still valuable for explicit assertion of invariants without going through the full service stack.

findings.title: set_payload public API is untested

findings.title: _stub_access_persist / _stub_state_persist are documented no-ops

They are invoked in every grant/revoke/update test (12+ call sites in test_route_access_admin.py alone) purely as leftover scaffolding. Git history (commit 4a04de47) shows they replaced actual `monkeypatch.setattr()` calls that stubbed bucket I/O during the SQLite migration. The stubs return `None` and never use their `monkeypatch` parameter. Their docstrings explicitly document they are "no-op post-cutover". They are invoked in 12+ call sites (test_route_access_admin.py lines 61, 71, 82, 96, 108, 119, 130, 146, 156, 175, 205, 232, 248; test_route_admin_actions.py line 52 definition + 15+ call sites). findings.title: _replace_state / _row reimplemented in three sibling test files with the same _seed_state delegation
findings.explanation: All three route tests define identical thin wrappers around `_seed_state` already exposed by conftest. The conftest also exports `seed_state` as a fixture. The duplicated `_row` builders only differ in trivial default kwargs (assignee_login=='prev' vs 'prev_owner' vs 'target_user'). This is exactly the BE seeding-helper duplication called out in the audit brief.
findings.proposed_action: Promote `_row` (a small dataclass-style spec builder) and `_replace_state` to conftest, or just delete them and have call sites call `seed_state(slug=..., state=..., assignee_hf_id=...)` directly. The fixture already exists.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is valid. Three sibling route test files (test_route_access_admin.py, test_route_claims.py, test_route_admin_actions.py) each define identical `_replace_state()` wrappers that loop and call `_seed_state()` from conftest. They also each define `_row()` dict builders with the same structure but different default `assignee_login` values ("prev", "prev_owner", "target_user"). Since conftest already exports `_seed_state` (line 172) as a callable and as a fixture (line 275), these thin wrappers create maintainability risk without adding sufficient value. The duplication could be reduced by either: (1) promoting a single `_row()` builder to conftest with a configurable assignee_login parameter, or (2) having test files call `seed_state(slug=..., state=..., assignee_hf_id=...)` directly. The current per-file pattern creates an unnecessary maintenance burden and violates DRY.

findings.title: test_revoke_force_releases_active_claim does not verify claim was actually closed or audit emitted
findings.explanation: The test posts to /api/admin/access/revoke and asserts only `body['auto_released_slugs'] == ['test_slug']`. It does not check that (a) `repo_claims.open_claims_for_user('u-target')` is empty afterwards, (b) the delivery state transitioned back to AWAITING_REVIEW, or (c) a `reciter.released` transition row was appended alongside `access.role_revoked`. The route docstring explicitly advertises all three side effects. If the cascade wire-field assembly drifted from the actual cascade (e.g. response said 'released' but the state row never flipped) this test would still pass.
findings.proposed_action: After the 200, also assert: `repo_state.get('test_slug').state == 'awaiting_review'`, `repo_state.get('test_slug').assignee_hf_id is None`, and at least one transition row each for events `reciter.released` and `access.role_revoked` exists for the slug/actor.
findings.verifier_notes: The test at inspector/tests/routes/test_route_access_admin.py:166-196 only verifies that `body['auto_released_slugs'] == ['test_slug']`. The route's docstring explicitly advertises three side effects: (1) cascade-release of claims, (2) state transition to AWAITING_REVIEW, and (3) audit trail with both `access.role_revoked` and `reciter.released` transitions. The implementation calls `access_service.revoke()` which invokes `_state_service._apply_event(conn, slug, "reciter.released", ...)` to persist state changes via `_h_released()` handler and `repo_transitions.append()`. The test infrastructure supports post-request verification (via `repo_state.get_row()` and `repo_transitions.for_slug()`) but doesn't perform any. If the `_apply_event()` calls were accidentally disabled or the state mutations failed silently, the test would still pass because it only checks the returned wire field. The finding is valid.

findings.title: File docstring claims '409 on already-active member' but no such test exists
findings.explanation: The module docstring's coverage bullet 'Coverage: ... 409 on already-active member' is unmet — there is no test that grants a member twice to exercise the `MemberAlreadyActive` → 409 branch in routes/admin/access.py:84-85. The closest test in test_repo_access.py is `test_double_active_grant_blocked` at the DB level (IntegrityError), not at the route level.
findings.proposed_action: Either remove the claim from the docstring or add a test that seeds an existing maintainer and POSTs `/grant` for the same hf_user_id, asserting 409. (Listed as convention since the docstring is misleading; the missing test itself is a separate GAP finding.)
findings.verifier_notes: The docstring in test_route_access_admin.py line 7 claims coverage for "409 on already-active member". The route handler at inspector/routes/admin/access.py lines 84-85 catches MemberAlreadyActive and returns 409. The service at inspector/services/auth/access.py lines 119-122 raises this exception when a grant is attempted for an existing member. However, examining test_route_access_admin.py (lines 1-256), there is no test function that: (1) seeds an existing active member, (2) POSTs /api/admin/access/grant for the same hf_user_id, and (3) asserts a 409 response. The db-level test test_double_active_grant_blocked in test_repo_access.py tests the IntegrityError constraint, not the route-level MemberAlreadyActive exception. The docstring claim is unmet.

findings.title: No test for the GET /api/admin/permissions anonymous → 401 vs missing-Origin behavior on POST toggle
findings.explanation: test_get_matrix_anonymous_unauthorized covers GET. The POST toggle route stacks @require_same_origin BEFORE @require_capability('manage_permissions'); an anonymous cross-origin POST returns 403 from the Origin check, not 401 from the capability check. No test asserts the anonymous-POST behavior. The interaction with `require_capability` for an anonymous caller on a non-anon-eligible cap is also untested at the route layer.
findings.proposed_action: Add `test_toggle_anonymous_missing_origin_returns_403` and `test_toggle_anonymous_with_origin_returns_401_or_403` to pin the gate order.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is confirmed. The POST toggle route (/api/admin/permissions/<cap>/<tier>) uses @require_same_origin followed by @require_capability("manage_permissions"). Tests verify: (1) GET anonymous returns 401 (line 33-34), (2) POST with valid Origin headers from signed-in users (multiple tests). However, the tests do NOT cover: (1) anonymous POST without Origin header (would return 403 from require_same_origin), or (2) anonymous POST with valid Origin (would return 401 from require_capability). The test_set_role.py file (line 122-127) establishes a pattern for testing missing Origin behavior on protected POST routes, and the permissions route should follow this pattern. The gap exists and should be addressed, though severity is correctly labeled as LOW since the behavior is correct and the decorators are independently sound. Both missing tests are justified for route-layer regression detection.

findings.title: repo_access.resolve_role returns a raw str for members but annotates -> Role
findings.explanation: resolve_role returns `row[0]` (a Python str like 'maintainer') for members but Role.CONTRIBUTOR (a Role enum member) for non-members. The annotation is `-> Role`. Tests pass because Role is a str-Enum and `'maintainer' == Role.MAINTAINER` is True, but downstream code that does `isinstance(x, Role)` or pattern-matches on enum members will behave inconsistently between the two return paths. The docstring documents this as intentional ('preserve wire/str behavior') but it is still a hazard: any caller using `resolve_role(x).value` will crash for members.
findings.proposed_action: Either wrap the member branch in `Role(row[0])` and update the docstring, or change the return annotation to `Role | str` and audit downstream callers. At minimum add a regression test asserting `isinstance(resolve_role('u1'), Role)` to surface intent.
findings.verifier_notes: The bug is real and confirmed by multiple pieces of evidence: (1) resolve_role(hf_user_id) returns row[0] (a raw string like "maintainer") for members but Role.CONTRIBUTOR (an enum member) for non-members, violating the -> Role annotation; (2) Python test verification confirms isinstance("maintainer", Role) is False while isinstance(Role.MAINTAINER, Role) is True; (3) Multiple production code locations have added defensive hasattr(x, "value") checks to handle this inconsistency (inspector/services/auth/access.py:193, inspector/routes/auth/auth.py:243, inspector/routes/segments/edit.py:29); (4) The User dataclass at auth.py:270 annotates role: Role but receives either a string or Role enum; (5) Any code calling resolve_role(x).value for a member user would crash with AttributeError. The docstring acknowledges intentional legacy wire-compatibility, but this creates a type-safety and runtime hazard throughout the codebase.

findings.title: Dead `_stub_*_persist` helpers + duplicated `_replace_state` / `_row` makes the access-admin test harness opaque
findings.explanation: A new contributor reading test_route_access_admin.py sees `_stub_access_persist(monkeypatch)` and a `_replace_state` helper in every test and reasonably assumes bucket-persistence is being mocked and that `_replace_state` is doing something nontrivial — neither is true. The conftest already exposes `seed_state` and `seed_role` as fixtures, and bucket uploads are already disabled by `_substrate_db`. The dead scaffolding hides which lines are actually load-bearing.
findings.proposed_action: Strip the dead stubs, switch to the `seed_state` / `seed_role` fixtures, and leave a comment at the top noting that the autouse `_substrate_db` fixture handles the DB substrate.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is valid. Code inspection confirms: (1) _stub_access_persist and _stub_state_persist are literal no-ops returning None with post-cutover comments at inspector/tests/routes/test_route_access_admin.py:44-52; (2) the autouse _substrate_db fixture at conftest.py:117-150 already disables bucket uploads with set_sync_enabled(False) at line 133, documented in the fixture docstring; (3) _replace_state and _row helpers are duplicated identically across test_route_access_admin.py, test_route_admin_actions.py, and test_route_claims.py, each wrapping the shared _seed_state from conftest; (4) seed_state and seed_role fixtures exist at conftest.py:275-284 as direct alternatives. The stubs and duplicated helpers create dead code that signals importance to new readers when the actual load-bearing work is handled by _substrate_db and conftest fixtures.

findings.title: `_TTLCache` expiry path (the whole point of the cache) is never exercised
findings.explanation: `_TTLCache.get` evicts and returns None when `expires_at < now`, and `.set` opportunistically purges expired entries once the store grows past 256. Neither path is verified. The state-roundtrip test passes `set_state_data` with `self.expires_in` (Authlib default), but no test ever simulates time advancing past expiry, nor the >256-entry eviction backstop, nor the abandoned-login purge. A regression that broke TTL handling (e.g. flipping the comparison) would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests that monkeypatch `services.auth.auth.time.time` to advance past `_RETURN_PATH_TTL` and assert expired keys disappear; also test the >256-entry backstop by injecting many entries.
findings.verifier_notes:
The `_TTLCache` implementation in C:\Users\ahmed\Documents\Work\my-projects\quranic-universal-audio\.claude\worktrees\elated-heyrovsky-aa8bb0\inspector\services\auth\auth.py (lines 78-119) has two expiry mechanisms:

1. Time-based expiry in `get()` (lines 99-101): Returns None when `expires_at < now`
2. Opportunistic purge in `set()` (lines 109-114): Drops expired entries when store size > 256

The test file at inspector\tests\services\test_auth_oauth_state.py (lines 20-49) only tests the happy path: immediate set/get without time passing. No tests:
- Monkeypatch `time.time()` to simulate expiry
- Verify expired keys are evicted on `get()`
- Create 256+ entries to test the purge backstop
- Verify abandoned login cleanup works

The route auth tests (test_route_auth.py:11) explicitly state "OAuth callback exchange is integration-shaped (authorizes against HF) and is covered by manual smoke during deploy rather than a mocked unit test."

The `FlaskIntegration` parent class (verified via direct import) provides default `expires_in=3600`, so entries ARE being created with TTL, but the expiry behavior is untested.

findings.title: Open-redirect defense `_safe_return_path` has zero direct tests
findings.explanation: `_safe_return_path` rejects absolute URLs (`scheme`/`netloc`), protocol-relative URLs (`//evil.example`), and falls back to `/`. It is the single defense between an attacker-controlled `?return=...` query param and the post-OAuth redirect. There is no test for any branch — neither `safe path passthrough`, `protocol-relative rejection`, `absolute URL rejection`, `plain relative path normalization`, nor `None/empty fallback`. The companion route test only covers 503-on-unconfigured for `/api/auth/login`, never the return-path piping. A regression that returns the raw `raw` would be silently exploitable.
findings.proposed_action: Parametrize `_safe_return_path` with `('/foo', '/foo')`, `('//evil.com/x', '/')`, `('https://evil.com/x', '/')`, `('foo', '/foo')`, `(None, '/')`, `('', '/')`.
findings.verifier_notes: The `_safe_return_path` function (inspector/routes/auth/auth.py:40-57) is indeed untested directly. I verified: (1) no parametrized or direct unit tests exist for this function; (2) the return-path cache tests (test_auth_oauth_state.py:43-56) validate the cache round-trip but NOT the sanitization logic itself; (3) route tests (test_route_auth.py) never exercise the `?return=...` parameter. The function is a critical open-redirect defense called twice during OAuth (lines 90 and 127) and validates all six cases mentioned: None/empty, protocol-relative, absolute URLs, relative paths, and normalization. While the code is correct and simple (leveraging urlparse reliably), the lack of tests creates a regression risk. The function is idempotent so double-wrapping doesn't break behavior, but defensive tests would confirm each branch and prevent future refactoring bugs.

findings.title: `/api/auth/callback` happy path + error branches are entirely untested
findings.explanation: The module docstring explicitly notes 'OAuth callback exchange is integration-shaped (authorizes against HF) and is covered by manual smoke during deploy rather than a mocked unit test.' That is reasonable for the live HF token exchange, but the surrounding behavior is mockable and unverified: (a) the `?error=access_denied` early return at line 114-125, (b) the `userinfo missing sub/login` 400 at 152-154, (c) the `ensure_user` / `touch_last_login` non-fatal exception path at 161-166, (d) the `secure/samesite` cookie attributes flipping on `_BEHIND_PROXY`, (e) the `pop_return_path` integration with the same-origin redirect. All of these can be tested by monkeypatching `oauth.huggingface.authorize_access_token` to return a synthetic token dict.
findings.proposed_action: Add a callback test fixture that monkeypatches `auth_service.get_oauth().huggingface.authorize_access_token` and `.userinfo`, and assert: HF-error branch returns 400 with the error code; missing-sub returns 400; ensure_user-raise is swallowed; SET-COOKIE has `Secure; SameSite=None` under `INSPECTOR_BEHIND_PROXY=1` and `SameSite=Lax` (no Secure) without; the post-login redirect lands on the `pop_return_path`-resolved target.
findings.verifier_notes: The `/api/auth/callback` endpoint routes/auth/auth.py:108-185 lacks unit test coverage for its happy path and error branches. The test file explicitly documents this as intentional ("OAuth callback exchange is integration-shaped and is covered by manual smoke during deploy"). However, the surrounding logic (error handling, cookie attributes, redirect targeting) is mockable and testable: lines 114-125 (HF error handling), 161-166 (exception swallowing), 181-182 (BEHIND_PROXY conditional cookie attributes), and 127 (return path integration) are all unit-testable by monkeypatching oauth.huggingface.authorize_access_token (as already done with monkeypatch in conftest.py). The proposed action to add callback fixture tests with mocked OAuth is technically sound and feasible. The documented decision to defer to deploy-time smoke tests is reasonable for the token exchange itself, but the surrounding error handling and cookie logic should have unit coverage.

findings.title: QF OAuth routes (login, callback, logout) have no direct route tests

The existing test_route_auth.py demonstrates the appropriate testing pattern (using monkeypatch for config and mocking service calls), making this an actionable gap that mirrors the exact pattern from HF OAuth route tests. findings.title: Signed-cookie `SignatureExpired` and `MissingSecret` branches in `decode_session` untested
findings.explanation: `decode_session` swallows three failure modes (SignatureExpired, BadSignature, MissingSecret) and returns None. Only `BadSignature` is exercised (the tampered-cookie test at line 145). A cookie signed > 1 week ago (SignatureExpired path) and a deploy with the session secret unset mid-flight (MissingSecret path) are not verified. There is also no test that `current_user()` actually surfaces None when the payload is missing required fields (`hf_user_id`/`login`) at line 291-292.

Only BadSignature handler (lines 256-257) is covered by test_me_with_tampered_cookie_returns_anonymous. findings.title: Bearer-token cache TTL expiry + 256-entry backstop untested

The cache's role-mutability contract ('role is resolved fresh every call') is also not explicitly tested — a test should grant OWNER, mint a token, demote, and assert the second call raises NotOwner without a second whoami.
findings.proposed_action: Add a TTL-expiry test that monkeypatches `services.auth.token_auth.time.time` to advance past `_TOKEN_TTL_SECONDS`. Add a role-mutability test that demotes between two `resolve_owner_from_token` calls.
findings.verifier_notes: The test file (inspector/tests/services/test_token_auth.py) has an autouse fixture that clears the token cache before and after every test. The only cache test (test_token_cache_avoids_second_whoami, lines 92-107) verifies the hit path within milliseconds, never testing TTL expiry, the 256-entry backstop, or role mutability between calls. The TTL comparison logic (token_auth.py:75, hit[0] > now) is correct, but without a monkeypatch of time.time() or test covering cache overflow, the proposed scenarios remain untested.
