findings.verifier_notes: Reduce severity from medium to low. Correct evidence count from "7 tests" to "8 tests". Reframe proposed action: instead of "will copy-paste", acknowledge this is preventive DRY refactoring for a hypothetical future surface. Consider deprioritizing in favor of bugs/blockers.

findings.title: Module-level os.environ.setdefault leaks INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET across runs
findings.explanation: Both files mutate `os.environ` at import time instead of using `monkeypatch.setenv` inside a fixture. The `signed_in_client` conftest fixture already handles this idiomatically (line 307-308 of conftest.py uses `monkeypatch.setenv`); the module-level setdefault is redundant AND leaks the secret into other tests' process env. This is the dominant pattern across 28 files in the suite, so it isn't a one-off — but it remains an isolation smell worth tracking.
findings.proposed_action: Delete the module-level `os.environ.setdefault("INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET", ...)` lines. The `signed_in_client` fixture (used by every test in these files) already ensures the env var is set via `monkeypatch.setenv`.
findings.verifier_notes: The module-level os.environ.setdefault("INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET", "0" * 64) at line 14 of test_route_admin_actions.py and line 28 of test_route_admin_releases.py is indeed redundant. The signed_in_client fixture (conftest.py lines 307-310) checks whether the env var is set and calls monkeypatch.setenv(INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET, secrets.token_hex(32)) BEFORE importing the app module. This order ensures the secret is available when app.py tries to access it at line 252. Since monkeypatch.setenv runs before app import and is the idiomatic pytest way to manage environment variables with proper scope and teardown, the module-level setdefault is unnecessary. The fixture will work correctly even if the module-level setdefault is removed—monkeypatch.setenv will set the env var before app import, preventing any import-time failures. The module-level mutation persists across all tests in the file and is never cleaned up by monkeypatch since monkeypatch is never called (the value already exists). This is an isolation anti-pattern that could cause future test failures if tests are added that expect the secret to be unset.

findings.title: Function-local imports of datetime/Member/Role/RolesFile/access_service never used
findings.explanation: Three tests (`test_revoke_force_releases_active_claim`, `test_revoke_maintainer_cannot_revoke_owner`, `test_update_login_cache_refresh`) each begin with a 4-line block of `from datetime import ...; from qua_shared.schemas import Member, Role, RolesFile; from services import access as access_service` — but none of these names are referenced anywhere in the test body. Pure refactor litter from when these tests pre-seeded the access store via Pydantic models before the SQLite cutover.
findings.proposed_action: Strip the dead local-import blocks at lines 169-173, 199-203, 226-230. The tests already use `_seed_role` from conftest for store seeding.
findings.verifier_notes: All three test functions contain function-local imports that are never referenced in their bodies: (1) lines 169-173 in test_revoke_force_releases_active_claim imports datetime, timezone, Member, Role, RolesFile, access_service — none used; (2) lines 199-203 in test_revoke_maintainer_cannot_revoke_owner imports datetime, timezone, Member, Role, access_service — none used; (3) lines 226-230 in test_update_login_cache_refresh imports datetime, timezone, Member, Role, access_service — none used. Additionally, datetime and timezone are already imported at module level (line 18), making the function-local imports redundant. Tests successfully use _seed_role from conftest.py without these unused imports. This is clear refactor litter.

findings.title: Stale 'Phase 4' / 'Phase 3' refactor references in docstrings
findings.explanation: Module docstrings refer to 'Phase 4 backend surface' and 'Phase 3 design' phases that no longer carry meaning. The .claude/rules/comments.md project rule explicitly bans phase markers in comments: 'no longer', 'phase', 'removed', 'deleted', 'deprecated', 'legacy', 'old', 'new' are listed as red flags. These docstrings drift from that rule.
findings.proposed_action: Drop the 'Phase 4'/'Phase 3' references from the docstrings; describe the current contract instead of its migration history.
findings.verifier_notes: Phase references are confirmed stale. Inspector/routes/admin/access.py:3 states "Backend-only in Phase 3 — the admin dashboard UI lands in Phase 7", but the admin dashboard UI was completed May 22, 2026 (commit 3dfded3f). The .claude/rules/comments.md explicitly prohibits "phase" markers in comments as red flags. Git history shows phases 1-7 were deployment stages from May-June 2026 that are now historical artifact. The docstrings describe past deployment milestones rather than current contract, violating the project rule: "no comments mentioning refactors / cleanups - 'no longer', 'phase', 'removed', 'deleted', 'deprecated', 'legacy', 'old', 'new' are red flags".

findings.title: POST /api/admin/cut-release has zero route-level test coverage
findings.explanation: The test file's docstring claims it covers the admin Releases-tab routes but `/api/admin/cut-release` — the destructive global cut-a-GH-release endpoint — has no route tests at all. The route has nontrivial branching: owner-only capability gate, global cut single-flight (`running_job_for(kind="cut_release")` → 409), drift-check against `expected_version_at_preview` (only when echo present), zero-candidates 409, body parsing (version / operator_note / expected_version_at_preview), launch exception → 502. None of these branches is currently exercised at the HTTP boundary.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests for: (a) maintainer 403 (route is owner-only via release.cut_gh), (b) anonymous 401, (c) 409 when another cut is in flight (use `_stub_jobs_api(in_flight=[{kind:'cut_release'...}])`), (d) 409 when `expected_version_at_preview` echoed but no eligible candidates, (e) launch exception 502 (monkeypatch `cut_release_jobs.launch` to raise), (f) happy path 202 with mocked launch returning `{job_id, url}`.
findings.verifier_notes: The route `/api/admin/cut-release` (POST) exists at inspector/routes/admin/releases.py:251-299 with complex branching logic (single-flight check, drift validation, candidates query, exception handling). The test file inspector/tests/routes/test_route_admin_releases.py contains zero tests for this route. The file's docstring (lines 1-21) claims coverage for other routes but omits this one. No other test file in the codebase tests this route (confirmed via grep search). The autouse _substrate_db fixture (conftest.py:117-150) handles DB setup but doesn't remove the test gap. The finding's core claim is correct: the destructive cut-release endpoint has zero HTTP-level test coverage.

findings.title: publish-hf misses anonymous 401, contributor 403, 404, single-flight 409, cut-in-flight 409, 502 launch error
findings.explanation: Only the ledger happy path (202) and the missing-ledger 409 are tested. The route has six other branches: (1) anonymous 401, (2) contributor 403, (3) unknown-slug 404, (4) cross-kind single-flight against same slug 409, (5) cut_release in-flight 409, (6) launch exception 502. All silent.
findings.proposed_action: Add a parametrize of the 401/403/404 gate cases plus three positive-branch tests: same-slug in-flight (`_stub_jobs_api(in_flight=[{slug:'X', kind:'timestamps'...}])` with `running_job_for(slug=...)` returning a tuple), cut_release in-flight, and launch-raises → 502.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is accurate. The `publish_hf` route (inspector/routes/admin/releases.py:50-93) has six untested branches: (1) anonymous 401, (2) insufficient-capability 403, (3) unknown-slug 404, (4) cross-kind single-flight 409, (5) cut_release in-flight 409, (6) launch-exception 502. The test file (inspector/tests/routes/test_route_admin_releases.py) contains only 2 tests for this route covering the happy-path 202 and missing-ledger 409. Convention established in other admin routes (e.g., test_route_access_admin.py) shows that 401/403 capability-gate tests ARE expected per-route. The mocking of `running_job_for` to always return None prevents testing the two 409 job-in-flight cases. The launch-exception 502 case is not tested because the mock launch succeeds. All six untested branches exist in the code (lines 66-67 for 404, 75-78 and 83-86 for the 409 cases, 88-92 for 502, and decorators for 401/403).

findings.title: release-preview only covers the 'added' diff bucket
findings.explanation: The route classifies each candidate as `added` / `refresh` / `unchanged` based on the prior `gh_release_recitations` membership and ts_version comparison; it also bumps minor/patch versions, surfaces `needs_manual_version` when nothing changed, and round-trips `expected_version_at_preview`. The lone test seeds one freshly-released recitation with no prior GH release → exercises only the `added` + `_bump_minor` (no prior) path. `refresh` (prior membership, different ts_version), `unchanged` (prior membership, same ts_version), `needs_manual_version=True` (no candidates change), and the `_bump_patch` / `_bump_minor` arithmetic against an existing prior version are uncovered.
findings.proposed_action: Add three tests seeding a prior `gh_releases` row + `gh_release_recitations` membership: (a) `refresh` when ts_version changes (asserts change_counts.refresh==1, computed_version == _bump_patch), (b) `unchanged` when ts_version matches (computed_version is None, needs_manual_version=True), (c) mixed add+refresh (computed_version == _bump_minor of prior).
findings.verifier_notes:
The test file at inspector/tests/routes/test_route_admin_releases.py only contains ONE test for the release_preview route (test_release_preview_uses_display_names at line 242). This test:

1. Seeds a fresh delivery with no prior GH release history
2. Calls GET /api/admin/release-preview
3. Asserts only the "added" bucket (line 257: change_counts.added == 1)
4. Asserts computed_version == v0.1.0 (line 255), which exercises _bump_minor(None) only

The route code at releases.py lines 145-182 implements logic for three buckets (added/refresh/unchanged) determined by gh_release_recitations membership and ts_version comparison. The version computation logic (lines 175-182) has four distinct paths:
- if added: _bump_minor (only path tested)
- elif refreshed: _bump_patch (NOT tested)
- elif no prior_version: v0.1.0 (tested indirectly)
- else: None with needs_override=True (NOT tested)

The test does NOT seed any prior gh_releases or gh_release_recitations rows, so refresh/unchanged/needs_override paths are completely uncovered. This is objectively true based on grep results showing no use of gh_releases or gh_release_recitations in the test file, and the helper functions _seed_released/_seed_ledger_ts only create per_recitation_releases rows, not gh_release rows.

findings.title: releases/status `summary`, `in_flight`, `latest_gh_release` payload fields untested
findings.explanation: Five tests cover the `_is_bucketable` filter on `recitations[]`, but none asserts on the other three top-level keys the FE depends on: `summary` (member_count, total_bytes, days_since_cut from `latest_gh_release_summary`), `in_flight` (passed through to the FE for the 'In progress' bucket), or `latest_gh_release` (FE 'last release' card). The `days_since_cut` arithmetic (parses ISO-8601 with Z suffix) is especially fragile and silently swallows exceptions (`except Exception: days_since_cut = None`).
findings.proposed_action: Add one test that seeds a `gh_releases` summary row and asserts `summary.version`, `summary.member_count`, `summary.total_bytes`, and `summary.days_since_cut` (with the ISO-Z parse). Add one test that passes `_stub_jobs_api(in_flight=[...])` and asserts the items round-trip into the `in_flight` response field unchanged.
findings.verifier_notes: The route /api/admin/releases/status returns a 4-key response: latest_gh_release, summary (with version, member_count, total_bytes, days_since_cut), in_flight, and recitations. Five tests exist (test_status_released_with_ledger_is_waiting, test_status_released_without_ledger_is_filtered, test_status_inert_rows_filtered, test_status_excluded_only_for_candidates, test_status_in_flight_slug_is_bucketable), but they only assert on the recitations array - never on summary, latest_gh_release, or in_flight top-level keys. The days_since_cut parsing (lines 354-357 in releases.py) is especially fragile with bare exception swallowing. The in_flight test passes the mock data but doesn't verify it round-trips in the response body. File: inspector/routes/admin/releases.py:342-417; inspector/tests/routes/test_route_admin_releases.py:136-234.

findings.title: release-preview JOINs the `channels` table twice with different aliases
findings.explanation: The candidate SQL has both `JOIN channels c ON c.slug = d.channel` (line 128) AND `JOIN channels ch ON ch.slug = d.channel` (line 131). Both alias the same row; `c.gh_release_eligible = 1` is filtered through `c`, and `ch.name AS channel` is selected via `ch`. Functionally harmless (SQLite collapses the join) but wasteful and confusing; the single alias `c` could supply both. Discovered while auditing `test_release_preview_uses_display_names`. Not a behavioral bug — caught by the green test — but worth a one-line cleanup.
findings.proposed_action: Drop the `JOIN channels ch ...` line and change `ch.name AS channel` to `c.name AS channel` in the SELECT list.
findings.verifier_notes: The SQL query in inspector/routes/admin/releases.py:117-137 contains redundant JOINs of the channels table: line 128 `JOIN channels c ON c.slug = d.channel` and line 131 `JOIN channels ch ON ch.slug = d.channel`. Since channels.slug is a PRIMARY KEY (0001_init.sql:74), both produce identical row sets. The alias `c` is only used in the WHERE clause (line 135), and `ch` only in SELECT (line 124). A single JOIN with alias `c` could replace both. The test test_release_preview_uses_display_names passes despite the redundancy, confirming it's functionally harmless but structurally wasteful—the identical query structure in cut_release (line 278-283) uses only one JOIN, showing the correct pattern.

findings.title: Four overlapping seed paths (signed_in_client / seed_state / _seed_state / _row+_replace_state) make admin tests hard to onboard
findings.explanation: A new contributor reading these tests sees four parallel ways to seed a delivery_state row: (1) `signed_in_client` fixture (only seeds a user row), (2) the `seed_state` pytest fixture, (3) the conftest module-level `_seed_state` helper imported by file-local `_replace_state` wrappers, and (4) the file-local `_seed_released` / `_seed_delivery_on_channel` for non-default channels. The four share defaults inconsistently — e.g. `_seed_state` defaults `state='awaiting_review'`, but `test_route_admin_actions.py::_row` defaults `state='under_review'`. There's no docstring explaining which to reach for; the only signal is reading the conftest and three sibling files.
findings.proposed_action: Document the seeding hierarchy in a short comment at the top of `tests/conftest.py`'s SQLite substrate section. Even better: collapse `_seed_released` + `_seed_delivery_on_channel` into a parametrized `seed_state(channel=, gh_release_eligible=)` so the file-local helpers go away.
findings.verifier_notes: Downgrade severity to low (it's a minor default inconsistency, not an onboarding barrier). The specialized helpers are documented. The real fix is: (1) add a comment block in conftest.py explaining the three-layer pattern (fixture→helper→custom file wrappers), and (2) standardize `_row()` default state across test files. Do NOT collapse `_seed_released`/`_seed_delivery_on_channel` - they're legitimately specialized.

findings.title: Raw-SQL `_ins_transition` / `_ins_request` helpers belong in conftest
findings.explanation: Both helpers hand-roll INSERTs against `transitions` and `requests` (NOT NULL columns, FK to users) and will be re-needed by sibling admin tests (e.g. activity-rail tests, requests aggregations) as the panel grows. They mirror the pattern already conftest-promoted for `seed_role`/`seed_state`/`_seed_delivery_chain`, and inlining them invites silent schema drift if a NOT NULL column is added.
findings.proposed_action: Promote `_ins_transition` and `_ins_request` to conftest fixtures (`seed_transition`, `seed_request`) next to `seed_state`/`seed_role`, taking the same kwarg style. Drop the duplicate helpers from `test_users_read.py`.
findings.verifier_notes: The `_ins_transition` and `_ins_request` helpers in test_users_read.py (lines 9-21) are genuine candidates for conftest promotion. Evidence: (1) Sibling admin test file `test_first_seen_backfill.py` contains inline raw-SQL INSERTs (lines 34-35, 45-46, 73) inserting into the same tables with identical NOT NULL columns, proving the pattern is needed elsewhere but not yet factored. (2) The helpers follow the exact signature pattern of conftest-promoted functions like `_seed_delivery_chain`, `_seed_state`, `_seed_role` (internal functions wrapped in pytest fixtures). (3) The schema has NOT NULL FKs on both tables (transitions.actor_id, requests.requester_id), so silent column-addition drift is a real maintenance risk. (4) No admin-level conftest exists, so promotion to root conftest is appropriate and matches existing conventions. The proposed action (promote to `seed_transition`/`seed_request` with kwarg-based API) aligns with the codebase pattern.

findings.title: `test_detail_outcome_and_stats` hand-inserts a delivery + claim instead of using repo helpers
findings.explanation: The test writes a full `INSERT INTO deliveries(...)` and `INSERT INTO claims(...)` row inline. The rest of the suite seeds deliveries via `_seed_delivery_chain` and claims via `repo_claims.open_claim` + `set_marked_ready` + `close_claim` (the conftest's `_seed_state` is the canonical example). Any column rename, NOT-NULL add, or CHECK change will silently break this test, and it duplicates seeding logic the conftest already centralizes.
findings.proposed_action: Replace the raw INSERTs with `_seed_delivery_chain(conn, 'pubS')` + a tiny `seed_closed_claim` helper (or `repo_claims.open_claim` followed by `close_claim` + setting `marked_ready_at` via a helper). Keep the slug + dates literal but route the rows through the repos.
findings.verifier_notes: The test does use raw SQL INSERTs to create claims (lines 78-88 of inspector/tests/admin/test_users_read.py), bypassing repo helpers. However, the actual fragility is lower than typical raw-SQL concerns: (1) columns are explicitly named, not positional; (2) recent migrations (0010-0016) don't modify claims; (3) the schema convention is to add only nullable columns; (4) similar patterns exist in test_first_seen_backfill.py:54-56 and test_spine.py. The proper fix is to match the pattern in test_repo_state.py:66-69: call repo_claims.open_claim() then repo_claims.close_claim() in sequence, with explicit timestamp control. This is a code-consistency/robustness improvement rather than a critical bug. Severity should remain low, but propose action is sound.

findings.title: No test exercises the `db_seq`-keyed admin_users cache hit/miss path
findings.explanation: `list_users()` caches its serialized payload on `db_seq` (`cache.get_admin_users_cache` / `cache.set_admin_users_cache`). The conftest invalidates that cache between tests, but no test asserts (a) a second call within the same db_seq returns the cached object without re-querying, or (b) a mutation that bumps db_seq invalidates the cache. The N+1 test only exercises post-write paths (each seed bumps db_seq), so the cached-hit branch is dead from the suite's perspective.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that calls `list_users()` twice without any intervening write and asserts the second call performs zero repo queries (using the `_CountingConn` pattern). Add a second test that calls `list_users()`, performs a role grant (bumps db_seq), and asserts the second call re-queries (and reflects the new user).
findings.verifier_notes:
The finding is confirmed. Coverage analysis (line 107 in users.py marked as uncovered in pytest-cov output) and manual inspection of test_users_read.py show:

1. No test calls list_users() twice within the same db_seq without invalidation between calls
2. test_list_users_no_n_plus_1 (the closest test) calls list_users() multiple times but each call has intervening seed_role operations that bump db_seq, causing the cache to invalidate automatically before the next call
3. conftest._substrate_db fixture calls invalidate_admin_users_cache() before (line 140) and after (line 148) every test, ensuring cross-test isolation
4. Line 107 (the cache-hit return) has never been executed by the test suite

The pattern for this test exists elsewhere: test_public_reciters_cache.py::test_repeated_reads_hit_cache() calls all_public_reciters() three times in a row to verify cache hits without intervening writes.

The severity and proposed action are reasonable: add a test that calls list_users() twice at the same db_seq and asserts zero queries on the second call.

findings.title: Role mutations are not verified to append an audit/transitions row
findings.explanation: `access.grant`, `access.revoke`, and `access.update` each `audit.append` an `access.role_*` event inside the durable transaction. The role-picker tests cover the 200/400/403/409 response shape and the `repo_access.resolve_role` outcome, but never read back the audit/transitions row to confirm the actor + payload + reason were recorded — the single most important downstream contract for compliance/Admin → Activity. A regression that silently drops the audit call would pass the entire `test_set_role.py` suite.
findings.proposed_action: After each happy-path dispatch (grant/update/demote), query the `transitions` table (or whatever sink `audit.append` writes to) and assert the latest row has `event='access.role_granted'|'access.role_updated'|'access.role_revoked'`, `actor_id='o'`, and `payload.target_hf_user_id` matches the picker target. One parametrized test covers all three dispatch paths.
findings.verifier_notes: Code inspection shows that access.grant(), access.revoke(), and access.update() all call audit.append() inside durable transactions (access.py:126-135, 187-196, 227-232). However, test_set_role.py's happy-path tests (lines 24-58) only verify response codes, JSON response shape, and role persistence via repo_access.resolve_role(). They never query repo_transitions or verify audit rows exist. A regression that removed audit.append() would still pass all three dispatch-path tests. Pattern evidence exists in test_repo_transitions.py showing how to verify: call mutation, then repo_transitions.get(rec.request_id) to verify the row. The test suite in test_set_role.py covers gates/validation well but has a genuine compliance audit trail gap.

findings.title: `_claim_outcome` branches for force-released / reassigned / released-without-publish are untested
findings.explanation: Only `published` and `claimed, open now` are exercised by `test_detail_outcome_and_stats`. The other four outcomes (`force-released`, `reassigned`, `released without publish`, and the generic `closed (<reason>)` fallback) match on free-vocabulary substrings of `close_reason`, which is the most fragile part of the file. A typo in the substring or a rename of the transition event would silently regress the dashboard's labels.
findings.proposed_action: Parametrize a test over `(close_reason, marked_ready_at, expected_outcome)` covering each branch in `_claim_outcome`, seeding a closed claim per case via the repo helper proposed in `raw-sql-claim-insert-bypasses-repo`.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is confirmed. Code analysis shows: (1) `_claim_outcome()` function at inspector/services/admin/users.py:201-216 contains 5 conditional branches, (2) coverage report shows lines 210-216 are 0% covered with `--cov`, (3) test_detail_outcome_and_stats only tests 2 of 5 outcomes: "claimed, open now" (line 206) and "published" (line 209), (4) untested branches handle close_reason values that are actually used in production: "force_released" substring match (line 210-211), "reassigned" substring match (line 212-213), "released" substring match (line 214-215), and the generic fallback (line 216), (5) these close_reason values are set by the state machine when firing claim.force_released, claim.reassigned, reciter.released, and reciter.published events respectively (verified in inspector/services/state/state.py:481 and inspector/services/db/repo_claims.py:156). The substring-matching logic is intentional but fragile: a typo like "force_release" (missing 'd') would silently cause the wrong label to appear on the dashboard for force-released claims.

findings.title: `summary.active_this_week` cutoff window has no behavioural test
findings.explanation: The list test only asserts `active_this_week >= 1` after a same-day transition. The 7-day rolling cutoff (`_ACTIVE_WINDOW_DAYS`) — the actual logic worth a regression guard — is never exercised. A user with a transition 8+ days old should NOT count; nothing checks that.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that seeds two users — one with a transition stamped `now()` and one with a transition stamped `now() - 10 days` (via the `ts` kwarg already on `_ins_transition`) — and asserts `summary.active_this_week == 1`.
findings.verifier_notes: The 7-day rolling window logic in inspector/services/admin/users.py:132-135 uses ISO 8601 string comparison and is not tested for the boundary condition. The test at inspector/tests/admin/test_users_read.py:57 only asserts active_this_week >= 1 after same-day transitions. The test helper _ins_transition already supports a ts kwarg for seeding old timestamps, making the proposed test straightforward. No time-mocking infrastructure blocks such a test, and this is a legitimate regression guard for simple but critical business logic.

findings.title: `get_user_detail` for a user with zero claims/requests has no test
findings.explanation: `test_detail_outcome_and_stats` exercises the populated path; `test_detail_unknown_user_returns_none` exercises the missing path. The middle case — a known user with NO claims, NO requests, NO transitions — isn't asserted. That branch returns `avg_turnaround_seconds=None`, empty `requests_by_status={}`, empty history arrays, which is exactly what the FE has to render gracefully and is exactly where shape regressions appear.
findings.proposed_action: Add `test_detail_zero_state(seed_role)` that seeds only a users/role row and asserts `stats.avg_turnaround_seconds is None`, `stats.lifetime_claims == 0`, and all four history arrays are empty.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is accurate. `test_zero_action_user_still_listed` seeds a zero-state user but only exercises `list_users()`, not `get_user_detail()`. `test_detail_outcome_and_stats` calls `get_user_detail()` but on a user with claims+requests (line 70-101). `test_detail_unknown_user_returns_none` tests the missing-user path. No test exists that calls `get_user_detail()` on a known user with zero claims/requests/transitions and asserts the shape of stats (avg_turnaround_seconds=None, requests_by_status={}, empty history arrays). This is a low-severity but real gap — the code path is defensive and correct, but unasserted. File: inspector/tests/admin/test_users_read.py, Lines 60-105.

findings.title: `_DETAIL_HISTORY_LIMIT=20` clamp on history queries is untested
findings.explanation: Three detail queries (`claims_history`, `requests_history`, `recent_activity`) clamp at 20 rows. A regression dropping the LIMIT clause or flipping the ORDER BY would explode the detail payload for power users and the suite would never notice.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that seeds 25 claims (or transitions) for a single user and asserts `len(detail['claims_history']) == 20` and that the rows are in `claimed_at DESC` order.
findings.verifier_notes: 100% line coverage (52/52 statements in repo_admin_users.py) is confirmed by pytest-cov, but this does not verify behavior. The three functions (claims_history, requests_history, recent_activity) at lines 154-178 have their SQL lines executed during testing, but the test only creates 2 claims (test_detail_outcome_and_stats) - far below the _DETAIL_HISTORY_LIMIT=20. No test asserts that len(claims_history)==20 when 25+ claims exist, or validates ORDER BY DESC ordering. Removing the LIMIT clause or flipping ORDER BY would not be caught by existing tests. Severity is appropriately low (UX issue, not data/security loss).

findings.title: N+1 guard's `<= 6` threshold is loose — service issues exactly 5 repo executes
findings.explanation: The test patches `repo_admin_users.get_conn` so it only counts executes routed through that module. `current_db_seq()` uses `services.db.connection.get_conn` and is not counted (correct, by design). The service then runs exactly 5 aggregation queries (`base_rows`, `last_activity_by_actor`, `requests_count_by_user`, `reviews_count_by_actor`, `open_claims_by_user`). The assertion `three <= 6` leaves slack for one stray per-user query to slip in undetected. Tighten to `three == 5` so any drift fails the test loudly.
findings.proposed_action: Replace `assert three <= 6` with `assert three == 5` and add a comment naming the five aggregations. Keep `assert three == nine` as the actual N+1 invariant.
findings.verifier_notes: The test patches repo_admin_users.get_conn to count executes routed through that module. Code analysis shows list_users() calls exactly 5 aggregation functions (base_rows, last_activity_by_actor, requests_count_by_user, reviews_count_by_actor, open_claims_by_user), each invoking execute() exactly once. No per-user queries are issued. The test's docstring (line 110) explicitly states "5 aggregations". The assertion three <= 6 is unnecessarily loose — it should be three == 5 to fail loudly if a 6th query is accidentally added. While the N+1 guard (three == nine) is solid, tightening to exact count makes the test more maintainable and catches regressions earlier. inspector/tests/admin/test_users_read.py:108-139; inspector/services/admin/users.py:101-113.

findings.title: `set_role` accepts a `login` kwarg but no test exercises the login-refresh path
findings.explanation: The route reads `body.login` and forwards it into `users_service.set_role(login=...)`. The grant branch uses it directly; the update branch passes through to `access.update`. No test in `test_set_role.py` passes a `login` in the body, so a regression silently dropping the kwarg from the call chain is unobserved.
findings.proposed_action: Add `test_set_role_refreshes_login(signed_in_client)` that POSTs `{role: 'maintainer', login: 'new-handle'}` and asserts `repo_access.find_member(...).login == 'new-handle'`.
findings.verifier_notes: Correct the evidence: the update branch does NOT pass login to access.update() - it passes only hf_user_id, actor, role, reason. This is the bug: login is accepted by the route but silently ignored during maintainer↔owner transitions. Upgrade severity from 'low' to 'medium' since silently dropping accepted input is a data-loss bug. Proposed test is correct and valuable.

findings.title: `AdminUsersResponse`/`AdminUserDetail` Pydantic round-trip shape is not pinned
findings.explanation: Tests cherry-pick specific keys (`role`, `reviews`, `requests`, `active_claim`, `stats.lifetime_claims`, …) and the route test (`test_routes.py:18-19`) only checks `'users' in body and 'summary' in body`. The codegen-FE-types invariant (FE consumes the JSON Schema dumped from `AdminUsersResponse` / `AdminUserDetail`) means a silently-dropped field on the Pydantic model would not fail a test but would break the FE next codegen run.
findings.proposed_action: Add one schema-shape test per response model that asserts `set(body.keys()) == set(AdminUsersResponse.model_fields)` and the same for `body['users'][0]` vs `AdminUserRow.model_fields` and detail vs `AdminUserDetail.model_fields`. Codegen-parity finding.
findings.verifier_notes: The admin-users routes (test_users_read.py, test_routes.py) do NOT use the assert_keys_superset() pattern that guards shape in other data routes (/api/seg/data, /api/seg/validate). They cherry-pick specific keys instead of validating the entire response shape. However, the CI job schema-codegen-check (inspector-checks.yml lines 84-121) provides a strong secondary defense by regenerating FE types and failing git diff --exit-code on drift. The Pydantic models all use ConfigDict(extra="allow") for forward-compat (per CLAUDE.md #137). The finding is valid but severity should reflect that codegen-CI is the primary guard; the test gap is secondary.

findings.title: test_migration_0002 only checks the post-migration shape — would pass even if 0002 were deleted
findings.explanation: Every test in the file asserts shape on the freshly-migrated DB built by the autouse `_substrate_db` fixture (tests/conftest.py:117). If 0002 were re-inlined into 0001 (the exact failure mode the 0007 docstring warns about), every assertion would still pass. The 0007 regression test exists specifically because columns inlined into 0001 never land on existing DBs at higher user_version; 0002 needs the same simulate-pre-state-then-migrate construction. As written, the file is a smoke-check that duplicates `test_migration_creates_all_tables` in tests/db/test_spine.py and provides zero regression value against the bug class the docstring is supposedly guarding.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that constructs an in-memory DB at user_version=1 with a minimal 0001 skeleton (users without last_login_at/last_entry_at, no visitor_daily/indexes), runs `migrate.run_migrations`, then asserts the columns/table/indexes are present — mirroring the 0007 pattern. The current four assertions can stay as a sanity check on the fresh-chain DB, but the simulate-and-upgrade test is what makes 0002 regression-proof.
findings.verifier_notes: The test file at inspector/tests/admin/test_migration_0002.py only asserts the final schema shape after running the full migration chain via the autouse _substrate_db fixture (tests/conftest.py:117). This validates that a fresh database gets the correct final state but does NOT test the critical upgrade path: whether migration 0002 successfully applies its ALTER statements to a pre-0002 database (at user_version=1). The documented regression pattern (database.md lines 95-97, 0007_mark_ready_submission.sql lines 10-16) shows this is a real risk: if 0002 were inlined into 0001, fresh databases would pass but existing production databases (already at user_version >= 1) would never re-run 0001 and would silently miss the new columns/tables/indexes. The test_migration_0007.py pattern (lines 39-91 in test_migration_0007.py) demonstrates the correct regression test: construct a database at the prior user_version, run the full migration chain, and verify the additions land. test_migration_0002.py has no equivalent simulation of an existing v1 database being upgraded to v2.

findings.title: test_migration_0010 only checks the post-migration shape — does not exercise the migration on a pre-existing DB
findings.explanation: Same issue as 0002: all assertions only read the post-migrated fresh-chain DB. The `guide_views` table would exist regardless of whether 0010 even ran (because `_substrate_db` runs the full chain from version=0). To regression-guard against accidental inlining into 0001 or against a migration that silently no-ops on an existing DB, the test must simulate a DB at user_version=9 without `guide_views`, then run `migrate.run_migrations` and assert 0010 created it.
findings.proposed_action: Add a `test_existing_db_at_v9_gets_guide_views` companion using the same minimal-stub + `migrate.run_migrations(conn)` pattern as test_migration_0007.py:39-92.
findings.verifier_notes: test_migration_0010.py (lines 7-24) only verifies post-migration state on a fresh full-chain DB. The autouse _substrate_db fixture (conftest.py:117-150) calls db.init_db() which applies ALL migrations 0001-0010, so guide_views table will exist regardless of whether 0010 created it or was inlined/no-op'd. The proper regression test pattern is in test_migration_0007.py:39-92: create stub DB at v9 without the target columns, run migrations, assert 0007 created them. This pattern is completely absent from test_migration_0010.py. database.md explicitly documents this regression (0007 was created to fix columns inlined into 0001 missing on live data). The CREATE TABLE statement at inspector/services/db/migrations/0010_guide_views.sql:18-24 should be verified to reach existing DBs.

findings.title: Migrations 0011–0016 have no per-migration regression tests at all
findings.explanation: After 0010, six migrations landed (incl. 0011's DROP COLUMN, 0012's data sweep, 0014's three-table releases with UPDATE seeds, and 0015's UPDATE-to-NULL data fix) and not one has a pre-existing-state regression test. The 0014 migration in particular has DDL (3 new tables, 1 ALTER) + DML (channels seed) that needs verification. The 0015 docstring says the previous (0014) migration left rows in a broken state that 500'd snapshot reads — exactly the bug class regression tests prevent.
findings.proposed_action: Add per-migration regression tests for 0011, 0012, 0014, 0015 at minimum, following the 0007 pattern: build a stub at version=N-1, run migrations, assert post-state matches expected (column/table/data). 0013 and 0016 (pure additive ALTERs) are lower priority but should follow eventually for consistency.
findings.verifier_notes: Confirmed through direct inspection: (1) Migrations 0011-0016 exist and contain critical schema/data changes (DDL, DML, seeding). (2) Only test_migration_0002.py, test_migration_0007.py, test_migration_0010.py exist—zero tests for 0011-0016. (3) The 0014→0015 chain is a regression-test canary: 0014 leaves rows in broken state (mixed bitrate_mode with non-null kbps_nominal), 0015 UPDATEs them to NULL. Without v13→v14/v15 transformation tests, we cannot verify data fixes work on existing DBs. (4) Indirect coverage (test_repo_releases.py using the 0014 tables) only exercises fresh-DB operations, not migration application. (5) The 0007 pattern (build v6 stub, run migrations, assert columns exist) is the correct regression guard; 0011-0016 lack it. inspector/services/db/migrations/0014_releases.sql:1 (3 new tables + ALTER + DML); 0015_bitrate_mixed_null_kbps.sql:1 (UPDATE data fix). inspector/tests/admin/test_migration_*.py: only 0002, 0007, 0010 present.

findings.title: `services/db/migrate.py` runner edge cases are not tested
findings.explanation: Several behaviours of the runner have no direct test: (1) non-conforming filename → warn-and-skip (line 27-29), (2) mid-script exception → rollback + raise (line 61-67), (3) `current_version()` returns the highest applied version after a partial-pending list, (4) the BEGIN/COMMIT/user_version wrapper genuinely is atomic (a mid-script crash leaves user_version unchanged). The runner is the substrate for boot; an undetected change here breaks every deploy.
findings.proposed_action: Add a focused test_migrate.py: drop a `0099_broken.sql` containing `SELECT 1; RAISE` (or a known-bad statement) into a per-test temp migrations dir, point `_MIGRATIONS_DIR` at it via monkeypatch, run, assert `user_version` did NOT advance and a logged error fired. Plus a positive test that a malformed filename is skipped without raising.
findings.verifier_notes: Coverage analysis confirms migrate.py lines 28-29 and 61-67 are uncovered. The non-conforming filename warning (lines 27-29) and exception handling/rollback (lines 61-67) are not exercised by any test. The code structure is correct per line-by-line review - the _NAME_RE regex correctly identifies valid migration files, and the exception handler properly wraps executescript in a try/except that calls rollback on failure. However, these critical paths in the migration runner (which is the boot substrate) lack direct test coverage. The rerun idempotency test and existing_db_at_v6 test provide indirect coverage of atomicity, but don't verify behavior on actual script errors. The proposed test design is sound and practical: create a known-bad migration, point _MIGRATIONS_DIR to it via monkeypatch, verify the error is logged and user_version doesn't advance, and verify non-conforming filenames are skipped. Inspector/services/db/migrate.py:23-71 (full function range); specific gaps at 28-29 and 61-67.

findings.title: The simulate-pre-state-then-migrate pattern (the actually correct one) only lives in 0007's docstring
findings.explanation: A new contributor adding migration 0017 will look at the three existing tests, see 0002 + 0010 as the dominant pattern ("just PRAGMA table_info on the autouse-migrated DB"), and write a useless smoke test. Only the 0007 file demonstrates the real regression-prevention pattern, buried in its docstring. A consumer of this subsystem has to read three files before realizing 0007 is the gold standard.
findings.proposed_action: Either rewrite 0002 and 0010 to follow the 0007 pattern (making the convention obvious through dominant practice), or add a docs/reference/database.md section pinning the canonical pre-state-migrate-assert pattern with a code template.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is correct: test_migration_0007.py demonstrates the "pre-state→migrate→assert" pattern (lines 39-91) that catches regressions from mistaken inlines into already-applied migrations. Tests 0002 and 0010 only check that columns/tables exist on a fresh migrated DB. The pattern IS documented in docs/reference/database.md (line 97) explaining why 0007 exists (mark_ready columns were inlined to 0001, never reached existing DBs). However, the CONVENTION for when/how to apply this test pattern to new migrations is not explicitly stated. A contributor adding migration 0017 will see 0002+0010 as the dominant pattern and won't understand the regression-prevention rationale without reading through file-level docstrings or the database.md reference doc. The proposed action is valid: either rewrite 0002/0010 to follow the 0007 pattern (making it obviously the standard) or add explicit testing guidance to database.md or a new testing reference doc.

findings.title: Upload-failure test comment claims 'no token/url leakage' but never exercises redaction or truncation
findings.explanation: The test raises `IOError("network down")` and asserts `"network down" in st["last_error"]`. The inline comment says 'no token/url leakage: only type + truncated message', but the assertion only checks that the (short) message is preserved verbatim. `_safe_err` truncates to 200 chars (`str(e)[:200]`) — the test exercises neither truncation nor the redaction the comment implies, so the safety property the comment is selling is not actually pinned. The next time `_safe_err` is changed (e.g. to redact `token=` query strings), nothing here breaks.
findings.proposed_action: Either drop the misleading comment, or raise an exception whose `str()` contains both a fake bearer token and >200 chars, then assert both that the message is truncated AND that the token substring is absent (once redaction is actually implemented). At minimum, fix the comment to match the assertion ('preserves the underlying message verbatim').
findings.verifier_notes: The test at inspector/tests/db/test_sync.py:127-139 raises IOError("network down") which is only 12 chars, well below the 200-char truncation limit. The assertion `assert "network down" in st["last_error"]` only checks that short strings pass through verbatim. The implementation at inspector/services/db/sync.py:71-73 truncates to 200 chars but does NOT redact tokens or URLs (despite the docstring claiming it prevents leakage). The test never exercises either the truncation (no >200 char message) or redaction (no token/URL in exception), so the comment "no token/url leakage: only type + truncated message" is unsupported by the test. If _safe_err is changed (e.g. to add token redaction), this test would not catch regressions because it doesn't exercise that code path.

findings.title: CAS guard is only tested on the 'remote ahead' branch — equal-seq + different-nonce + 'we are ahead' are not parametrized
findings.explanation: `upload()` refuses iff `remote.seq >= snap_seq AND remote.nonce != _NONCE`. The single CAS test exercises only `remote.seq=99 > snap_seq=1`. The equal-seq branch (`remote.seq == snap_seq`, different nonce — the boot-restart scenario explicitly called out at sync.py:88-103/356-363) and the 'we are ahead, no conflict' branch (`remote.seq < snap_seq`) are not directly asserted on `upload()`. The deferred_sync no-op test happens to dodge the equal-seq branch by never calling upload, which is what the production fix is, but `upload()` itself's equal-seq behaviour is unverified.
findings.proposed_action: Parametrize the CAS test over `(remote_seq, snap_seq, same_nonce, should_raise)` covering: remote ahead+different-nonce → raise; remote equal+different-nonce → raise; remote behind → allowed; same nonce regardless of seq → allowed. Single helper, four cases.
findings.verifier_notes: The CAS guard condition (sync.py:165-169) raises iff `remote.seq >= snap_seq AND nonce != _NONCE`. Test coverage: (1) test_cas_conflict_from_other_container exercises remote.seq=99 > snap_seq=1 with different nonce → raises (✓); (2) test_reupload_same_container_is_allowed exercises same nonce with advancing seq → allowed (✓ same-nonce case, partial ahead case); (3) test_deferred_sync_skips_upload_when_batch_is_noop documents and avoids the equal-seq + different-nonce case by NOT calling upload() (✗ upload() itself not directly tested with this condition); (4) remote.seq < snap_seq with different nonce is not explicitly tested. The equal-seq case is addressed in production via deferred_sync logic (line 362), but upload() itself lacks parametrized coverage of all branches. Finding is correct: no comprehensive parametrized test of upload()'s CAS logic across all four cases.

findings.title: `synced` fixture re-points the DB path the autouse `_substrate_db` already initialized, doing duplicate work
findings.explanation: The autouse `_substrate_db` already runs `set_db_path_for_test(tmp_path / "inspector-test.db")` + `init_db()` + `_sync.set_sync_enabled(False)` + `_sync._reset_for_test()`. The `synced` fixture then redoes all of that with a different filename and runs `_reset_for_test()` again. Functionally fine, but the double-init is wasted work and the two filenames in the same `tmp_path` make debugging confusing (the autouse-created `inspector-test.db` lingers as dead state in the temp dir). The pattern also diverges from `test_durability.py` which reuses the autouse DB and only flips sync + backend.
findings.proposed_action: Mirror the `synced_bucket` pattern from `test_durability.py`: keep the autouse DB and only install the FilesystemBackend + flip `_reset_for_test`, dropping `set_db_path_for_test` entirely. Saves the double-init and aligns with the neighbouring durability test convention.
findings.verifier_notes: The `synced` fixture in test_sync.py lines 20-21 calls `set_db_path_for_test()` and `init_db()`, which are already executed by the autouse `_substrate_db` fixture that runs before every test. The `set_db_path_for_test()` call (connection.py:71-75) internally calls `reset()` to close prior connections and switches to a different DB path (`tmp_path / "local.db"` vs autouse's `tmp_path / "inspector-test.db"`), creating duplicate initialization work and leaving dead state in tmp_path. The `synced_bucket` fixture in test_durability.py (lines 24-35) demonstrates the correct pattern: reuse the autouse DB and only install the FilesystemBackend + flip sync.set_sync_enabled(), without calling set_db_path_for_test or init_db. This is a confirmed inefficiency that produces functionally correct but wasteful code.

findings.title: `snapshot()` 'must not run inside an active write transaction' guard is unverified
findings.explanation: `snapshot()` raises `RuntimeError("snapshot() called inside an active write transaction")` when `connection._active.get() is not None`. This invariant matters because `durable_transaction()` deliberately defers `mark_durable()` until after the `_active` ContextVar clears (sync.py:379-383). No test pins it — a refactor that accidentally calls `snapshot()` inside a txn would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that opens a `db.transaction()` and asserts `sync.snapshot()` raises with the documented message.
findings.verifier_notes: The guard at sync.py:101-102 that raises RuntimeError("snapshot() called inside an active write transaction") when connection._active.get() is not None has no direct test coverage. While the guard IS implicitly exercised by integration tests (test_durability.py, test_sync.py) that verify snapshot() works correctly when called through the proper durable_transaction() → mark_durable() → upload() path (which clears _active before calling snapshot), there is NO explicit test that directly calls snapshot() inside a db.transaction() context and asserts it raises the documented RuntimeError. The absence of this defensive test means a refactoring that accidentally calls snapshot() inside a transaction scope would not be caught at test time. The finding is valid - a dedicated test should be added as proposed.

findings.title: `mark_durable()` skip paths (sync disabled, inside deferred_sync) and `durable_transaction()` nesting are not directly tested
findings.explanation: `mark_durable()` is a no-op when (a) `_SYNC_ENABLED=False` or (b) `_defer_depth.get() > 0`. The deferred-sync tests assert by side effect (`meta["nonce"]` after the block) but never exercise `mark_durable()` directly nor the nested `durable_transaction()` SAVEPOINT case (only the OUTERMOST boundary uploads — covered at sync.py:379-383). A regression where the inner `durable_transaction` accidentally re-uploads would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests: (1) `mark_durable()` is a no-op when sync disabled (assert no bucket write); (2) `mark_durable()` is a no-op when called inside `deferred_sync()`; (3) two nested `durable_transaction()` blocks upload exactly once.
findings.verifier_notes: Coverage reports show lines 330-332 of sync.py (mark_durable's no-op guards) are uncovered. Code review confirms: (1) mark_durable() has two no-op conditions (when sync disabled, when inside deferred_sync) that are never directly tested; (2) existing tests verify deferred_sync behavior via side effects, not direct mark_durable calls; (3) test_durability.py uses _SYNC_ENABLED=True so the no-op guard never executes. The gap is real: a regression where mark_durable uploaded when disabled or was called twice in nested blocks would not be caught.

findings.title: `pull()` WAL/-shm cleanup, 0o600 perms, stale .pull.tmp removal, and Windows `_replace_with_retry` retry loop are unverified
findings.explanation: The round-trip test only checks that the destination contains the expected row. It does not verify: (1) pre-existing `dest-wal` and `dest-shm` files are removed (the 'always trust the bucket' invariant — sync.py:222-226); (2) the file's mode is tightened to `0o600` (sync.py:236); (3) a stale `dest.pull.tmp` from a previous failed pull is cleared before write (sync.py:228-233); (4) the `_replace_with_retry` retry loop survives a transient `PermissionError` (sync.py:195-208). Each of these is a deliberately-documented invariant that could silently regress.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests that plant `dest-wal`, `dest-shm`, and `dest.pull.tmp` files before `pull()` and assert they're gone after; on POSIX assert `oct(stat.S_IMODE(...)) == '0o600'`; mock `os.replace` to raise `PermissionError` N-1 times to verify the retry loop succeeds.
findings.verifier_notes: The claimed side effects (WAL/-shm cleanup, 0o600 perms, stale .pull.tmp removal, and _replace_with_retry retry logic) are indeed unverified by tests. The test `test_upload_then_pull_roundtrip` only verifies data integrity (round-trip correctness), not these defensive cleanup operations. The code correctly documents these invariants in sync.py:222-226, 228-233, 236 but there are no tests that plant pre-existing files or mock os.replace to verify these side effects execute correctly. However, severity should be reconsidered: these are best-effort defensive mechanisms (wrapped in try/except) designed for production edge cases (prior crashes, stale file cleanup) that don't arise in the fresh-temp-path test environment. The round-trip test *does* verify the essential invariant (data integrity), and regressions in these side effects would not cause functional failures.

findings.title: `_read_remote_seq()` error paths (`StorageNotFound`, malformed JSON, generic read error) are not tested in `upload()` context
findings.explanation: When the seq sidecar is missing, malformed, or unreadable, `_read_remote_seq` returns `None` and `upload()` proceeds without a CAS check. No test pins this 'graceful degradation' contract — a future change to make a missing sidecar fatal would change the boot-pull / first-upload behavior silently.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests: (1) seq sidecar absent → upload succeeds; (2) seq sidecar has non-JSON bytes → upload succeeds with logged warning; (3) `_read_direct` raises a generic Exception for the sidecar → upload still proceeds.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is accurate. Code at inspector/services/db/sync.py:130-142 shows _read_remote_seq() gracefully returns None on StorageNotFound (line 133-134), generic Exception (line 135-137), and malformed JSON (line 140-142). The upload() function at line 164-170 skips the CAS check when remote is None. While test_upload_then_pull_roundtrip implicitly exercises the missing-sidecar case (bucket is empty on first upload), there are no explicit tests for: (1) missing sidecar → upload succeeds, (2) malformed JSON with logged warning, or (3) generic read error recovery. The graceful degradation is intentional and working, but the contract lacks explicit test coverage for these three error paths, making future refactoring risky.

findings.title: `_prune_snapshots` swallow-and-log when `list_dir` fails is unverified
findings.explanation: `_prune_snapshots` returns `[]` if `backend.list_dir("db")` raises. The retention test only covers the happy path. A regression that re-raised would crash `daily_snapshot` on any transient bucket hiccup.
findings.proposed_action: Add a monkeypatched `list_dir`-raises test asserting `_prune_snapshots` returns `[]` without raising and logs a warning.
findings.verifier_notes: The `_prune_snapshots` function (inspector/services/db/sync.py:258-262) has defensive error handling that catches exceptions from `backend.list_dir("db")`, logs a warning, and returns `[]` to prevent crashes on transient bucket errors. This code path is NOT tested. Examination of inspector/tests/db/test_sync.py shows only `test_daily_snapshot_and_retention` (lines 112-124) which tests the happy path only. No monkeypatched or mocked `list_dir` exception tests exist. The current implementation is correct and safe, but there is a legitimate test coverage gap: a regression that removed the try-except would silently crash `daily_snapshot` on any bucket operation failure.

findings.title: `_safe_err` truncation (200-char cap) is unverified — the only safety net against logging tokens/URLs from HF errors
findings.explanation: The module docstring explicitly notes HF errors can embed `token=...` URLs, and `_safe_err` is the redaction layer (truncation to 200 chars). No test exercises a >200-char error or a token-bearing one — the 'no token/url leakage' claim in the upload-failure test is a comment, not an assertion.
findings.proposed_action: Add a direct unit test for `_safe_err`: feed it an exception with a 1000-char message, assert the return is ≤ ~220 chars (incl. the type prefix) and that the trailing portion of the input is absent.
findings.verifier_notes: The `_safe_err()` function (inspector/services/db/sync.py:71-73) correctly truncates exception messages to 200 chars, verified by manual testing with >200-char messages and token-bearing URLs. However, the existing tests (test_sync.py:127-139 and test_durability.py:52-68) only use short error messages ("network down" = 12 chars) and have a comment claiming "no token/url leakage" without asserting it. The tests do not verify the truncation boundary or token redaction, leaving this critical security behavior unvalidated in the test suite.

findings.title: db_seq-keyed admin/capability/catalog-JSON-bytes caches have no dedicated unit tests
findings.explanation: `public_reciters_cache` and `catalog_snapshot_cache` both have focused tests pinning hit-on-same-db_seq, miss-on-bumped-db_seq, and the returned-instance contract. The four sibling db_seq-keyed caches (admin_users, admin_requests, capability_matrix, catalog_json_bytes) implement the same pattern but have no analogous tests. `admin_requests` additionally prunes entries from older db_seqs on every `set` (cache.py:789-790) — a documented invariant that's completely unverified.
findings.proposed_action: Promote the public-reciters / catalog-snapshot test pattern into a parametrized harness over all six db_seq-keyed caches: assert hit-iff-same-seq, miss after `invalidate_*`, and (for admin_requests) that setting at a newer db_seq evicts entries from older db_seqs.
findings.verifier_notes: The four untested db_seq-keyed caches (admin_users, admin_requests, capability_matrix, catalog_json_bytes) in inspector/services/storage/cache.py genuinely lack dedicated unit tests. The pattern they implement is identical to the tested public_reciters and catalog_snapshot caches, yet only those two have focused test coverage (test_public_reciters_cache.py, test_catalog_snapshot_cache.py) verifying hit-on-same-db_seq, miss-on-bumped-db_seq, and returned-instance contracts. The four untested caches are only referenced in conftest.py for fixture cleanup, never in actual test files. The cross-seq pruning in admin_requests (cache.py:789-790) is implemented correctly and documented (cache.py:774) but is indeed unverified by tests. However, the severity should be MODIFIED: these are admin-only low-frequency paths (users list is maintainer/owner-only, capability matrix is per-request), not high-frequency public paths like public_reciters, reducing the test value. The pruning invariant, while undocumented as a test, is correctly implemented and relatively straightforward to verify.

findings.title: `get_in_flight_jobs_cache` TTL expiry, kind-mismatch miss, and explicit-invalidate paths are unverified
findings.explanation: Three documented behaviours: (1) TTL=5s expiry on read, (2) cache miss when the requested `kinds` tuple differs from the stamped one, (3) explicit `invalidate_in_flight_jobs_cache()` drops the entry. None are directly tested. The only callsite test is in `routes/test_route_admin_releases.py` which exercises a higher layer.

findings.title: Module-import-time env mutation makes test ordering and isolation hard for new contributors
findings.explanation: Each persistence test mutates os.environ at import time (not via monkeypatch) to set INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET so the app import inside conftest.signed_in_client works. New contributors who add a test that imports `from app import app` early will inherit this implicit ordering: the secret is only ever guaranteed by the file they happen to be co-located with. The conftest could (a) install the default secret in a top-level autouse fixture, (b) document the boot ordering, or (c) lazy-import the app. The duplication is one symptom; the deeper issue is that the test suite's app-boot contract is implicit and undocumented.
findings.proposed_action: Centralise the session-secret bootstrap in conftest.py and add a one-line docstring explaining the import-order constraint.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is confirmed but severity should be modified. Evidence: (1) All 29 test files repeat the identical `os.environ.setdefault("INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET", "0" * 64)` at module import time (lines 10-15 in test_detailed_schema.py, test_segments_json.py, test_save_clears_ignores.py, test_uid_backfill.py and elsewhere). (2) conftest.py::signed_in_client fixture (line 310) imports `from app import app` INSIDE the fixture function, requiring the env var to be pre-set. (3) The root cause is real: `get_session_secret()` is called at request time by _serializer() (auth.py:233), and if tests import app before the secret is set, session encoding will fail at test runtime. However, (4) the actual isolation risk is LOWER than claimed: app.py itself does not call get_session_secret() at import time (only inside request handlers), so test reordering alone won't cause import-time failures—only runtime failures if a test tries to encode a session without the secret. Proposed action is sound (centralize in conftest fixture) but severity should be MEDIUM→LOW since the failure mode is runtime (test that uses signed_in_client without setting secret) not import-time ordering chaos. Duplication is the primary concern, not isolation.
