A test adding a case like _FakeBackend({static_refs.QPC_BUCKET_PATH: b'not gzip data'}) and asserting load_qpc_bytes() == b'' would cover this genuine gap.

findings.title: static_refs: bucket backend raising non-FileNotFoundError is uncovered
findings.explanation: The except Exception in load_qpc_bytes is wired specifically to degrade on bucket transient failures (network, auth, throttling) — yet the tests only exercise the StorageNotFound-equivalent path (FileNotFoundError from the fake). A test where the fake raises e.g. RuntimeError('network down') and the function returns b"" instead of propagating would lock that intent in.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test where _FakeBackend.read_bytes raises a non-FileNotFoundError exception (e.g. RuntimeError) and assert load_qpc_bytes() returns b''.
findings.verifier_notes: The `_FakeBackend` mock in test_reference_resource_bytes.py only raises FileNotFoundError (lines 23-27), never exercising the broader `except Exception` path in static_refs.py:69 that explicitly degrades on bucket transient failures. The BucketBackend.read_bytes() (hf_bucket.py:354-368) can raise unhandled exceptions from hffs.cat_file() which flow to the exception handler. The test gap is real: a test where _FakeBackend raises RuntimeError/IOError and assert load_qpc_bytes() returns b'' would lock the graceful degradation intent. However, the severity remains low because the fallback is correct, the code is defensive by design (never raise), and production usage would surface regressions.

findings.title: Audit-spec code-under-test paths don't exist
findings.explanation: The audit task lists code under test as `inspector/services/reference/resource.py` and `inspector/services/reference/validator.py`. Neither file exists — the test file actually imports `services.storage.static_refs` and `services.reference.timestamps`. The `services/reference/` package contains `public_state.py`, `quran_refs.py`, `tajweed.py`, `timestamps.py` — there is no `resource.py` or `validator.py`. New contributors landing on this subsystem from the (presumably auto-generated) audit description will spend cycles hunting modules that don't exist. The test file's own docstring correctly identifies the real subjects.
findings.proposed_action: Update whatever generates the audit-subsystem map to point at the real modules (`services/storage/static_refs.py` for byte resolution, `services/reference/timestamps.py::_build_resource_bytes` for manifest resources). If a future `validator.py`/`resource.py` is planned, leave a redirect comment in `services/reference/__init__.py`.
findings.verifier_notes: The actual test file at inspector/tests/services/test_reference_resource_bytes.py correctly imports and tests services.storage.static_refs and services.reference.timestamps (confirmed in lines 15-16 of the test file and the actual module contents). These are the real code-under-test. The modules inspector/services/reference/resource.py and inspector/services/reference/validator.py do not exist in the codebase (verified via ls of inspector/services/reference/ directory which contains only: __init__.py, public_state.py, quran_refs.py, tajweed.py, timestamps.py). The test file's own docstring correctly identifies the real subjects: static_refs.load_qpc_bytes and _build_resource_bytes. The issue is that some audit specification/mapping system lists non-existent modules as the code-under-test, creating confusion despite the test itself being correct.

findings.title: Zero direct unit coverage for FilesystemBackend, BucketBackend, get_backend/set_backend/reset_backend, `_ensure_posix`
findings.explanation: `test_bucket_guard.py` is the only test in this subsystem and exercises just `resolve_bucket_repo`. Nothing directly tests: (1) `_ensure_posix` rejecting absolute paths, backslashes, or empty paths; (2) `FilesystemBackend` atomic-write tmp-cleanup-on-error, `iter_jsonl` with blank lines / missing file, `copy`/`move`/`delete` on dirs vs files, `list_dir('')` returning `_root` contents; (3) `BucketBackend._is_not_found` heuristic against `HfHubHTTPError(404)`, fsspec FileNotFoundError, and KeyError; (4) mount-vs-API switching (mount-exists fast path, mount-missing falls back to API, mount-set-but-doesn't-exist disables itself per line 325-331); (5) `write_bytes_direct` / `read_bytes_direct` bypassing the mount; (6) singleton lifecycle (`get_backend` caches, `reset_backend` re-reads env, `set_backend` swaps); (7) `INSPECTOR_BACKEND=filesystem` requiring `INSPECTOR_FILESYSTEM_ROOT`; (8) `auto_mount()` skip conditions (under pytest, behind proxy, prod-without-opt-in). These are not just edge cases — they are the core surface area of the substrate. Conftest uses `FilesystemBackend` extensively (lines 354, 438, etc.) but only indirectly through higher-level fixtures.
findings.proposed_action: Add a `test_filesystem_backend.py` covering atomic writes (and tmp-cleanup on write failure), JSONL append concurrency, list_dir/copy/move/delete dir-vs-file semantics, and StorageNotFound paths. Add a `test_backend_factory.py` covering the singleton (cache + reset + filesystem-root requirement). Add unit tests for `_ensure_posix`. For `BucketBackend`, at minimum test `_is_not_found` against fake exceptions, and the mount-vs-API decision (mount-set-but-missing → mount cleared), via monkeypatching `huggingface_hub` imports.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is correct: test_bucket_guard.py only tests resolve_bucket_repo(). While FilesystemBackend is extensively USED indirectly by conftest.py fixtures (lines 354, 438) in integration tests, there are zero DIRECT unit tests for: (1) FilesystemBackend edge cases (tmp cleanup on error, JSONL blank lines, list_dir(''), copy/move/delete on dirs), (2) _ensure_posix validation (backslashes, empty paths), (3) BucketBackend._is_not_found against real exception types, (4) mount-vs-API switching logic, (5) write_bytes_direct/read_bytes_direct, (6) auto_mount() skip conditions. The smoke test (_storage_smoke.py) exercises some paths but is a standalone manual script, not pytest-integrated. Conftest uses these backends extensively but only indirectly—if a backend method has a bug that doesn't affect the happy path (e.g., incorrect tmp cleanup on write error, wrong exception mapping), it won't be caught. This is a real, significant gap in direct unit test coverage for critical substrate code.

findings.title: `_clear(monkeypatch)` helper is private to this file but pattern is reusable
findings.explanation: `_clear()` resets the three guard-related env vars. It's repeated at the top of every test (lines 28, 33, 39, 45, 51, 58, 65). Each call site is correct, but every test calls it identically — this is a textbook autouse-fixture candidate. The cost of the current shape is minor (small file), but the convention across the broader suite is to promote shared env-clearing helpers into a fixture; e.g. `test_route_auth.py` and `test_ts_webhook.py` likewise scope env-clearing per-test rather than as fixtures.
findings.proposed_action: Convert `_clear` to an `@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)` that clears those three env vars before every test in the module. Removes the seven manual call sites without changing semantics.
findings.verifier_notes: The `_clear(monkeypatch)` helper in test_bucket_guard.py (lines 18-24) is called identically 7 times at the start of distinct tests. This is a textbook autouse-fixture candidate that follows established patterns in the suite (e.g., test_token_auth.py's `_clear_token_cache` autouse fixture). The repetition is avoidable, and promoting it to `@pytest.fixture(autouse=True)` removes boilerplate without changing semantics. The finding's evidence citations are somewhat misleading (test_route_auth.py's _clear_state is a no-op; test_ts_webhook.py doesn't use a helper), but the core recommendation is valid and aligns with codebase conventions.

findings.title: `iter_jsonl` corrupt-line and blank-line behaviour is unpinned
findings.explanation: Both backends iterate JSONL by stripping each line and feeding non-empty lines to `orjson.loads`. Per CLAUDE.md, append-only `edit_history.jsonl` / `edit_history_peaks.jsonl` round-trip through Pydantic models — corrupt lines should raise rather than skip. Today, the behavior on a corrupt line is to raise (which is correct), but on a blank line (e.g. trailing newline after the last append) the iterator silently skips, which is what you want. Neither path is tested, so a future change adding lenient orjson handling could silently drop records. Schema round-trip coverage gap also flagged for `edit_history.jsonl` / `edit_history_peaks.jsonl` shape per CLAUDE.md guidance.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests pinning: (1) `iter_jsonl` over an empty file yields nothing without raising; (2) trailing newline after a valid record is tolerated; (3) embedded blank lines are skipped; (4) a corrupt mid-stream line raises `orjson.JSONDecodeError`.
findings.verifier_notes: Both `FilesystemBackend.iter_jsonl` (lines 181-192) and `BucketBackend.iter_jsonl` (lines 389-400) exhibit the claimed behavior: empty lines are skipped, trailing newlines tolerated, corrupt JSON raises orjson.JSONDecodeError. Manual testing confirms all four edge cases work as expected. However, the behavior is only smoke-tested (happy path with 3 records in `_storage_smoke.py` lines 63-72), not unit-tested with dedicated edge-case tests. The lack of pinned unit tests creates a real regression risk: future changes to orjson handling or the iteration logic could silently break the contract. Per CLAUDE.md line 137, append-only `edit_history.jsonl` / `edit_history_peaks.jsonl` should round-trip through Pydantic models, but production code (`history_query.py` line 93, `peaks_history.py` line 196) bypasses validation entirely and collects raw dicts. The proposed tests are valuable: they document the contract and prevent future regressions, even though current behavior is correct.

findings.title: `BucketBackend._bucket_upload` cache-invalidation contract unpinned
findings.explanation: After every upload, `_bucket_upload` calls `hffs.invalidate_cache(self._bucket_uri(path))` and falls back to `invalidate_cache()` if that errors. The comment (line 411-412) says this is required for read-after-write consistency inside the same process. A regression that drops the invalidation call would silently break post-save reads — a high-cost bug — but there is no test verifying this contract.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that monkeypatches `huggingface_hub.batch_bucket_files` and `huggingface_hub.hffs` with stand-ins, then asserts that after `write_bytes_atomic` (mount=None code path), `hffs.invalidate_cache` was called with the bucket URI. Also assert fallback to no-arg `invalidate_cache()` when the path-specific call raises.
findings.verifier_notes: BucketBackend._bucket_upload (line 404-419 in inspector/services/storage/hf_bucket.py) calls hffs.invalidate_cache() after bucket writes to ensure read-after-write consistency. The code comment (lines 411-412) explicitly states this is required. However, the standard pytest test suite only uses FilesystemBackend, which doesn't exercise this code path. Only the manual smoke test (inspector/tests/smoke/_bucket_smoke.py) exercises BucketBackend, and it's not part of the standard test suite (requires manual invocation with HF_TOKEN). A regression that removed the invalidate_cache calls would not be caught by pytest—the contract is unpinned.

findings.title: `BucketBackend.list_dir` and `.exists` swallow all non-404 exceptions, returning a misleading false-empty
findings.explanation: Both methods catch any exception, log a warning, and return `False`/`[]`. A 500 from the HF API or an auth error becomes 'file doesn't exist' to the caller. For a substrate where 'doesn't exist' triggers fallback paths (e.g. CDN proxy when bucket audio is absent), this can mask real outages as silent missing-data. Whether this is a bug depends on caller expectations, but at minimum the contract is undocumented and unpinned by tests.
findings.proposed_action: Decide whether transient errors should bubble (probably yes for 5xx) or surface as a distinct exception class. If kept as-is, document explicitly and pin with a test that verifies log emission for non-404 errors.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified through code inspection. BucketBackend.exists() and .list_dir() suppress non-404 exceptions by catching all errors and returning False/[], logging a warning, while read_bytes() properly re-raises non-404 errors. This inconsistency masks transient failures (5xx, auth errors) as "file doesn't exist" to callers. FilesystemBackend never encounters HTTP errors, so the interface contract is violated. No tests pin the suppression behavior, indicating it's unintentional. Impact: scripts like backfill_boundary_adj.py that call list_slugs() -> list_dir() could silently proceed with empty reciter lists on API outages. File: inspector/services/storage/hf_bucket.py:511-515 (exists), 531-535 (list_dir).

findings.title: monkeypatch parameter declared but never used in split-group index test
findings.explanation: test_split_group_index_byte_equal_after_save_append accepts the monkeypatch fixture in its signature but never patches anything. The whole test operates on the in-process cache via public set_/pop_ helpers, so no monkeypatching is required. It's refactor litter from an earlier shape of the test.
findings.proposed_action: Drop the monkeypatch parameter from the test signature.
findings.verifier_notes: The test `test_split_group_index_byte_equal_after_save_append` at inspector/tests/services/test_cache_invariants.py:123 accepts a `monkeypatch` parameter but never invokes it. The test body (lines 126-168) exclusively uses cache public methods (`set_seg_history_batches`, `pop_seg_history_batches`, `pop_seg_split_group_index`) and the `build_split_group_index` function. No environment variables are patched, no objects are mocked. The parameter is unused and the test requires no monkeypatching. This is clearly refactor litter from an earlier test shape.

findings.title: Phase 3 pops the split-group index twice with no intervening write
findings.explanation: Line 146 pops _seg_split_group_index, then line 147 re-sets _seg_history_batches (which does NOT touch the derived index cache), then line 152 pops the derived index a second time. The second pop is a no-op — the entry was already absent. Either line 146 or line 152 should be removed for clarity.
findings.proposed_action: Keep one pop_seg_split_group_index call (the one immediately before the rebuild) and remove the redundant one.
findings.verifier_notes: Lines 146 and 152 in inspector/tests/services/test_cache_invariants.py both call cache.pop_seg_split_group_index(slug). Line 147 calls cache.set_seg_history_batches(), which per the cache module docstring (line 94-95) does NOT touch _seg_split_group_index. The _KeyedCache.pop() method at line 63-64 uses .pop(key, None), making it idempotent and safe. However, the second pop on line 152 is a no-op—the entry was already removed by line 146. The test passes and validates the correct invariant, but the redundant pop is dead code that confuses intent. Recommend keeping line 146 (pop before new state) and removing line 152.

findings.title: _SEG_CACHE_NAMES in conftest omits _seg_history_peaks_response
findings.explanation: The conftest _SEG_CACHE_NAMES tuple lists the seg caches that tmp_reciter_dir clears between tests. _seg_history_peaks_response is defined in cache.py (a per-reciter _KeyedCache holding serialized response bytes) and is invalidated by invalidate_seg_caches in production, but the test-time cleaner doesn't touch it. Tests that hit the history-peaks response route and rely on a clean slate could see cross-test bleed if a previous test installed a cached body for the same slug. The fix is to add _seg_history_peaks_response to the tuple (it has the same _KeyedCache.clear() interface as its siblings).
findings.proposed_action: Add '_seg_history_peaks_response' to inspector/tests/conftest.py:_SEG_CACHE_NAMES.
findings.verifier_notes: Production code at inspector/services/storage/cache.py:306 explicitly pops _seg_history_peaks_response on invalidate_seg_caches(), but test fixture at inspector/tests/conftest.py:362-376 omits it from _SEG_CACHE_NAMES tuple used to clear caches between tests. The cache comment at cache.py:104-107 confirms it holds serialized response bytes that should be invalidated on JSONL append. Cross-test bleed is real: successive tests using same reciter slug would see stale cached response bytes from prior test if different data was installed.

findings.title: _SingletonCache class has no direct test coverage
findings.explanation: The test file directly exercises _KeyedCache LRU semantics but the sibling _SingletonCache primitive (used by ~10 callers: _phoneme_sub_pairs, _qf_content_token, _qf_token_cooldown, _word_counts, _single_word_verses, _qpc, _dk, _dk_words_flat, _surah_info_lite, _public_reciters indirectly) has no get/set/clear contract test. It's a trivial class but it's a public extension point — clearing it (which set/clear/get interactions e.g. None replacement) is worth a focused unit.
findings.proposed_action: Add a small parametrized test that pokes get→None, set→get round-trip, and clear→None for _SingletonCache to lock the contract.
findings.verifier_notes: _SingletonCache (cache.py:22-35) has no dedicated unit test, though its methods ARE exercised indirectly via test fixtures (_clear_qf_cache in test_qf_content_audio.py lines 45-53 calls .clear() directly, and tests call .set()/.get() through wrapper functions). The contract is implicitly verified through fixture cleanup and test assertions, but no focused parametrized unit test exists to lock get→None, set→get round-trip, and clear→None explicitly. Severity is correctly assessed as low since the class is trivial (3 one-liner methods) and its contract is working. Proposed action (parametrized test poking the three operations) is reasonable but optional given the code simplicity.

findings.title: _PEAKS_RESPONSE_CACHE LRU + pop_reciter_peaks_response_cache untested at primitive level
findings.explanation: The 50-entry _PEAKS_RESPONSE_CACHE is the only handwritten (non-_KeyedCache) LRU in this module: it uses get→move_to_end (read-promotes-on-hit, opposite of _KeyedCache) and a separate lock. Its LRU semantics, the per-reciter pop_reciter_peaks_response_cache filter, and clear_peaks_response_cache are exercised only via integration tests (test_route_peaks.py touches the survives-invalidate_seg_caches case but not eviction). Worth a focused unit covering: 50-entry overflow eviction, read-promotion, pop-by-reciter only drops keys whose first tuple element matches.
findings.proposed_action: Add unit tests against get_peaks_response_cache/set_peaks_response_cache/pop_reciter_peaks_response_cache that lock in (a) read-promotes-on-hit semantics, (b) 50-entry LRU eviction, (c) per-reciter selective pop.
findings.verifier_notes: The _PEAKS_RESPONSE_CACHE (lines 395-431 in cache.py) implements read-promotion LRU semantics (get→move_to_end) that differ from _KeyedCache (which does NOT promote on read). The 50-entry LRU eviction is never tested in isolation at the primitive level. Integration tests in test_route_peaks.py (lines 102-147) exercise the cache through the HTTP route but do not trigger the 50-entry overflow condition. Unit tests in test_cache_invariants.py thoroughly cover _KeyedCache LRU behavior but do not cover _PEAKS_RESPONSE_CACHE. The conftest.py fixture (line 401) calls clear_peaks_response_cache() but does not test its behavior. Per-reciter pop filtering is exercised via the route but not as a focused unit test. The gap is real: LRU eviction semantics at the 50-entry ceiling are untested at the primitive level.

findings.title: _jobs_in_flight TTL + kinds-keying cache has no direct test
findings.explanation: _jobs_in_flight is a TTL+kinds-tagged singleton cache that wraps an external HF Jobs API call. It has three correctness gates (None on cold, None on kinds mismatch, None on TTL expiry) plus an explicit invalidator. None of these are exercised. A regression that flips the equality check on cached_kinds, or skips the TTL comparison, would silently serve stale or cross-kinds data.
findings.proposed_action: Add unit tests pinning: cold = None; same-kinds within TTL = value; different-kinds = None; stale (monkeypatched _time.time) = None; invalidate = None.
findings.verifier_notes: The three correctness gates in get_in_flight_jobs_cache (lines 855-861) are untested: (1) None on cold cache—implicitly covered but not directly verified; (2) None on kinds mismatch (cached_kinds != kinds)—NO unit test exercises different kinds values; (3) None on TTL expiry (time.time() - stamped_at > 5.0)—NO test monkeypatches _time.time to verify TTL logic. Invalidation is called in production (timestamps_jobs.py:306,526) but never tested. Integration test test_status_in_flight_slug_is_bucketable mocks list_in_flight_jobs() completely, bypassing the cache. Proposed unit tests (cold, same-kinds within TTL, different-kinds, stale, invalidate) are all missing. conftest._substrate_db does not clear _jobs_in_flight between tests, risking cross-test bleed (though keyed by kinds tuple mitigates in practice).

findings.title: db_seq-keyed caches (public_reciters, catalog_snapshot, catalog_json_bytes, admin_users, admin_requests, capability_matrix) not unit-tested at the cache primitive level
findings.explanation: All db_seq-stamped caches share the same shape: get returns value iff stored seq matches the asked seq, else None. The file documents this contract as the self-invalidation mechanism (any committed write bumps db_seq → transparent miss). There are integration tests for the wrappers (test_public_reciters_cache.py, test_catalog_snapshot_cache.py) but no primitive-level test of the get-when-seq-stale path for catalog_json_bytes, admin_users, admin_requests, capability_matrix. _admin_requests in particular has eviction logic — set_admin_requests_cache prunes entries from older db_seqs — that's worth pinning.
findings.proposed_action: Add a parametrized unit per db_seq-cache asserting: get(seq=N) after set(seq=N) returns the value; get(seq=N+1) after set(seq=N) returns None; invalidate clears. For admin_requests, also assert older-seq entries are pruned by set.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding correctly identifies a gap in primitive-level unit test coverage. While public_reciters and catalog_snapshot have dedicated tests (test_public_reciters_cache.py, test_catalog_snapshot_cache.py), the four other db_seq-keyed caches (catalog_json_bytes, admin_users, admin_requests, capability_matrix) only have integration-level tests through routes and services (test_static_catalog.py, test_users_read.py, test_route_requests.py, test_capabilities.py). There are no standalone unit tests that directly verify: (1) get returns value when seq matches, (2) get returns None when seq differs, (3) invalidate clears the cache, or (4) for admin_requests, the pruning of old db_seq entries. conftest.py shows these caches are invalidated between tests, confirming they exist and are used, but lack primitive-level coverage alongside the other two caches. Severity is appropriate: medium (integration tests prove correctness but primitive tests would pin the contract more directly).

findings.title: invalidate_audio_manifest_cache clears both slug-keyed caches but isn't covered here
findings.explanation: invalidate_audio_manifest_cache clears BOTH _audio_manifest AND _audio_manifest_url_index — the comment notes this is to prevent a stale sidecar from leaking old URLs after a re-extraction. test_manifest_invalidation.py covers manifest invalidation at a higher level but the cache-invariants file (which owns the LRU + paired-cache invariants) doesn't lock in the paired-clear contract.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that pre-populates both _audio_manifest and _audio_manifest_url_index for two slugs, calls invalidate_audio_manifest_cache(), and asserts both caches are fully drained for all slugs.
findings.verifier_notes: The code at cache.py:537-544 defines invalidate_audio_manifest_cache() which calls clear() on both _audio_manifest and _audio_manifest_url_index (paired caches). While this function IS exercised by the test_manifest_invalidation.py tests (which invoke timestamps.invalidate() which calls this function), there is NO direct test that verifies both caches are actually emptied. test_cache_invariants.py owns the cache-invariant testing (as evidenced by its module docstring and existing LRU eviction tests), making it the appropriate location to add a test that explicitly pre-populates both caches for multiple slugs, calls invalidate_audio_manifest_cache(), and asserts both are fully drained. The paired-cache contract (that invalidating one requires invalidating the other) is documented in the code comment but not locked in by a test in the cache-invariants file.

findings.title: _KEYED_CACHE_LRU_MAX default (20) and its boundary not exercised
findings.explanation: All _KeyedCache tests construct kc = _KeyedCache(max_size=3). The production default _KEYED_CACHE_LRU_MAX = 20 is the value every cache uses in practice. A regression that changed the default (or removed the cap argument default) wouldn't be caught. Worth a one-line test that instantiates _KeyedCache() with no args and verifies an entry survives at size 20 but not 21.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that verifies _KeyedCache() defaults to the 20-entry ceiling (e.g., set 20 keys, all readable; set a 21st, oldest evicted).
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is confirmed. Production creates 19+ _KeyedCache instances with no arguments (cache.py:80-514), relying on the default max_size=_KEYED_CACHE_LRU_MAX=20. The test suite only exercises max_size=3 (test_cache_invariants.py:176-216). A regression changing _KEYED_CACHE_LRU_MAX or removing the default parameter would not be caught. The LRU mechanism is tested correctly, but the specific boundary (20) used in production is untested. The conftest autouse fixtures do not clear per-reciter caches between tests, so cache isolation during tests relies on explicit invalidation that the cache-invariants test does not use.

findings.title: Module docstring claims 'keeps the parsed JSONL list in step with disk' but the tests never touch disk
findings.explanation: The header docstring sells the file as covering 'append_history_batch keeps the parsed JSONL list in step with disk so the next reader doesn't re-parse'. In reality every test in this file is pure in-memory — no edit_history.jsonl is written, no parse_history_for_reciter is called from a cold-cache scenario through the production path (data_dir.iter_edit_history). The convention elsewhere (see test_resolved_by_edit.py:378) wires through invalidate_seg_caches with a real fixture. The disk-parity claim should either be backed by a test or removed from the docstring.
findings.proposed_action: Either tighten the docstring to 'covers the in-memory cache primitives' or extend the test to cold-load through parse_history_for_reciter using a tmp_reciter_dir fixture.
findings.verifier_notes: The module docstring (lines 1-13 of test_cache_invariants.py) claims to cover "append_history_batch keeps the parsed JSONL list in step with disk" but the tests use only in-memory cache operations (cache.set_seg_history_batches, cache.get_seg_history_batches, cache.pop_seg_history_batches). No test writes to edit_history.jsonl or calls parse_history_for_reciter in a cold-cache scenario. The actual disk-sync validation exists in test_resolved_by_edit.py:349-389 (uses tmp_reciter_dir fixture, writes to disk, calls invalidate_seg_caches, triggers parse_history_for_reciter). The docstring should describe what THIS file tests (in-memory cache primitives), not the full disk-sync contract.

findings.title: Backfill SQL pulls from role_assignments.granted_at but no test exercises that source
findings.explanation: The CTE in 0003_backfill_first_seen.sql unions four sources (role_assignments.granted_at, claims.claimed_at, requests.submitted_at, transitions.ts). test_first_seen_backfill covers transitions (test_pulls_back_to_earliest_transition, test_idempotent_and_only_backwards), requests (test_min_across_sources_request_wins) and claims (test_claim_source) but never seeds a role_assignments row with an earlier granted_at than the existing first_seen. A change that dropped role_assignments from the UNION would not fail any test.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that ensure_user()s a user, inserts a role_assignments row with an earlier granted_at, runs the backfill, and asserts first_seen pulls back to granted_at. Mirrors the shape of test_claim_source.
findings.verifier_notes: The backfill SQL file /inspector/services/db/migrations/0003_backfill_first_seen.sql:27 includes role_assignments.granted_at as a union source. The test file /inspector/tests/admin/test_first_seen_backfill.py contains tests for transitions, requests, and claims sources but no test that seeds a role_assignments row with an earlier granted_at. The role_assignments table is real (0001_init.sql:39-52), grant_role() function is real (repo_access.py:140-160) and does insert into role_assignments with granted_at, but the test gap is genuine. A code change that removed role_assignments from the UNION would not fail any test.

findings.title: flush() day-boundary behaviour untested — counters collected on Day N can leak into Day N+1 row
findings.explanation: flush() resolves the target day from (now or datetime.now(...)), but _drain() unconditionally pulls today's in-memory bucket. If a tick fires just after UTC midnight, hits recorded during Day N are written into Day N+1's visitor_daily row. None of the existing tests exercise flush() with an explicit now= parameter (despite the signature exposing it), so this edge case is silently unprotected.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that records hits, then calls visitors.flush(now=<next-day timestamp>) and asserts the row lands under the appropriate day. Either confirm the current behaviour is intentional (and document) or fix flush to derive the day from the same instant at which the bucket was last reset.
findings.verifier_notes: The race condition is real. The _drain() function atomically reads the in-memory bucket, which can contain hits accumulated over an hour spanning a day boundary. Then flush() calls datetime.now(timezone.utc) AFTER draining, which can return a time on the next day if the flush daemon happens to wake after UTC midnight. This causes hits from Day N to be written to Day N+1's visitor_daily row. Example: if hits accumulate from 23:00 on Day N to 00:15 on Day N+1, and the flush tick fires at 00:15, those Day N hits will be attributed to Day N+1. The test gap is also confirmed—no existing tests call flush(now=...), leaving the edge case unprotected. The finding's proposed action is valid: capture the day before calling datetime.now(), or pass now= explicitly to flush() from the daemon loop. Severity (low) is appropriate given analytics are already acknowledged as approximate estimates. inspector/services/admin/visitors.py:122-132, inspector/tests/admin/test_visitor_analytics.py:20-65

findings.title: test_static_assets_skipped only exercises /assets/; /fonts/, /api/webhooks/, /healthz, /favicon.ico are uncovered
findings.explanation: _ANON_SKIP_PREFIXES is ('/assets/', '/fonts/', '/api/webhooks/') and _ANON_SKIP_PATHS is {'/healthz', '/favicon.ico'} (inspector/app.py:273-274). Only /assets/ is tested. A regression that removed /fonts/, /api/webhooks/, /healthz or /favicon.ico from the skip list would not be caught — webhooks in particular would start counting external traffic as anonymous user hits.
findings.proposed_action: Parametrize test_static_assets_skipped over every entry in _ANON_SKIP_PREFIXES and _ANON_SKIP_PATHS, or import them and iterate. One @pytest.mark.parametrize replaces the bespoke test with full coverage.
findings.verifier_notes: Test `test_static_assets_skipped` (inspector/tests/admin/test_visitor_analytics.py:89-92) exercises only the /assets/ prefix from the 5 skip entries defined in inspector/app.py:273-274. The other 4 entries (/fonts/, /api/webhooks/, /healthz, /favicon.ico) have no explicit test coverage. A refactoring that removed any of these from the skip lists would not be caught by the test suite, especially the critical /api/webhooks/ path which receives external HF job callbacks. The proposed parametrization solution is sound and would provide comprehensive regression protection.

findings.title: get_visitor_stats() recent[] field is not asserted by any test
findings.explanation: test_get_visitor_stats_includes_live only checks stats["today"]["anon_hits"]. The recent[] array (last 30 days of visitor_daily rows, materialized as VisitorDayStat instances) is never asserted. Removing or breaking repo_visitors.recent_days() would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Seed two non-today rows via repo_visitors.upsert_day with earlier dates, call get_visitor_stats(), and assert recent[] contains both with correct counts and in expected order (whatever recent_days promises).
findings.verifier_notes: The `recent` field is populated by `repo_visitors.recent_days()` at line 184 of visitors.py, but test_get_visitor_stats_includes_live() (lines 59-64 of test_visitor_analytics.py) only asserts today["anon_hits"] and never touches the recent array. The schema allows recent=[] (default_factory=list), so the test passes silently even if recent_days() is broken. No other tests in the file cover recent field validation. The fixture cleanup is proper (_reset_bucket, _substrate_db), so nothing prevents adding seed data with earlier dates to test the feature — the gap is real.

findings.title: start_flush_daemon idempotency + _flush_loop exception swallowing are uncovered
findings.explanation: start_flush_daemon() is documented as idempotent (gated by _FLUSH_STARTED) and _flush_loop swallows exceptions via logger.exception. No test exercises either: a regression that started a second daemon thread on a second call, or that re-raised on a flush() failure (crashing the daemon silently), would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that calls start_flush_daemon() twice and asserts only one thread is alive (or that the second call is a no-op via state inspection). Optionally monkeypatch flush() to raise once and assert the loop continues — though that requires shorter sleep tunables.
findings.verifier_notes:
The finding is confirmed. Code analysis shows:

1. IDEMPOTENCY: The `start_flush_daemon()` function has a working guard (`if _FLUSH_STARTED: return` at line 145), preventing a second call from starting another thread. However, NO direct unit test exercises this idempotency. The guard is correct and simple, but a test would provide defense in depth.

2. EXCEPTION HANDLING: The `_flush_loop()` function intentionally swallows exceptions via `try/except` with logging (lines 157-160). This is correct daemon practice (log + continue to avoid crashing the app). NO test verifies this behavior persists.

3. TEST COVERAGE: Flask integration tests do import the app, which calls `start_flush_daemon()` once (if `INSPECTOR_VISITOR_ANALYTICS=1`), but there is no direct unit test of the function itself. The `_reset_for_test()` fixture only resets the bucket state, not the global `_FLUSH_STARTED` flag.

The test gaps are real and verifiable (no test file calls `start_flush_daemon()` directly per grep search). The proposed test actions (call twice + verify idempotency, monkeypatch flush() to raise) are valid and would catch regressions.

SEVERITY ASSESSMENT: The risk is genuinely LOW because this is single-call bootstrap code unlikely to regress, but the test gap is measurable and the finding is accurate.

findings.title: test_identity_recency imports a private _serde module
findings.explanation: from services.db import _serde, repo_access — reaching into the underscored serde module to call _serde.now(). The neighbouring tests (test_users_read.py:6, test_first_seen_backfill.py implicitly) also use _serde; it is the dominant pattern within services/db tests, but the leading underscore signals package-private. Either accept that _serde.now is part of the test API (and rename / re-export under a public path) or have tests build their own datetime.now(timezone.utc).
findings.proposed_action: If _serde.now/to_iso are intended public test affordances, re-export them under services.db (drop the underscore) or services.db.testing. Otherwise have tests construct datetime.now(timezone.utc) inline.
findings.verifier_notes: Verdict should remain "modify" because: (a) the severity is correct but (b) the proposed action misfires. Change from "have tests construct datetime.now(timezone.utc) inline" to "document _serde.{now,to_iso} as intentional test affordances in CLAUDE.md testing section, OR re-export them under services.db without underscore for clarity". The issue is convention visibility, not correctness.

findings.title: maybe_touch_entry returns True for a missing users row even though nothing was written, and still opens a durable_transaction (bucket upload) per call
findings.explanation: maybe_touch_entry() returns True whenever it enters the durable_transaction block, regardless of whether touch_last_entry actually updated a row. touch_last_entry is UPDATE-only (repo_access.py:59-65), so for an absent users row it affects 0 rows. The test test_maybe_touch_entry_missing_row_does_not_raise actually asserts this behaviour (returns True, no last_entry_at stored) — i.e. the contract is 'returns True means we entered the write path' not 'returns True means we wrote'. The docstring says 'Returns True if it wrote' which contradicts the actual behaviour. Additionally, durable_transaction() in the no-op path still bumps db_seq and triggers a bucket upload for an UPDATE-affects-0-rows path; for a pre-feature signed-in user every /api/me hit produces a wasted full-file DB upload until they re-login.
findings.proposed_action: Either tighten the implementation to skip the durable_transaction when the row is missing (cheap SELECT first, no write/upload if absent) and align the docstring; or update the docstring to match the actual semantics ('returns True if it took the write path; may be a no-op UPDATE'). The current state silently incurs a per-request bucket upload for absent users.
findings.verifier_notes: The code genuinely returns True when entering durable_transaction for a missing user row, despite the docstring stating "Returns True if it wrote" (visitors.py:49). The UPDATE-only touch_last_entry affects 0 rows for absent users (repo_access.py:59-65), but durable_transaction unconditionally calls mark_durable()->upload() on exit (sync.py:382-383), triggering a bucket upload for each /api/me hit from pre-feature users. The test test_maybe_touch_entry_missing_row_does_not_raise explicitly validates this behavior (returns True, no row written), and with _SYNC_ENABLED=True in production, this incurs wasted full-file DB uploads per request.

findings.title: set_role() noop short-circuit returns {ok, role, noop} but non-noop returns {ok, member} — inconsistent wire shape
findings.explanation: When the target role equals the current role, set_role() returns {ok: True, role: <role>, noop: True} (users.py:61-62). For a grant/update it returns {ok: True, member: <member-dump>}. The demote-to-contributor branch returns yet a third shape {ok: True, role: 'contributor'} (no member, no noop). test_noop_same_role asserts both 'noop' and 'role' but never that 'member' exists, so the inconsistency is endorsed. A FE client that always reads body.member will crash on noop or demote.
findings.proposed_action: Either include the existing Member (repo_access has the data — fetch and dump) in the noop and demote branches for shape parity, or have set_role() document the union explicitly so the FE knows to gate on body.noop / body.role before reading member.
findings.verifier_notes: The service function set_role() in users.py returns three inconsistent response shapes: noop returns {ok, role, noop}; demote returns {ok, role}; grant/update returns {ok, member}. This violates API contract expectations. However, the current UI layer mitigates risk by: (1) early-returning before calling setUserRole() when role is unchanged (UsersCompartment.svelte:48), (2) the HTTP client discards the response body entirely. The finding is real but practically low-risk in the current UI — it would affect programmatic API consumers. The test suite validates this inconsistency as expected behavior.

findings.title: Stubs for running_job_for/launch are wired on tests that reject before reaching them
findings.explanation: `test_generate_ts_rejects_under_review_not_marked_ready`, `test_generate_ts_rejects_awaiting_review`, and `test_generate_ts_unknown_slug_404` all call `_stub_launch(monkeypatch)`, but the route returns 409/404 well before `running_job_for` or `launch` are reached. The stub setup is dead code in these tests and makes it look as if launch could fire (it can't).
findings.proposed_action: Drop the `_stub_launch(monkeypatch)` call in the three negative-path tests — they reject upstream of the launcher. Keep stubs only on the launching tests.
findings.verifier_notes: The route's generate_timestamps function returns 404/409 before reaching the stubbed calls. Line-by-line flow: unknown slug → 404 at line 110; invalid state → 409 at lines 113-119; valid state → continues to line 123 (running_job_for). All three negative tests reject upstream of line 123, so their stubs are dead code. Positive tests need stubs and correctly use them.

findings.title: Set-superset assertion is redundant after the exact widx-list assertion
findings.explanation: Line 107 already pins the exact list `widxs == [1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5]`; the very next line then asserts `set(widxs) >= {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}`, which is implied by the exact-list assertion. Cosmetic noise — first time a reader has to wonder which of the two is the load-bearing check.
findings.proposed_action: Drop the `set(widxs) >= {…}` assertion (the exact-list line carries the full-coverage invariant); or, if the author wants the coverage assertion to survive list-shape changes, keep the set assertion and replace the exact-list assertion with the within-pass loopback contract only (e.g. assert the repeated `3, 4` subsequence appears in order).
findings.verifier_notes: The exact-list assertion `widxs == [1, 2, 3, 4, 3, 4, 5]` (line 107) mathematically guarantees that `set(widxs) >= {1, 2, 3, 4, 5}` (line 108) is true. Companion tests in qua_shared/tests/test_segment_shard_dedup.py (e.g., lines 81, 93, 153) follow a consistent pattern: they use only exact-list assertions without set-superset checks. The set assertion is genuinely redundant and adds no unique coverage validation beyond what the exact-list already provides. Severity assessment (low) is correct — this is cosmetic noise, not a functional issue.

findings.title: Unknown-slug noop test doesn't assert state is None — passes even if the function returned a phantom state
findings.explanation: `complete_timestamps_job` returns `{slug, state: None, released: False, reason: 'unknown slug'}` for an unknown slug, but the test only asserts `released is False` and `reason == 'unknown slug'`. If a regression caused the function to default `state` to something non-None (e.g. an inferred from-row crash path), the assertion would still pass.
findings.proposed_action: Add `assert out['state'] is None` to `test_complete_unknown_slug_is_noop`.
findings.verifier_notes: The function `complete_timestamps_job` documents returning {slug, state, released: bool, ...} (line 461 inspector/services/admin/timestamps_jobs.py). For unknown slugs, it explicitly returns state: None (line 469-470). However, test_complete_unknown_slug_is_noop (line 239-242 inspector/tests/services/test_timestamps_jobs.py) only asserts released and reason, not the state field. A regression that changed state from None to any non-None value would pass the test. Notably, test_complete_publishes_marked_ready (line 111) DOES assert the state field, showing the pattern exists elsewhere. The function returns state as JSON to callers (line 74 inspector/routes/webhooks/ts_jobs.py), making it part of the documented contract that should be verified.

findings.title: Not-marked-ready noop test doesn't assert the reason string
findings.explanation: `test_complete_noop_when_not_marked_ready` asserts the released flag and state, but not the `reason` discriminator (`'not marked-ready / wrong state'`). Asserting the reason locks the branch the noop came from — otherwise a future regression that takes the `if not _has_any_shard` branch (returning the same `released=False` shape with `reason='no shards'`) would pass this test.
findings.proposed_action: Add `assert out['reason'] == 'not marked-ready / wrong state'` (or the equivalent canonical string from the function) to pin the discriminator.
findings.verifier_notes: The test `test_complete_noop_when_not_marked_ready` (lines 199-209) asserts `released=False` and state, but omits asserting the `reason` discriminator. The code path (line 473-478) returns `reason="not marked-ready / wrong state"`, but this specific reason string is not verified. While the monkeypatch prevents reaching other noop branches in practice, the finding is valid because: (1) other similar noop tests in the file DO assert reason (lines 152, 194, 221, 242), (2) asserting reason catches test setup regressions defensively, and (3) it makes the test more precise. The severity (low) is appropriate—the practical test coverage is adequate, but the assertion should be added for consistency and defensive programming.

findings.title: No tests for _parse_ts_settings input-validation branches
findings.explanation: The route's body-parser raises `ValueError` (→ 400) for bad `beam`, bad `probe_beams` types, out-of-range `workers`, and Pydantic ValidationError on the resulting `TsJobSettings`. None of these are covered. A regression that loosens validation (e.g. allowing a negative `beam` or a list-of-strings `probe_beams` through) would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add 400-path tests: (a) `beam: 0` → 400 'beam must be a positive integer'; (b) `probe_beams: ['10']` → 400; (c) `workers: 0` / `workers: 100` → 400; (d) malformed body that produces a Pydantic ValidationError. Use the same `_stub_launch` plumbing so the stub is never reached.
findings.verifier_notes: The validation logic in _parse_ts_settings (lines 152-153, 154-155, 161-162, 174-175) is implemented correctly and functions as intended when tested manually. However, the current test suite (inspector/tests/routes/test_route_generate_timestamps.py) contains only 5 tests, all of which pass valid data and do not exercise any of the error paths. The route correctly catches ValueError at line 130-131 and returns 400 responses, but no test cases verify this behavior. Manual verification confirms: beam=0, probe_beams=['10'], workers=0, workers=100, and invalid batch_size all correctly raise ValueError. The gap is real: a regression loosening validation would not be caught because there are no HTTP-level 400-path tests for these input-validation branches.

findings.title: No test for the single-flight 409 path (running_job_for returns an id)
findings.explanation: All five route tests stub `running_job_for` to return None. The 409 returned when an in-flight job exists ('a timestamps job is already running' + the existing job_id in the response) — the load-bearing race guard documented in the route docstring — is not exercised.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that stubs `running_job_for` to return `'j_in_flight'` against a marked-ready or released seed, asserts 409, and asserts the response body carries `job_id='j_in_flight'`.
findings.verifier_notes: The 409 path when running_job_for returns a non-None id is not exercised. The route implementation (reviews.py:123-126) checks for in-flight jobs and returns 409 with job_id. All five tests stub running_job_for to always return None via _stub_launch (test_route_generate_timestamps.py:19-28), leaving the existing-job branch untested. This is a documented single-flight guard (timestamps-job.md:72, route docstring at line 103-106). Production code is correct; test gap is real and the proposed test is straightforward: stub running_job_for to return a job id against a marked-ready or released seed and assert 409 with the job_id in response.

findings.title: No test that a user lacking reciter.publish is rejected (inline require_capability_or_403)
findings.explanation: The route gates on TWO capabilities: `reviews.generate_timestamps` (decorator) and `reciter.publish` (inline). All existing tests sign in as `maintainer`, which the capability matrix grants both to by default. A future capability-matrix tweak (or an inline gate inversion) that revoked `reciter.publish` from maintainers would silently let the route through.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that signs in as a role granted `reviews.generate_timestamps` but NOT `reciter.publish` (likely via owner override on a contributor, or by stubbing `can()`) against a marked-ready row and asserts 403.
findings.verifier_notes: The inline `require_capability_or_403(user, "reciter.publish")` call at inspector/routes/admin/reviews.py:120-122 lacks test coverage. All existing tests (test_route_generate_timestamps.py) sign in as "maintainer", which holds both "reviews.generate_timestamps" (decorator) and "reciter.publish" (inline) by default. No test verifies that a user lacking "reciter.publish" is rejected with 403. Per capabilities.md convention and the pattern in test_route_permissions.py:106-124, capability gates should be explicitly tested, especially dual gates (decorator + inline). A future capability-matrix override revoking "reciter.publish" from maintainers would silently pass all existing tests, leaving the inline gate untested.

findings.title: cancel_job orchestrator has no tests (record reconciliation + dot notify + HF failure path)
findings.explanation: `cancel_job` calls `huggingface_hub.cancel_job`, then reconciles the durable record (only when it's running/unknown, idempotent on re-cancel), and lights the reviews-tab dot. None of these branches has direct coverage: HF-cancel raising → `{canceled: False, reason: str(exc)}`; unknown slug → `{canceled: False, reason: 'unknown slug'}`; existing terminal record → no record rewrite; running record → rewrite to status='canceled' + ended_at. The route is also untested.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests stubbing `huggingface_hub.cancel_job` and `read_job_record`/`_write_job_record` to cover: (a) HF raises → returns `canceled=False, reason=str(exc)`, no record write; (b) running record → rewritten with status='canceled' + ended_at; (c) terminal record → no rewrite (idempotent); (d) unknown slug → early return. Then add a route test for `/api/admin/reciters/<slug>/jobs/<job_id>/cancel` covering the 200 / 404 / 502 paths.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified that cancel_job orchestrator (lines 590-631 in inspector/services/admin/timestamps_jobs.py) and route handler (lines 191-209 in inspector/routes/admin/reviews.py) both exist but have zero test coverage. Coverage report shows lines 601-631 (orchestrator body) and 201-209 (route handler) are 0% covered. No tests found in inspector/tests/services/test_timestamps_jobs.py (292 lines, 14 tests, none for cancel_job) or any route tests. The implementation correctly handles: (a) HF API failures with exception catching, (b) unknown slug early returns, (c) record reconciliation only when status is running/unknown, and (d) dot notification via _note_job_finished. All documented error paths (404/502/200) and branches exist but untested.

findings.title: read_job_record / list_job_records have no tests (per-reciter→legacy fallback, missing stubs, TsJobRecord forward-compat)
findings.explanation: `_read_record_bytes` reads the per-reciter path then falls back to the pre-2026-05 legacy `jobs/ts/<job_id>.json` path. `read_job_record` model-validates with a fallback to raw JSON (forward-compat). `list_job_records` synthesizes a `{job_id, slug, type: 'ts', status: 'unknown'}` stub for any id missing a record. None of these branches is covered — and they're exactly the kind of layered fallback that silently regresses (e.g. the legacy fallback being dropped or the stub shape changing).
findings.proposed_action: Add service tests using `tmp_reciter_dir` (filesystem backend): write a record at the legacy path → `read_job_record` returns it; write at per-reciter path → wins over legacy; missing → `list_job_records` returns a minimal stub matching the documented shape; write a record with an unknown field → falls back to raw JSON without raising.
findings.verifier_notes: The functions `read_job_record`, `list_job_records`, and their internal helpers (`_read_record_bytes`) are actively used in production routes (/reciters/<slug>/jobs/<job_id>/record, /reciters/<slug>/ts-jobs) and admin scripts, but they are not directly tested. Existing tests in test_timestamps_jobs.py mock read_job_record via monkeypatch rather than exercising the real implementation. The critical untested paths are: (1) the per-reciter→legacy fallback chain in _read_record_bytes (lines 328-340), (2) the TsJobRecord model validation with raw JSON fallback for forward-compat (lines 343-354), and (3) stub synthesis for missing records in list_job_records (lines 357-371). These are exactly the layered fallbacks prone to silent regression. The proposed test approach using tmp_reciter_dir is sound.

findings.title: job_status non-terminal and fetch_job_logs failure paths are not tested
findings.explanation: The existing three tests cover the terminal backstop. The non-terminal path (status='running' → no record rewrite, no complete/note dispatch), the `fetch_job_logs` raising path (logs stay empty, log_truncated False), and the log-truncation path (`len(logs) > log_tail` → trims + sets log_truncated) are unverified.
findings.proposed_action: Add (a) a non-terminal test asserting no record write, no complete dispatch, and the returned dict shape; (b) a fetch_job_logs-raises test asserting `logs=[]` + `log_truncated=False` + status still reported; (c) a truncation test producing > log_tail lines and asserting `log_truncated=True`.
findings.verifier_notes: Verified by reading the test file (inspector/tests/services/test_timestamps_jobs.py) and the implementation (inspector/services/admin/timestamps_jobs.py:374-436). All three existing tests exercise only the terminal-status path (when status in _TERMINAL, lines 401-433 execute). findings.title: _has_any_shard is only exercised via monkeypatched stubs — never against the real backend

findings.title: Most /api/ts/* routes (shard, validation, resource, config, tajweed) and their gating are not covered

findings.title: running_job_for and _resolve_launched_job_id are untested
findings.explanation: Both helpers filter `list_jobs()` by labels `{task: 'timestamps', reciter: slug}` and apply status logic. `running_job_for` is the single-flight guard; `_resolve_launched_job_id` reconciles the transient run_job() id with the canonical id list_jobs reports. The label-filter, status interpretation, and 'list_jobs raises → return None safely' branches are unverified, and a regression that flipped the label key would silently let two concurrent jobs race the same shards.

The risk of a label-key typo silently breaking the single-flight guard is real but mitigated by safe fallback behavior.

findings.title: launch() env composition (beams/persist_audio/workers) and webhook URL/secret threading are untested

findings.title: 502 branch when orchestrator raises is not exercised
findings.explanation: ts_job_complete catches any Exception from complete_timestamps_job/note_timestamps_job_failed and returns 502 with the error string (so HF retries). No test verifies this — neither the success path nor the failure path. A regression that lets the exception bubble (e.g. turning the 502 into a 500) would not be caught.

findings.title: Alternate success status 'completed' is not tested
findings.explanation: _SUCCESS = ('succeeded', 'completed') accepts both terminal-success spellings. Tests only cover 'succeeded'. If someone tightens _SUCCESS to ('succeeded',) the 'completed' webhook path (used by qua_jobs in some terminal-state shapes) would silently regress.
findings.proposed_action: Parametrize the success test over ['succeeded', 'completed'] (and arguably ['Succeeded', 'COMPLETED'] to lock the .lower() normalization).
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is confirmed. Code inspection shows: (1) `_SUCCESS = ("succeeded", "completed")` in ts_jobs.py line 35 accepts both statuses; (2) test_ts_webhook.py line 73's `test_webhook_publishes_on_success` only tests "succeeded" path; (3) no test coverage for "completed" status; (4) while the current qua_jobs code (generate_timestamps.py) only sends "succeeded", the defensive inclusion of "completed" in _SUCCESS (matching HF's TERMINAL status set in admin_hf_publish.py:27) means the test coverage gap is real and unguarded. If the tuple is tightened to only "succeeded", the "completed" path would regress silently without test detection. Parametrizing the test over both success statuses is the correct fix to prevent this regression.

findings.title: Status normalization (strip + lower) is not asserted
findings.explanation: The handler does `(body.get('status') or '').strip().lower()`. No test verifies that 'SUCCEEDED' or '  succeeded\n' still publishes, or that whitespace-only slug/job_id is rejected as 400. A regression dropping .lower() would let a caller send 'Succeeded' and silently skip publishing.
findings.proposed_action: Add a parametrized test feeding 'SUCCEEDED', ' succeeded ', 'Completed' and asserting publish. Add a separate test feeding {slug: '  ', job_id: ''} and asserting 400.
findings.verifier_notes: The status normalization code at inspector/routes/webhooks/ts_jobs.py:59 is functionally correct and handles uppercase, whitespace-padded, and mixed-case status values properly via .strip().lower(). The validation at lines 60-61 correctly rejects whitespace-only slug/job_id. However, the test file (test_ts_webhook.py) only tests with lowercase, non-whitespace status values ('succeeded', 'failed'), leaving edge cases unverified. A regression dropping .lower() or .strip() would cause external callers sending 'SUCCEEDED' or ' succeeded ' to silently trigger the failure path instead of publishing, since the normalized status would not match _SUCCESS = ("succeeded", "completed"). This is a real test gap, though the production code is currently correct.

findings.title: Module-level os.environ.setdefault sets a global session secret on import
findings.explanation: The file mutates os.environ at import time. This is the dominant pattern across inspector/tests (~25 files do the same), so it's not a divergence — but a session-scoped autouse fixture (or a project-level conftest line) would centralise this and avoid every new route-test file repeating the incantation. Worth flagging because it leaks env state across the run and is invisible to readers. The webhook tests use monkeypatch for INSPECTOR_WEBHOOK_SECRET correctly, so the contrast (one env var module-set, the other test-scoped) is itself confusing.
findings.proposed_action: Promote `os.environ.setdefault('INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET', '0'*64)` to an autouse session-scoped fixture in inspector/tests/conftest.py (or set it in pyproject pytest_env / a pytest_configure hook), then delete the line from every route-test file.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is technically accurate: 30 files across inspector/tests (not 25) contain module-level os.environ.setdefault("INSPECTOR_SESSION_SECRET", "0"*64) that mutates environ at import time. The pattern exists because Flask app.py reads this secret at module import time, so it must be available before conftest fixtures execute. The proposed refactoring (move to conftest.py at module level or pytest_configure hook) is technically sound and would eliminate repetition. However, severity should be "informational" not "low" — this is intentional initialization order logic, not an isolation bug. The webhook tests already use monkeypatch correctly for INSPECTOR_WEBHOOK_SECRET (line 44), showing conscious use of both patterns. Recommend documenting the architectural reason (app imports at module level) in a conftest docstring rather than repositioning, or implement the refactoring with clear comments explaining the pytest import order dependency.

findings.title: ts_job_complete re-inlines secret check instead of calling _check_secret
findings.explanation: The same secret/HMAC compare logic lives twice in this file: inline at lines 46-54 inside ts_job_complete, and again as the shared helper _check_secret at lines 77-89 used by the other two webhooks. Any future change (e.g. add a constant-time delay on bad secret, add structured logging, switch to a header allowlist) must be applied in two places or the endpoints drift. Not a runtime bug today, but a classic DRY violation directly contradicting the project's KISS/DRY rules; surfacing as a low-severity bug because it WILL drift.
findings.proposed_action: Refactor ts_job_complete to call `ok, err = _check_secret(); if not ok: return err` like the sister handlers. The test matrix at test_ts_webhook.py covers the same observable behaviour, so the change should be drop-in.
findings.verifier_notes: The file inspector/routes/webhooks/ts_jobs.py contains the identical HMAC secret-check logic in two places: inline within ts_job_complete (lines 46-54) and as a shared helper _check_secret (lines 77-89). The helper was added in commit fbe1b02b when two new webhooks (hf_publish_complete and release_cut_complete) were introduced, but ts_job_complete was not refactored to use it. The project's best-practices.md explicitly requires DRY ("Extract repeated logic into shared functions" + "Avoid copy-paste implementation drift"). All tests in test_ts_webhook.py pass and cover the secret-check behavior, confirming that refactoring to call _check_secret would be a safe drop-in change. This is a legitimate DRY violation that will lead to implementation drift if future changes are needed.

findings.title: Top-of-file docstring contradicts test_manifest_self_heals (and the code) about the authoritative invalidation hook
findings.explanation: The module docstring claims the manifest is 'cached behind a `_built` flag with no other invalidation hook,' framing the post-commit `invalidate()` as the only safety net. But test_manifest_self_heals_on_db_seq_without_explicit_invalidate explicitly pins the db_seq check as 'the AUTHORITATIVE rebuild trigger,' and the timestamps module's own `_built_seq` comment (lines 44-50) agrees. The file's framing is internally inconsistent and will mislead a future reader who only reads the header.
findings.proposed_action: Rewrite the module docstring to lead with the db_seq check as the authoritative self-healer and describe `invalidate()` as the belt-and-braces explicit drop (mirroring the wording already in timestamps.py:322 and the test_3 docstring).
findings.verifier_notes: The module docstring (lines 1-9) claims the manifest is "cached behind a `_built` flag with no other invalidation hook" and frames the post-commit `invalidate()` drop as essential to prevent stale caching until restart. However, commit d9c36787 added db_seq-based self-healing, which is now documented as the "authoritative rebuild trigger" in three places: (1) timestamps.py lines 42-50 ("no reliance on the explicit post-commit `invalidate()`"), (2) timestamps.py lines 323-330 (invalidate() docstring: "db_seq check is the authoritative rebuild trigger; this explicit drop is retained... as a belt-and-braces hook"), and (3) the test's own docstring (line 73: "The db_seq check is the AUTHORITATIVE rebuild trigger"). The module docstring predates this architectural change and is now misleading. The test `test_manifest_self_heals_on_db_seq_without_explicit_invalidate` (lines 72-93) explicitly proves that invalidate() is not necessary for correctness — db_seq advancement alone triggers the rebuild. The proposed action to rewrite the module docstring with db_seq as primary and invalidate() as belt-and-braces is correct and mirrors existing code documentation.

findings.title: ts_manifest._built / _built_seq / _served_slugs / _manifest_bytes / _shard_lru / _resource_bytes are never reset between tests
findings.explanation: The autouse `_substrate_db` fixture invalidates several keyed caches (public_reciters, catalog_snapshot, admin_*, capability_matrix) but does NOT call `ts_manifest.invalidate()`. The module-level `_built`, `_built_seq`, `_manifest_bytes`, `_served_slugs`, `_shard_lru`, `_resource_bytes` carry across tests in pytest's single-process run. Today the suite is saved by the fact that `db.reset()` resets the db_seq counter to 0 each test and the test's first commit bumps to 1 — but if a future test happens to leave `_built_seq=1` and the next test's first manifest read also lands at seq=1, the stale `_served_slugs` from the previous test would survive (`rec_a` carrying over from test 1 into a later test that uses `rec_a` and expects it absent at warm-time would now pass spuriously). Test 3's pre-condition `assert 'rec_a' not in ts_manifest._served_slugs` is precisely the kind of assertion vulnerable to this kind of bleed. Reset is also the conventional pattern in this codebase (see `_invalidate_seg_caches` and the 6 cache clears in `_substrate_db`).
findings.proposed_action: Add `ts_manifest.invalidate()` (or a local autouse fixture that resets the four module-level globals) to the file. Or promote to `_substrate_db` in conftest alongside the other cache clears.
findings.verifier_notes: 1) Verdict: confirmed (real code issue), but severity downgrade to "low" not "medium". 2) Root cause: incomplete global declaration and missing explicit reset, not actual test isolation failure. 3) The explanation's claim that "if a future test leaves _built_seq=1 and the next test lands at seq=1, stale _served_slugs would survive" misses that each test gets a fresh DB file (seq resets to 0), so identical seq values across test boundaries are impossible.

findings.title: Monkeypatched spies use a cryptic tuple-index trick instead of a named closure
findings.explanation: Both spies are written as `lambda: (calls.append(1), real())[1]` / `lambda block: (calls.append(1), real_build(block))[1]`. The tuple-and-index pattern is opaque, and the rest of the test suite (e.g. `test_reference_resource_bytes.py`) uses straightforward lambdas / `def`-closures. The pattern saves one line but loses readability.
findings.proposed_action: Replace with a `def _spy(...)` that calls `real(...)` and returns. Two lines per spy, but unambiguous.
findings.verifier_notes: Severity: downgrade or reclassify as "style" (not "convention"). Proposed action: reframe as optional—the tuple trick is intentional and consistent, but maintainers may prefer explicit def-based spies for readability (will not save lines, only improve clarity). Remove the line-count claim.

findings.title: No test verifies that invalidate() clears _shard_lru, _resource_bytes, and the audio-manifest sidecar cache
findings.explanation: `invalidate()` does five things: drops `_built`, `_built_seq`, `_manifest_bytes`, clears `_shard_lru`, clears `_resource_bytes`, and calls `cache.invalidate_audio_manifest_cache()`. The current suite only pins the first via `_built is False`. A regression that removed the shard-LRU clear (the exact bug class this file exists to prevent) or the audio-manifest-cache passthrough (the explicit safety against stale URL templates on a re-extracted reciter — documented in timestamps.py:326-329) would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add tests that (a) warm the shard LRU via `shard_bytes`, call `invalidate`, assert `_shard_lru == {}`; (b) warm a `_resource_bytes` entry, call `invalidate`, assert `_resource_bytes == {}`; (c) spy `services.storage.cache.invalidate_audio_manifest_cache` and assert it's invoked exactly once.
findings.verifier_notes:
Verified that invalidate() at inspector/services/reference/timestamps.py:322-340 clears _shard_lru (line 336), _resource_bytes (line 337), and calls cache.invalidate_audio_manifest_cache() (line 340). The test suite in inspector/tests/services/test_manifest_invalidation.py:38-109 contains zero assertions validating these side-effects: test_transition_drops_manifest_cache only checks _built is False; test_transition_invokes_invalidate_hook only verifies the function was called (via spy), not what it does; no test warms _shard_lru or _resource_bytes or spies the audio-manifest cache call. The audio-manifest cache invalidation is documented as a critical safety net (timestamps.py:328-329) against stale sidecars leaking old URLs. A regression removing any of these three clears would not be caught.</parameter>
<parameter name="modifications">Severity and action are appropriate. This is a real, actionable gap in test coverage for documented safety invariants and essential cache clearing logic.</parameter>
</invoke>

findings.title: Concurrency / re-entry: the inside-lock re-check at timestamps.py:212-213 is unexercised
findings.explanation: The build path acquires `_lock`, then re-reads `_built` and `_built_seq` to bail if a peer just rebuilt at the same seq. Single-worker invariant means this is defence-in-depth, but if it regresses (e.g. someone removes the re-check), two concurrent threads would both rebuild and one would clobber the other's `_served_slugs`. Currently untested.
findings.proposed_action: Drive two threads through `_ensure_built` at the same seq under a mock that counts `_build_manifest_dict` calls; assert exactly one build despite two concurrent readers.
findings.verifier_notes: The re-check at timestamps.py:207-208 is real and necessary. Analysis: (1) Production uses gunicorn-gthread with -w 1, so single worker process but multiple request threads run concurrently; (2) Without the inside-lock re-check, concurrent threads reading stale `_built/_built_seq` before acquiring the lock would both attempt to rebuild at the same db_seq, causing duplicate builds; (3) The test suite has no concurrent threading test for this scenario (test_manifest_invalidation.py is entirely single-threaded); (4) The code comment explicitly documents this ("Re-check inside the lock; another thread may have just rebuilt at seq"), proving it's intentional defense-in-depth; (5) The single-worker enforcement (inspector/app.py:225 _assert_single_worker()) confirms that threading scenarios ARE expected within one process. This is a valid untested codepath that would regress if the re-check is removed. Proposed test action is sound: spawn two threads, mock _build_manifest_dict, confirm it's called exactly once despite concurrent entry at same seq.

findings.title: Baseline parity table covers only 21 of ~117 (capability, tier) cells
findings.explanation: The `_PARITY` tuple list — described as encoding 'the pre-capability hardcoded truth table' — asserts only 21 cells out of 39 capabilities x 3 tiers (~117 meaningful cells). Whole groups have zero parity coverage: requests/intake (`request.reject_hard`, `intake.accept`, `intake.probe`, `intake.resolve`), claims (`claim.mark_ready`, `claim.unmark_ready`, `claim.mark_ready_skip_gates`, `review.send_back`, `user.lookup`), roles (`users.view`), lifecycle (`reciter.unpublish`, `reciter.unlock_for_revision`, `reciter.discard`, `catalog.edit`), admin (`reviews.generate_timestamps`, `timestamps.view_unreleased`, `timestamps.view_validation`), and releases (`release.publish_hf`, `release.cut_gh`). The docstring claims 'If any of these flips, the migration silently changed authz' — but a flip in any uncovered cell would still pass tests.
findings.proposed_action: Auto-generate the parity table from `CAPABILITIES` itself: parametrize over every (cap.id, tier) cell where `cap.applicable(tier)` is True, asserting `caps.can(_caller(tier), cap.id) is cap.default_for(tier)`. This makes the parity check exhaustive by construction and self-updating when new capabilities are registered.
findings.verifier_notes: The baseline parity test covers only 21 of 78 applicable (capability, tier) cells. Verified by: (1) counting all capabilities (38 total) × tiers (3: anonymous, contributor, maintainer) and filtering for `cap.applicable(tier)` = 78 cells; (2) examining test_capabilities.py which explicitly parametrizes `test_baseline_parity` over only 21 hard-coded entries in `_PARITY`; (3) confirming that 20 capabilities (e.g., catalog.edit, claim.mark_ready, intake.accept, request.reject_hard, review.send_back, release.publish_hf, timestamps.view_unreleased, users.view, etc.) are completely absent from the parity list. The docstring says the test checks "the pre-capability hardcoded truth table" and detects regressions if any entry "flips" — but a flip in any of the 57 uncovered cells would silently pass this test. The resolver implementation IS exhaustive (resolve_grants() iterates all applicable cells), but the test suite does not validate all those defaults. Auto-generating the parity table from CAPABILITIES itself would make the test exhaustive and self-updating.

findings.title: `resolve_grants` db_seq cache invariants are uncovered
findings.explanation: `resolve_grants` is documented as 'cached on db_seq' and the module docstring claims 'a committed override write bumps db_seq and transparently invalidates the cache, so a toggle takes effect on the very next request with no restart'. `test_override_flips_then_resets` checks the externally observable behavior but doesn't verify the cache mechanism: it doesn't assert (a) the matrix is identity-cached across repeat calls at the same db_seq, (b) bumping db_seq replaces the cached value, (c) `invalidate_capability_matrix_cache()` forces a rebuild. A regression that disabled caching (e.g. dropping `seq = current_db_seq()` and always re-running the loop) would still pass every existing test.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test asserting `resolve_grants() is resolve_grants()` at the same db_seq (identity cache hit), and that after a `connection.transaction()`-wrapped override write the returned matrix object is a new instance reflecting the new override.
findings.verifier_notes: The cache mechanism is NOT covered by identity/mechanism tests. The autouse `_substrate_db` fixture clears the cache before each test, and `test_override_flips_then_resets` only verifies external observable behavior (capability toggles work), not the caching contract itself. A regression removing the `seq = current_db_seq()` line or the cache getter/setter would pass all existing tests because `resolve_grants()` rebuilds the same result each time. Unlike `catalog_service.snapshot()` which has explicit identity tests (`assert a is b is c`), there is no assertion that `resolve_grants()` returns the same object instance at the same db_seq, nor explicit verification that the cache is keyed/invalidated correctly. The finding is correct: cache invariants (a) identity-cached across repeat calls at same db_seq, (b) cache invalidation on db_seq bump, (c) `invalidate_capability_matrix_cache()` forcing rebuild are all untested. inspector/services/auth/capabilities.py:51-76; inspector/tests/services/test_capabilities.py:82-88; inspector/tests/conftest.py:142 confirms cache is cleared but not verified to work.

findings.title: `resolve_grants` filters for unknown cap_id / owner_only_fixed / inapplicable cells are uncovered
findings.explanation: Lines 69-73 of `capabilities.py` silently drop override rows whose `cap_id` is unknown, whose cap is `owner_only_fixed`, or whose `(cap, tier)` cell is inapplicable (e.g. anonymous on a non-anon cap). The owner-only-fixed branch is partially covered via `test_manage_permissions_is_owner_only_and_immutable`, but a stale cap_id row left over from a removed capability or an inapplicable anonymous override row (e.g. `_set_override('claim.acquire', 'anonymous', True)` in `test_anonymous_only_where_eligible`) only checks the resolver's anon-eligibility short-circuit at line 94, not the resolve_grants filter at line 71.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that (a) inserts an override row for an unknown cap_id and asserts `resolve_grants()` does not contain it / `can()` still raises ValueError for it, and (b) verifies the inapplicable-anon row does not appear as a key in the resolved matrix.
findings.verifier_notes: The filters at capabilities.py:69-73 that drop unknown cap_id, owner_only_fixed, and inapplicable cells are not directly tested. The existing tests (test_manage_permissions_is_owner_only_and_immutable and test_anonymous_only_where_eligible) verify end-to-end behavior via can() which has defensive short-circuits (lines 90-91 and 94-95), but they never call resolve_grants() directly to verify the matrix itself is clean. A true test would assert that resolve_grants() does not contain these filtered-out keys. This is a real gap: the contract in the docstring (line 52-57) states inapplicable cells are dropped, but this is not validated by tests. However, the impact is low because can() behaves correctly due to defense-in-depth checks.

findings.title: `test_registry_self_consistency` duplicates a module-level assert
findings.explanation: Line 126 asserts `len(CAPABILITIES_BY_ID) == len(CAPABILITIES)`, but the module itself already runs `assert len(CAPABILITIES_BY_ID) == len(CAPABILITIES), "duplicate capability id"` at import time (qua_shared/schemas/capabilities.py:398). Any duplicate id would fail collection before this test ran. The second assertion (every default_grants tier key is a real tier) is non-redundant in spirit but also already enforced by the Pydantic `_validate_shape` validator at qua_shared/schemas/capabilities.py:71-87 which rejects unknown tier keys with ValueError at model construction.
findings.proposed_action: Either remove the test (both invariants are validated at import time) or repurpose it to test something the registry doesn't self-enforce — e.g. that `MANAGE_PERMISSIONS` exists in the registry, or that every group label appears in `GROUP_ORDER`.
findings.verifier_notes: Both assertions in test_registry_self_consistency are provably redundant. Assertion #1 (line 126) duplicates the module-level assert at capabilities.py:398 which runs at import time, preventing module load if violated. Assertion #2 (lines 128-129) re-checks data that Pydantic's _validate_shape validator (capabilities.py:71-87) already enforced at model construction. No scenario exists where the test catches something the system doesn't already guarantee at import/construction time. The test provides zero additional validation value.

findings.title: Hardcoded event-name snapshot will fail-open on new gated events
findings.explanation: `test_event_capability_map_is_complete_and_valid` asserts the keys of `_EVENT_CAPABILITY` exactly equal a 16-element hardcoded literal set. The intent (per docstring) is 'a missing entry would un-gate a transition' — but the actual check is symmetric: adding a NEW correctly-gated event also fails. The forward-direction check at lines 139-141 (every mapping entry points to a real handler + a real capability) is the load-bearing one.
