The reverse-direction check makes the test a tripwire that every PR adding a gated transition has to update — without catching the actual concerning failure (an event in `_HANDLERS` whose handler should be gated but isn't in the mapping).
findings.proposed_action: Replace the equality check with a directional check: assert every key in `_EVENT_CAPABILITY` is in `_HANDLERS` and points to a valid capability (already done), and separately enumerate a list of known-non-gated events (server-driven `reciter.alignment_completed`, ownership-only `reciter.released`) that legitimately should NOT appear in `_EVENT_CAPABILITY`. That catches the un-gating regression without breaking on additive changes.
findings.verifier_notes: Severity: low (correct) but rationale incomplete. Finding correctly identifies maintainability pain but mischaracterizes the effectiveness of the current check at catching the actual regression. Proposed action needs refinement: instead of just enumerating known-non-gated events, the test should assert (1) every event in _HANDLERS is either in _EVENT_CAPABILITY OR in a documented non-gated list, and (2) never in both. This catches both un-gating regressions AND overgating regressions while tolerating additive changes. File paths correct: inspector/tests/services/test_capabilities.py:132-159, inspector/services/state/state.py:246-263.

findings.title: `capabilities_for` not tested for contributor or maintainer tiers
findings.explanation: `capabilities_for` powers the FE's `/api/me` payload so the UI can pre-gate controls. The tests cover only the two extremes (owner → all caps; anonymous → exactly the two anon defaults). There's no assertion that a contributor's list contains `claim.acquire`, `segment.edit`, `request.submit` and excludes `catalog.add`, `reciter.publish`; no assertion that a maintainer's list reflects the matrix and an override change is reflected in the returned list (the live UI gating path).
findings.proposed_action: Add `test_capabilities_for_contributor_baseline` and `test_capabilities_for_maintainer_reflects_override` — the latter sets an override and asserts the changed cap appears (or disappears) in the returned list.
findings.verifier_notes: The gap is real and confirmed. While `test_baseline_parity` provides good indirect coverage of individual `can()` calls for contributor and maintainer tiers (covering ~5 of 7 contributor capabilities and ~15 of 23 maintainer capabilities), there are NO explicit tests for: (1) `capabilities_for(contributor)` that verify the complete aggregated list, (2) `capabilities_for(maintainer)` that verify the complete aggregated list, or (3) the integration with overrides (e.g., setting an override and verifying it changes the returned list). The `/api/me` route test (test_route_auth.py:68-78) calls `capabilities_for()` indirectly via signed-in users but doesn't assert the capabilities list for contributor/maintainer. The concern about the "live UI gating path" with overrides is also unaddressed by the existing test suite. The finding correctly identifies that while the implementation is simple enough that it should work via composition (`can()` + loop), explicit end-to-end tests would provide better regression protection, especially for the override case.

findings.title: Route tests for /api/ts/tajweed live in tests/services/ instead of tests/routes/
findings.explanation: The dominant repo convention places HTTP route tests under inspector/tests/routes/ (e.g. test_route_validate.py, test_route_save.py, test_route_history.py, etc.), with services/ reserved for pure-function service tests. test_tajweed.py mixes both: service unit tests for bridges_for_verse plus four route tests (test_route_no_stops, test_route_with_stops_query_param, test_route_empty_stops_param_is_treated_as_no_stops, test_route_compound_verse_ref) using flask_client. This makes the route surface harder to discover and breaks the area separation enforced everywhere else.
findings.proposed_action: Split the four route tests into inspector/tests/routes/test_route_ts_tajweed.py (or add to an existing timestamps route test module). Keep the service-level tests in tests/services/test_tajweed.py.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is confirmed by thorough investigation. test_tajweed.py is the ONLY file in inspector/tests/services/ that contains flask_client usage (lines 107-144), violating the established convention where route tests live in tests/routes/. All 34 other service test files are pure (no flask_client), and precedent exists in the codebase (test_capabilities.py + test_route_permissions.py are properly split). The file itself marks the split with explicit comments at line 102-104. The CLAUDE.md architecture doc confirms routes/services separation. No architectural reason prevents this split. Severity (low) is appropriate — this is a convention violation, not a bug.

findings.title: test_stops_order_independent_via_tuple_key does not exercise stop ordering
findings.explanation: The test is named 'order_independent' and the docstring states 'the same set of stops in a different order is a different cache key'. But the actual code calls bridges_for_verse('2:8', ('2:8:3',)) twice with the IDENTICAL one-element tuple. It does not test order at all - it just re-checks the lru_cache identity behaviour already covered by test_lru_cache_returns_identical_tuple. The test passes for the wrong reason relative to its claimed intent.
findings.proposed_action: Either delete the test (redundant with test_lru_cache_returns_identical_tuple) or change one of the calls to use a different ordering (e.g. ('2:8:3', '2:8:5') vs ('2:8:5', '2:8:3')) and assert 'a is not b' to actually lock the documented behaviour.
findings.verifier_notes: The test at line 83-89 calls bridges_for_verse("2:8", ("2:8:3",)) twice with IDENTICAL arguments and asserts the returned tuples are the same object (cached). This tests lru_cache identity behavior already covered by test_lru_cache_returns_identical_tuple (line 74-80). The docstring claims the test "locks" behavior that "the same set of stops in a different order is a different cache key", but the test never uses different orderings. To actually test order-independence behavior, it would need to call the function with ('2:8:3',) vs ('2:8:5', '2:8:3') and assert they are different objects. The test is either redundant or testing the wrong thing relative to its stated purpose.

findings.title: MISSED_BASMALA_FLAG_MIN_DELETED boundary (N-1 vs N) only tested on one side
findings.explanation: _busy_deleted() builds a deletion set of size exactly MISSED_BASMALA_FLAG_MIN_DELETED (the >= threshold). The test_missed_basmala_suppressed_below_threshold case uses size 1 ({5}), well below the threshold. There's no test for the inclusive boundary (size == N flags, size == N-1 suppresses). If a developer later changes the comparison from >= to > or vice versa, the suite silently passes when len == N - this is the exact edge the rule documents and the most likely off-by-one regression site.
findings.proposed_action: Add a parametrized test: one case with len(deleted) == MISSED_BASMALA_FLAG_MIN_DELETED - 1 (suppressed) and one with len(deleted) == MISSED_BASMALA_FLAG_MIN_DELETED (flagged), asserting symmetry with the documented inclusive boundary.
findings.verifier_notes: The production code at inspector/services/validation/detail.py:425 uses `len(deleted_basmala_chapters) >= MISSED_BASMALA_FLAG_MIN_DELETED` (inclusive comparison). Test coverage includes size 1 (well below threshold, suppressed) and size 11 (above threshold, flagged), but NO explicit test for the boundary case of size 10 (at threshold, must be flagged) or size 9 (below threshold, must be suppressed). An accidental change from >= to > would NOT be caught by the current suite, since size 10 would silently flip from flagged to suppressed while the below-threshold test (size 1) would remain suppressed in both cases. This is precisely the kind of off-by-one regression the threshold documents and the test suite should prevent.

findings.title: Empty deleted_basmala_chapters set (vs None) is not directly tested
findings.explanation: test_missed_basmala_inert_when_param_is_none covers None. The production code accepts set[int] | None and treats an empty set with len 0 < threshold as 'no augmentation' too, but there's no test that explicitly passes deleted=set() (the realistic intake case when pipeline_meta exists but the reciter stripped zero basmalas). A regression to 'is None' instead of 'len() < threshold' would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add test_missed_basmala_inert_when_deleted_set_is_empty(): pass deleted=set() and assert basmala_amin is empty (excluding the canonical 1:1/1:7 overlap behaviour).
findings.verifier_notes: Verdict should be: test gap exists but is low-severity. The proposed test is valid for clarity but not essential. Severity should remain low. The regression described (changing to `is None` without len check) would actually still be caught by the existing None test.

findings.title: Three of the eight BRIDGE_RULES are never asserted positively
findings.explanation: BRIDGE_RULES enumerates 8 cross-word rules. The tests positively assert: IDGHAM_GHUNNAH_NOON (2:8), IDGHAM_SHAFAWI (39:34, 37:151), IDGHAM_GHUNNAH_TANWEEN (2:5, 2:36, 11:42), IDGHAM_MUTAJANISAYN_KAMIL (11:42). Never directly asserted: IDGHAM_BILA_GHUNNAH_NOON, IDGHAM_BILA_GHUNNAH_TANWEEN, IDGHAM_MUTAMATHILAYN, IDGHAM_MUTAQARIBAYN. A phonemizer-side regression that drops one of these rules silently would not fail the suite.
findings.proposed_action: Add a parametrized case per missing rule using a known Quranic boundary - e.g. mutamathilayn at a well-known cross-word duplicate-letter pair, bila-ghunnah-noon at a (ن → ل/ر) boundary. Treat the parametrized list as the contract for BRIDGE_RULES coverage.
findings.verifier_notes: Correct the count: only 3 of 8 rules are untested-but-actually-fire (not 4, and not MUTAQARIBAYN). Proposed action remains valid: add parametrized test cases for IDGHAM_BILA_GHUNNAH_NOON (e.g. 2:5), IDGHAM_BILA_GHUNNAH_TANWEEN (e.g. 2:2), and IDGHAM_MUTAMATHILAYN (e.g. 3:12). Do NOT add a case for IDGHAM_MUTAQARIBAYN since it never occurs as a cross-word rule in the Qur'an.

findings.title: Route does not validate verse_ref shape; unhappy paths untested
findings.explanation: _resolve_word_idx returns 0 for malformed locations and the caller skips, but neither the service nor the route is tested for: (a) a verse_ref that the phonemizer rejects (e.g. '999:1'), (b) stops=' ,, ' or stops with malformed refs, (c) stops referencing words outside the verse. All four would surface as either a 500 or a silently-empty bridges array; only the happy path is locked.
findings.proposed_action: Add route tests covering: invalid verse_ref (assert specific status code - likely 500 today, candidate for hardening), stops with garbage entries (assert they're filtered or rejected), and stops that pause inside a word range (assert no over-firing). For the service: cover malformed verse_ref via direct call to bridges_for_verse.
findings.verifier_notes: The route has no try/except and passes verse_ref directly to the phonemizer without validation. Invalid verse_refs (e.g., '999:1') cause the phonemizer to raise ValueError, which bubbles up to the global error handler and results in a 500 response. The test suite only covers happy paths (valid refs like 2:8, 39:34) and never tests error cases: invalid verse_ref, out-of-bounds stops, or stops pausing inside word ranges. All three unhappy paths are untested. The service's _resolve_word_idx() only defends against malformed *locations* (muqattaat forms) within valid verses, not invalid verse refs. Verified via direct phonemizer call: pm.phonemize(ref='999:1') raises ValueError immediately. File: inspector/routes/timestamps/timestamps.py:157 (no error handling); inspector/services/reference/tajweed.py:152 (unguarded phonemize call); inspector/tests/services/test_tajweed.py:107-144 (happy path only).

findings.title: Chapter 1 with both 1:1 and 1:7 segs is the only multi-overlap test
findings.explanation: test_basmala_amin_order_is_first11_last17_rest11_then_missed asserts ordering for chapter 1 + two other chapters, but doesn't cover: (a) a chapter where the first seg straddles 1:1 AND 1:7 (the dedup branch on line 462-467), (b) a chapter 1 with zero 1:1 segs (no first11 candidate) - what does the output look like?, (c) a chapter 1 with only 1:7 segs all suppressed.
findings.proposed_action: Add three small tests under test_missed_basmala_rule.py or test_classify_per_category.py covering these edge cases - the dedup key (chapter, seg_index, segment_uid) on line 462 is otherwise untested.
findings.verifier_notes: The dedup logic on line 462-467 in detail.py is correctly implemented and handles all three claimed edge cases. The code is explicitly documented as "collapsing the overlap when a single seg spans both 1:1 and 1:7 (synthetic short fixtures)" — meaning it's defensive code for unrealistic test scenarios. Line 465 (the continue statement) IS uncovered by tests — no fixture exists that triggers the dedup condition. The three edge cases are correctly handled by the code, but the specific dedup execution path is untested defensive logic for synthetic scenarios where a single segment unrealistically spans both ayah 1:1 and 1:7.

findings.title: Backend↔frontend symmetry is load-bearing but never asserted in a test
findings.explanation: Both module docstrings and the test docstring declare the BE `normalize_arabic` must produce identical output to the FE `normalizeArabic`, and `/api/public/reciters?search=` filters/sorts using the BE while the UI filter uses the FE. Yet no test compares BE output against FE output for the same input string (e.g. a fixed table of inputs with expected normalized output, derived from the FE regex). Any future tweak to one regex range that the other doesn't get (e.g. a new Quranic mark) will silently desync search results between the live filter and the server query — the exact bug the symmetry promise exists to prevent.
findings.proposed_action: Add a parametrized table-driven test in `test_search_normalize.py` that asserts `normalize_arabic(x) == EXPECTED[x]` for a fixed set of inputs covering every regex range (tashkeel, dagger alef, Quranic annotations U+0610-U+061A, U+06D6-U+06DC, U+06DF-U+06E4, U+06E7-U+06E8, U+06EA-U+06ED, alif variants, taa-marbuta, alif-maqsura). The same table can be checked into a JSON fixture and consumed by the FE vitest `fuzzy-match.test.ts` so both languages assert against the same source of truth.
findings.verifier_notes: Both backend (search_normalize.py:1-9) and frontend (fuzzy-match.ts:7-10) module docstrings declare mutual parity as "load-bearing", and the test docstring (test_search_normalize.py:3-5) reinforces this. The backend normalization is used live in /api/public/reciters?search= (routes/public/public.py:183, 192) for filtering and sorting, while frontend uses normalizeArabic for client-side filtering. However, inspection of test_search_normalize.py (full file) and fuzzy-match.test.ts (full file) shows only isolated unit tests per language. The integration test (test_route_public.py:210) only verifies the feature works, never compares BE output against FE output. No cross-language test exists in CI. The regex patterns show notation differences (BE concatenates separate strings, FE uses range literals with different breakpoints) that could diverge. Without an assertion table validating both produce identical output for inputs covering every regex range (tashkeel U+064B-U+065F, Quranic U+0610-U+061A, etc.), silent search-result divergence is possible.

findings.title: `matches()` has no negative-case test
findings.explanation: All three `matches()` tests assert `is True`. There is no assertion that `matches("Husary", "afasy")` returns `False`. The FE counterpart has this exact negative case (`fuzzy-match.test.ts:46-48`). Without a False assertion, a regression that makes `matches` always return True would pass the suite.
findings.proposed_action: Add `assert matches("Husary", "afasy") is False` (mirroring the FE test on line 46-48) plus one negative Arabic case to confirm the substring check actually rejects non-matches.
findings.verifier_notes: Backend test suite in inspector/tests/services/test_search_normalize.py lines 44-61 contains three test cases: empty needle (True), Arabic normalized substring (True), and Latin substring (True). All assert True. The frontend counterpart (fuzzy-match.test.ts:46-48) explicitly includes the negative case `expect(match('Husary', 'afasy')).toBe(false)`. The backend implementation (search_normalize.py:51-55) is a simple substring check that could regress to always returning True without detection by the current test suite. The finding is load-bearing: a bug making `matches()` always return True would silently pass all existing backend tests. The proposed action mirrors the FE test and is appropriate.

findings.title: Dagger alef and Quranic annotation marks are unstripped in tests
findings.explanation: The diacritic regex covers six ranges including the dagger alef `ٰ` (U+0670) and Quranic annotation marks (U+06D6-U+06ED). Only the tashkeel range (`ً-ٟ`) is exercised by the existing test. The catalog contains real reciter names with Quranic-style annotation (and verse-text search may reach this code in the future per the docstring), so the unstripped ranges represent untested behaviour — a regex typo dropping the dagger-alef range would not fail any test.
findings.proposed_action: Add cases covering dagger alef (e.g. `normalize_arabic("اللّٰه")` vs `normalize_arabic("الله")`) and at least one Quranic annotation mark (e.g. U+06D6 or U+06E5/U+06E6 boundary checks).
findings.verifier_notes: The finding should be retitled and refocused: "Quranic mark U+06E5/U+06E6 missing from backend regex — FE/BE parity gap". The backend regex lines 20-30 are missing U+06E5 and U+06E6; this should be fixed to match the frontend "۟-۪" range. Proposed action remains valid: add test cases for dagger alef AND a test case for the missing Quranic marks (e.g., normalize_arabic("الله" + chr(0x06E5)) to verify stripping). The severity remains medium as this affects Quranic verse search (per the docstring mentioning future verse-text search), though currently only reciter names are searchable and dagger alef itself works.

findings.title: `normalize_arabic("")` guard branch is uncovered
findings.explanation: `normalize_arabic` has an explicit `if not s: return ""` early return that no test exercises. The FE counterpart has the parity test `expect(normalizeArabic('')).toBe('')` (line 28-30). Without it, removing the guard or accidentally returning `None` from this branch would not fail the suite.
findings.proposed_action: Add `assert normalize_arabic("") == ""` (mirrors `fuzzy-match.test.ts:28-30`).
findings.verifier_notes: Coverage instrumentation confirms line 43 (the early return in `normalize_arabic("")` guard) is uncovered. The backend function has an explicit `if not s: return ""` guard, while the frontend implementation has no guard but naturally handles empty strings via chained `.toLowerCase()` and `.replace()` calls. Frontend test `fuzzy-match.test.ts:28-30` explicitly tests the empty case with `expect(normalizeArabic('')).toBe('')`. Backend test suite has no equivalent. The guard is defensive (unreachable via current API paths due to `if search:` check at public.py:182) but aligns with the stated parity principle: "same input string normalizes to the same output in both languages". The proposed action correctly mirrors the FE test and improves backend coverage to match FE parity. Severity is appropriately low since the guard is defensive and unreachable in production paths.

findings.title: Module docstring references the pre-move path `inspector/services/search_normalize.py`
findings.explanation: Both docstrings (BE module at line 1-12 and FE module at line 8) reference the path `inspector/services/search_normalize.py`, but the file actually lives at `inspector/services/activity/search_normalize.py` (the legacy alias in `services/__init__.py:78` is what keeps `from services.search_normalize import ...` working). An agent searching by the docstring path will land on a non-existent file. Additionally the BE module ends with `Slice B of phase 6.` (line 11) — this is a phase/refactor comment the repo's `.claude/rules/comments.md` explicitly bans.
findings.proposed_action: Update both docstrings to reference `inspector/services/activity/search_normalize.py` (or the legacy alias `services.search_normalize`), and drop the `Slice B of phase 6.` trailer per the comment rules.
findings.verifier_notes: 1. Correct the evidence claim: BE docstring does NOT reference the path (remove that from finding). Only FE docstring at line 8 references `inspector/services/search_normalize.py`. 2. Clarify that while the FE path is outdated, the module is functionally accessible via the legacy alias, so it's not a "landing on non-existent file" bug. 3. Reframe the primary issue as the `Slice B of phase 6.` comment violation in BE module line 11 (actual rules violation). 4. Proposed action should focus on: (a) Remove the "phase 6" comment from BE line 11 (mandatory per rules), (b) Optionally enhance FE docstring to reference the actual filesystem path for clarity, but this is secondary.

findings.title: JobStagingError on missing REQUIRED_STATIC_FILES not exercised
findings.explanation: test_stage_job_code_raises_when_entrypoint_missing only covers the entrypoint branch. The static-file branch — where _resolve_required_static() returns (None, None) because neither data/qpc_hafs.json.gz nor the uncompressed data/qpc_hafs.json exists, or surah_info.json / repo.yml / LICENSE is missing — is not tested. That branch is exactly the second half of REQUIRED_STATIC_FILES the docstring says is being pinned against Dockerfile drops, so this leaves the headline contract half-covered.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that points REPO_ROOT at a tmp_path where all REQUIRED_ENTRYPOINTS exist but data/surah_info.json (or .github/config/repo.yml, or LICENSE) is missing, and assert JobStagingError contains the missing static path and stub_batch is empty. Bonus: parametrize over each static file to lock the contract per-entry.

findings.title: Most of base.py has no tests at all - single-flight, record I/O, poll worker, helpers
findings.explanation: The audit description ("HF Job base class, staging, submission, status tracking") covers the whole module, but the only test file is *_staging.py and it only touches stage_job_code(). Untested: running_job_for() filter rules (cross-kind mutex when kind=None, the slug=None,kind!=None global filter that excludes per-slug jobs via labels.task/labels.reciter), list_in_flight_jobs() including its 5s TTL cache hit/miss/invalidation contract and the started_at vs created_at preference, read_record_bytes() legacy_job_record_path fallback when the v2 path 404s with StorageNotFound, write_record_bytes() swallow-on-error behavior, job_record_path() global vs slug, _poll_terminal_jobs() dispatcher (only TERMINAL_SUCCESS dispatched, slug='_global' -> None coercion, handler exceptions logged not raised), register_handler/start_poll_worker idempotency, and the helpers env_int/hf_status_str/hf_job_id/now_iso. Several of these have subtle invariants (label-based filtering, idempotent registration, cache invalidation) that are the kind that silently break under refactor.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test_jobs_base.py (or rename _staging.py) covering: (1) running_job_for kind/slug filter matrix with stubbed list_jobs returning a small fixture; (2) list_in_flight_jobs caching - second call returns cached without re-listing, failures don't cache, hf_publish.launch invalidation path; (3) read_record_bytes falls back to legacy path on StorageNotFound; (4) _poll_terminal_jobs dispatches only registered kinds, only on TERMINAL_SUCCESS, coerces slug '_global' -> None, swallows handler exceptions; (5) start_poll_worker idempotency; (6) helper edge cases (env_int empty/garbage -> None, hf_status_str unwraps .status.stage vs .status).
findings.verifier_notes: Coverage report shows services/admin/jobs/base.py at 42.9% coverage with only stage_job_code() tested. Direct code inspection confirms: running_job_for() (lines 109-134, filter logic with _global/None coercion), list_in_flight_jobs() (lines 137-191, cache contract and TTL), read_record_bytes() (lines 207-220, legacy path fallback on StorageNotFound), write_record_bytes() (lines 200-204, swallow-on-error), _poll_terminal_jobs() (lines 360-385, handler dispatch and TERMINAL_SUCCESS filtering), register_handler() (lines 350-357), start_poll_worker() (lines 392-404, idempotency), and helpers (lines 65-84) are all completely untested. Test file mocks these functions rather than testing them (e.g., test_route_admin_releases.py line 46-49). All cited line ranges match actual function bodies and control flow paths that exercise the subtle invariants mentioned (label-based filtering, slug coercion, cache invalidation paths, handler exception swallowing). The finding accurately describes both the missing tests and the risk profile (refactor-silent label filter invariants, cache contract violations, idempotent registration failures).

findings.title: Auto-gzip success path doesn't verify the tempfile is unlinked
findings.explanation: test_stage_job_code_auto_gzips_qpc_when_only_uncompressed_present asserts the upload payload but doesn't assert the temp staging file (stagedref_*.json.gz under tempfile.gettempdir()) is unlinked after batch_bucket_files succeeds. The finally-block cleanup is the failure-mode the test docstring explicitly calls out ("auto-gzipped temp sources are deleted in stage_job_code's finally block"). If somebody refactors that finally away (e.g. moves to a context manager and gets the scope wrong), a temp-file leak ships silently.
findings.proposed_action: After the successful base.stage_job_code() call, capture the snapshotted source path (it starts with the system tempdir + 'stagedref_') and assert Path(src).exists() is False - the finally-block must have removed it.
findings.verifier_notes: The test `test_stage_job_code_auto_gzips_qpc_when_only_uncompressed_present` (lines 59-81) snapshots file blobs DURING the `batch_bucket_files` mock call (before cleanup), but never verifies that the temp files created via `tempfile.mkstemp()` at line 310 are actually unlinked by the finally-block at lines 332-333. The stub_batch fixture explicitly documents this scenario in its docstring ("auto-gzipped temp sources are deleted in stage_job_code's finally block"), but the test only asserts on the snapshot contents, not on the cleanup. If the finally-block were deleted or broken, the test would still pass while temp files leak in the system temp directory (/tmp or Windows equiv).

findings.title: Happy-path test walks the real repo and depends on real on-disk files
findings.explanation: test_stage_job_code_uploads_every_required_path does not monkeypatch REPO_ROOT, so it rglobs the actual qua_shared/ and qua_jobs/ trees and depends on data/qpc_hafs.json[.gz], data/surah_info.json, .github/config/repo.yml, LICENSE being present in whatever checkout runs it. The branch taken inside _resolve_required_static (real .gz vs gzip-from-uncompressed) flips between dev machines and CI runners depending on whether qpc_hafs.json.gz is checked in / generated. The test still passes because the assertion is a superset-check, but it's not hermetic and slows over time as qua_shared/qua_jobs grow. Same hermetic-isolation pattern that the other two tests already use (monkeypatch REPO_ROOT -> tmp_path with synthesized stubs) should be applied here too - letting the test still assert that every REQUIRED_* path lands in adds without scanning the real repo.
findings.proposed_action: Mirror the tmp_path setup from the other two tests: stub the entrypoints under tmp_path/qua_jobs/, drop empty qua_shared/__init__.py, materialize all REQUIRED_STATIC_FILES paths, monkeypatch base.REPO_ROOT, then assert. Keep one separate explicit "real repo wired up correctly" smoke test if you want - but it should be marked as such, not the canonical contract test.
findings.verifier_notes: The test test_stage_job_code_uploads_every_required_path does not monkeypatch REPO_ROOT (line 45 fixture has no monkeypatch param), so it scans the actual qua_shared/ and qua_jobs/ trees from the real repository. This is confirmed by executing the test code and observing that all real .py files from those directories are included in the upload manifest. The test also depends on real static files (qpc_hafs.json.gz, surah_info.json, .github/config/repo.yml, LICENSE) existing. The _resolve_required_static function contains conditional logic (lines 264-270) that branches differently depending on whether qpc_hafs.json.gz exists vs only qpc_hafs.json - the .gz path returns immediately while the .json-only path triggers gzip compression. The test passes due to a superset assertion (lines 53-56 just verify all required paths are present, not checking specific upload mechanics). Docstring explicitly states "Happy path against the real repo tree" indicating this is intentional design, not a bug. The test serves a legitimate purpose as a smoke test verifying the real repository is in a correct deployable state. The finding is technically accurate but should be classified as a design/clarity issue rather than a correctness bug - the test works as intended and is distinct from the contract tests that use synthetic repos.

findings.title: stub_batch reads file without a context manager
findings.explanation: `blob = open(src, 'rb').read()` leaks the file handle on success (only closed by GC). Project best-practices.md is explicit about explicit error handling and clean utilities. Trivial to fix.
findings.proposed_action: Replace with `blob = Path(src).read_bytes()` and let the OSError branch keep blob=None.
findings.verifier_notes: The code at line 35 uses `open(src, "rb").read()` which creates a file handle that is not explicitly closed on success—it relies on garbage collection instead. While Python will eventually clean it up via GC, this pattern violates the project's explicit resource management conventions visible in conftest.py (lines 472-482, 478) where context managers are consistently used. The error handling path (OSError → blob=None) is correct, but the success path should follow the same pattern as the rest of the test suite. The proposed fix to `Path(src).read_bytes()` is valid and would maintain the same exception behavior while ensuring explicit resource cleanup. This is confirmed as a style/convention issue, not a functional bug.

findings.title: Happy path doesn't assert target dedup invariant
findings.explanation: stage_job_code maintains a seen_targets set to dedup overlapping entries (e.g. a static file path that also matches a walked .py path, or future overlap if a REQUIRED_STATIC_FILES entry sits inside qua_shared/). The test asserts every required target is *present* but not that there are no duplicate targets in adds, so a regression that double-uploads silently would pass.
findings.proposed_action: After collecting targets, assert `len(targets) == len([t for _s, t in stub_batch[0]['add']])` (i.e. no duplicate target paths in the manifest).
findings.verifier_notes: The test at inspector/tests/services/test_jobs_base_staging.py:52 converts the manifest's adds list to a set via `targets = {target for _src, target in stub_batch[0]["add"]}`, which silently deduplicates. If the same target appeared twice in the adds list (from overlapping walk results + static files), the set would hide it. The code at inspector/services/admin/jobs/base.py:287-315 never checks for duplicates before calling batch_bucket_files; it only uses seen_targets to verify all required files are present (line 318). While duplicates are currently impossible by design (walk directories and static paths don't overlap), the test is brittle to future refactors. The proposed assertion `len(targets) == len([t for _s, t in stub_batch[0]['add']])` would catch regressions. Verdict confirmed: test is missing dedup invariant assertion. However, consider downgrading severity because: (1) duplicates can't occur with current path structure, (2) Xet bucket system deduplicates by content hash, and (3) this is defensive future-proofing rather than a current bug.

findings.title: huggingface_hub stub uses a different pattern from the neighbor test file
findings.explanation: test_timestamps_jobs.py (the closest neighbor, same subsystem) unconditionally creates `types.ModuleType('huggingface_hub')` and pins it into sys.modules. test_jobs_base_staging.py instead does `sys.modules.get(...)`, falls back to a new ModuleType only if absent, then setattr's onto whichever module it found - which means in CI (where huggingface_hub is installed and already imported) the fake is patched onto the real module instead of a fully-isolated stub. Both work because monkeypatch.setattr reverses on teardown, but the inconsistency forces a reader to reason about two different stubbing strategies for the same boundary. Pick one.
findings.proposed_action: Align with the neighbor: always create a fresh `types.ModuleType('huggingface_hub')`, attach `batch_bucket_files` to it, and `monkeypatch.setitem(sys.modules, 'huggingface_hub', mod)`. Simpler and fully hermetic.
findings.verifier_notes: Both test files stub huggingface_hub for the same boundary (HF job bucket operations). test_jobs_base_staging.py:26-29 uses sys.modules.get() with a conditional create pattern, while test_timestamps_jobs.py:33-36 unconditionally creates a fresh ModuleType. Both work due to pytest's isolation and monkeypatch teardown, but the inconsistency forces readers to reason about two different strategies. The `.get()` pattern appears defensive rather than intentional (no docstring explains it), and the unconditional approach is more hermetic. Aligning to the unconditional pattern would improve clarity without functional downside. Evidence: lines 26-29 vs 33-36 of cited files, lack of explanatory docstrings, all tests passing both patterns.

findings.title: Test duplicates production _STATUS_FOR_ARCHIVE mapping inline
findings.explanation: `_STATUS_FOR_KIND = {"completed": "accepted", "returned": "returned", "discarded": "discarded"}` in the test is character-for-character identical to `_STATUS_FOR_ARCHIVE` in repo_requests.py. If production mapping ever evolves (e.g. a new terminal status) the test silently drifts and would seed via the wrong status — masking a real bug.
findings.proposed_action: Either import the production map (`from services.db.repo_requests import _STATUS_FOR_ARCHIVE`) or, cleaner, drive the seed through the existing `pending_requests` service (`pending_requests.archive_returned/discarded/apply_and_archive_completed`) rather than calling `repo_requests.resolve` with a raw status string. That eliminates the duplication and exercises the layer above.
findings.verifier_notes: The test duplicates the production `_STATUS_FOR_ARCHIVE` mapping inline (repo_requests.py:27 vs test_request_archive.py:35, both are identical dicts). The test's `_archive()` function bypasses higher-level pending_requests service methods (archive_returned/archive_discarded/apply_and_archive_completed) and calls `repo_requests.resolve()` directly with a manual status map. If production mapping ever changes, the test's hardcoded mapping would silently diverge, masking bugs. The cleaner fix is to use pending_requests.archive_* functions instead, which encapsulate the mapping and are already available in the test (imported via services).

findings.title: fresh_archive yields backend but no test uses it
findings.explanation: The fixture yields `(request_archive_service, backend)` and every single test unpacks it as `svc, _ = fresh_archive` — the backend is never used. That's expected (archive is a pure-SQLite read facade) but the fixture API advertises it. Dead second tuple element.
findings.proposed_action: Yield `request_archive_service` alone and have tests bind `svc = fresh_archive`. Or, if reusing `state_persistence` per the previous finding, drop this fixture entirely.
findings.verifier_notes: The `fresh_archive` fixture at inspector/tests/services/test_request_archive.py:26 yields a tuple `(request_archive_service, backend)`. Examination of all 7 tests that use this fixture (lines 65, 71, 80, 95, 106, 113) shows they all unpack it identically: `svc, _ = fresh_archive`, discarding the backend element entirely. The request_archive module itself (inspector/services/state/request_archive.py) only reads from SQLite via repo_requests and does not access the FilesystemBackend at all. The _archive() helper function uses db.transaction() and repo_requests, not the backend. The backend setup is still necessary for global state, but yielding it from the fixture advertises it as part of the fixture's contract when tests never bind or use it. This matches the pattern in state_persistence (conftest.py:339) which does identical backend setup but yields only the backend itself, not a tuple.

findings.title: hydrate() is exposed in __all__ but untested
findings.explanation: `hydrate()` is a documented no-op kept for legacy callers and re-exported in `__all__`, but no test calls it. Low priority — it's intentionally trivial — but a one-line test pins the API surface so a future refactor doesn't quietly drop it.
findings.proposed_action: Add `def test_hydrate_is_noop(fresh_archive): svc, _ = fresh_archive; assert svc.hydrate() is None` to lock the contract.
findings.verifier_notes: The function `hydrate()` is defined in request_archive.py (line 25-27) as a documented no-op and exported in __all__ (line 46), but the test file inspector/tests/services/test_request_archive.py (6 tests total: lines 64-120) contains no test that calls it. A grep of the entire codebase confirms hydrate() is never called on request_archive in production or tests. The pattern matches other state modules (state.py, pending_requests.py) which also have untested no-op hydrate() functions for legacy API compatibility. Adding a simple test to pin the contract is reasonable housekeeping, and low severity is appropriate since this is intentional API preservation, not a functional bug.

findings.title: Per-ArchiveKind read tests are not parametrized
findings.explanation: `test_archive_via_resolve_is_readable` only exercises COMPLETED. `test_multiple_entries_per_slug_chronological` only exercises RETURNED. The DISCARDED + RETURNED chronological-order behavior + COMPLETED multi-entry behavior aren't asserted. The status mapping in repo_requests.py (`accepted`/`returned`/`discarded`) is the per-kind switch, so parametrizing over `ArchiveKind` would close the gap cheaply.
findings.proposed_action: Parametrize the round-trip + multi-entry tests over `ArchiveKind` so each terminal status is exercised the same way.
findings.verifier_notes: The gap is real and correctly identified. `test_archive_via_resolve_is_readable` (line 70) only exercises COMPLETED, and `test_multiple_entries_per_slug_chronological` (line 92) only exercises RETURNED. The per-kind read logic (repo_requests.get_for_slug, lines 284-293) is identical across all three kinds (COMPLETED, RETURNED, DISCARDED) — the mapping `_STATUS_FOR_ARCHIVE[archive_kind]` converts kind to status, then the same SQL query `ORDER BY resolved_at, submitted_at, id` runs. However, the actual code paths are not kind-specific; the ordering and retrieval logic is stateless. The finding correctly identifies a test coverage gap (COMPLETED and DISCARDED are not exercised with multiple entries), but the severity is overstated: this is a test symmetry/hygiene issue, not a functional correctness issue. All three kinds are exercised in `test_kinds_isolated` (lines 79-89), and the ordering logic is tested for RETURNED (the documented use case for multi-entry loops). Parametrization would improve maintainability and symmetry but would not catch logic errors in the actual code.

findings.title: FilesystemBackend setup signals 'this touches the bucket' when it doesn't
findings.explanation: A new contributor reading this test sees `INSPECTOR_FILESYSTEM_ROOT` + `FilesystemBackend` setup and reasonably concludes the archive lives in bucket files. It doesn't — post-cutover archive reads go through SQLite via `repo_requests.get_for_slug`/`all_archived`. The bucket fixture is ceremonial: needed only because `submit` walks through `repo_access.ensure_user` and other code paths that may incidentally touch backend-registered modules. The misleading scaffolding hides the actual seam being tested.
findings.proposed_action: Either reuse the autouse SQLite substrate alone (the archive tests don't need a bucket backend at all if the seeder uses repo paths) or add a one-line comment in the fixture explaining 'bucket backend is configured for parity with sibling tests; archives themselves live in SQLite'.
findings.verifier_notes:
The FilesystemBackend setup in `fresh_archive` is confirmed to be ceremonial and misleading:

1. **request_archive.py:25-27** explicitly states `hydrate()` is a no-op under SQLite
2. **request_archive.py:30-40** shows all archive reads go purely through SQLite (repo_requests.get_for_slug, all_archived)
3. **test_request_archive.py:64-120** all tests use the pattern `svc, _ = fresh_archive` discarding the backend entirely
4. **Verified experimentally** that tests pass without FilesystemBackend setup at all
5. **repo_requests.submit() on line 46** calls `repo_access.ensure_user` (repo_requests.py:88), which is purely SQLite (repo_access.py:24-40 - just INSERT/UPDATE to users table), never touches the bucket

The fixture's docstring "FilesystemBackend for any content + the substrate DB (autouse) for state" is misleading because there is no content that needs the backend. The autouse `_substrate_db` fixture (conftest.py:117) is sufficient. The proposed action is sound: either remove the ceremonial setup OR add a clarifying comment. The finding's explanation of why the backend is kept ("needed because submit touches backend-registered modules") is slightly inaccurate—it's purely unnecessary/ceremonial, not conditionally needed.

findings.title: Status assertion is a no-op tautology
findings.explanation: `assert body["status"] in ("ok", "degraded")` accepts every legal value the route can return — those are the only two statuses health.py ever emits (`status: "ok" if healthy else "degraded"` at routes/auth/health.py:52). The assertion cannot fail short of a typo or a totally rewritten route, so it has no regression-protection value. In this test's specific scenario (no `INSPECTOR_BUCKET_MOUNT` env, so `bucket_ok` is False), the route deterministically returns `degraded` — the test should pin that.
findings.proposed_action: Replace with `assert body["status"] == "degraded"` (and add an `assert body["mode"] == "local"` to anchor the no-mount branch). Or add a sibling test that sets `INSPECTOR_BUCKET_MOUNT` to a tmp path with `db/inspector.db` present and asserts `status == "ok"`.
findings.verifier_notes: The assertion `assert body["status"] in ("ok", "degraded")` is a no-op tautology. Code analysis shows: (1) health.py:52 defines status as a ternary `"ok" if healthy else "degraded"` with no other branches — these are the only two possible values; (2) the test doesn't set INSPECTOR_BUCKET_MOUNT, so bucket_ok=False, healthy=False, status="degraded" deterministically; (3) the assertion will always pass regardless of logic errors. The test provides zero regression protection. Proposed action is valid: assert the specific expected value ("degraded") or add a companion test with the mount configured to verify the "ok" path. File: inspector/tests/db/test_boot_health.py:29, inspector/routes/auth/health.py:52.

findings.title: `test_healthz_db_open_reflects_healthcheck` is a near-duplicate of `test_healthz_reports_db_section`
findings.explanation: Both tests assert `body["db"]["open"] is True` against the same autouse-migrated DB. The second test claims to verify that healthz "reflects" the underlying `db.healthcheck()`, but it just checks both return True independently — there's no equality assertion tying the route payload to the direct call, and no scenario where one would diverge from the other. The single load-bearing line over the first test is `assert db.healthcheck()["open"] is True`, which is already implied by the route's assertion. Either the test should actually compare the two (e.g. mutate the writer to force `open: False` and assert both flip), or it's stale duplication.
findings.proposed_action: Either delete the second test, or strengthen it by closing the writer connection (`db.reset()`-then-no-init or monkeypatch `get_writer` to raise) and asserting both `db.healthcheck()["open"] is False` AND `body["db"]["open"] is False`. That actually exercises the reflection claim.
findings.verifier_notes: Both tests assert `body["db"]["open"] is True` on an initialized DB from the autouse `_substrate_db` fixture. Test 2's only incremental assertion is `db.healthcheck()["open"] is True`, which is redundant with Test 1's route-based assertion. Test 2 claims to verify "reflection" but doesn't actually test covariance — it only checks that both return True independently. Within the fixture setup, the DB is always open, so divergence testing requires monkeypatching. The healthz route clearly calls `_db.healthcheck()` (routes/auth/health.py:70) and uses its return value (73-74), but Test 2 doesn't exercise failure modes or demonstrate that the route's value would change if the underlying function returned False. Per best-practices.md DRY principle, this duplication should be addressed either by deletion or by strengthening with failure-case coverage.

findings.title: No test covers `healthcheck()` failure branch / `/healthz` degraded-on-db path
findings.explanation: `healthcheck()` has an explicit `except Exception` branch returning `{open: False, error: ...}`, and `/healthz` propagates `healthy = healthy and bool(db_health.get("open"))` then returns 503 in deployed mode. Neither path has a test — both audited tests only exercise the happy path on a freshly-migrated DB. A regression that lets the route return 200/healthy when the DB writer is dead (e.g. someone catches the exception too high up) would slip silently.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that closes/breaks the writer (e.g. `db.reset()` without re-init, or monkeypatch `connection.get_writer` to raise) and asserts both `db.healthcheck()["open"] is False` AND a `/healthz` GET surfaces `body["db"]["open"] is False`. Add a second test that sets `INSPECTOR_BUCKET_MOUNT` to a populated tmp dir and confirms `status == "ok"` + 200, then breaks the DB and confirms 503 in that mode.
findings.verifier_notes: The `healthcheck()` function at /c/Users/ahmed/Documents/Work/my-projects/quranic-universal-audio/.claude/worktrees/elated-heyrovsky-aa8bb0/inspector/services/db/__init__.py:34-39 has an explicit `except Exception` branch returning `{"open": False, "error": ...}`. The `/healthz` endpoint at inspector/routes/auth/health.py:70-84 uses this to conditionally return 503 in deployed mode. However, test_boot_health.py contains only two tests (lines 18-35), both exercising the happy path on a freshly-migrated DB with `body["db"]["open"] is True`. There is no test that breaks the DB connection and verifies either (1) `db.healthcheck()["open"] is False` or (2) `/healthz` returns 503 in deployed mode. A regression allowing the route to return 200/healthy when the DB is broken would slip silently.

findings.title: Durability tests don't cover `deferred_sync()` or `UploadConflict` propagation
findings.explanation: The audited file says it verifies the `durable_transaction → mark_durable → upload` path end-to-end, but the upload-side guardrails are untested at this seam: (a) `deferred_sync()` is the bucket-storm fix for boot/batch loops — coalescing N commits into 1 upload only if the seq advanced. Nothing in `test_durability.py` arms `deferred_sync()` around a `durable_transaction` and asserts exactly one upload fires (or zero on a no-op batch). (b) `UploadConflict` is what happens when a rolling-deploy overlap advances the remote seq under a different nonce — the docstring says the route surfaces 5xx, but the seam isn't tested through `durable_transaction`.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that opens a `deferred_sync()` block, runs 2-3 `catalog.add_reciter` calls inside it, and asserts `_write_direct` was called exactly once (use a counter via monkeypatch). Add a second test that pre-writes a seq sidecar with a higher seq + different nonce, then runs an `add_reciter` and asserts it raises `UploadConflict` and `last_error` reflects the CAS message.
findings.verifier_notes: Change severity from medium to low-medium. Narrow the proposed action: only request a test for UploadConflict propagation through durable_transaction service boundary (e.g., monkeypatch the seq sidecar, then call catalog.add_reciter). Remove the deferred_sync test request since it's already adequately covered in test_sync.py.

findings.title: Boot path `pull → init_db → run_migrations` lacks an integration test
findings.explanation: The boot contract is: `sync.pull()` lands the bucket DB locally, `init_db()` then applies pending migrations on top. `test_sync.py::test_upload_then_pull_roundtrip` exercises a manual pull→`init_db` (with migrations no-op), but no test covers the more interesting case — bucket DB at version N, code with migrations through M>N, and `init_db()` brings it up. A regression that breaks the post-pull migration leg (e.g. a migration that doesn't fail-fast) would not be caught.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that writes a fixture DB at an older `PRAGMA user_version` into the FilesystemBackend bucket, pulls + inits, and asserts `current_version()` matches the latest migration and the on-disk schema is upgraded.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is accurate. Current test coverage includes: (1) individual migration tests (test_migration_0007.py) that create older-version DBs and verify migrations apply, (2) sync.pull() testing, and (3) a pull+init_db roundtrip test in test_upload_then_pull_roundtrip. However, the roundtrip test pulls a fully-migrated DB (explicitly noted: "migrations already applied in the pulled file → no-op"), so it never exercises the scenario of pulling an older-versioned DB from the bucket and applying pending migrations. A regression in the post-pull migration leg (e.g., silent migration failure, SQL syntax error) would not be caught by current tests despite the boot contract explicitly covering this sequence. The finding correctly identifies this gap with accurate file:line evidence (inspector/services/db/__init__.py:25-31 shows init_db contract, sync.py:211-241 shows pull, migrate.py:39-70 shows migrations). Severity LOW is appropriate because: migrations are tested in isolation, boot errors are logged/caught, and the scenario (bucket/code version mismatch) is infrequent.

findings.title: Reader must trace the autouse `_substrate_db` from a sibling conftest to read either test
findings.explanation: Both audited tests rely on autouse magic in `inspector/tests/conftest.py` (parent of `tests/db/`) — `_substrate_db` migrates a fresh DB, disables sync, and clears caches. A new reader of `test_boot_health.py::test_healthz_reports_db_section` sees `body = client.get("/healthz")` with only an in-test comment hinting at `# The autouse _substrate_db fixture has opened + migrated a DB.` The durability file's module docstring explains the inversion (autouse disables sync, the test re-arms it), but a new contributor has to read the parent conftest to understand the boundary. There's no broken contract, just a navigation tax.
findings.proposed_action: Add a one-line cross-reference in `tests/db/conftest.py` pointing at the parent autouse: `# Parent conftest provides autouse _substrate_db (fresh migrated DB + sync disarmed); fresh_db here is the bare equivalent for tests that want explicit setup.` Optionally also pull the durability seam fixture (`synced_bucket`) into `tests/db/conftest.py` per `synced-bucket-private-reset`.
findings.verifier_notes: The autouse `_substrate_db` fixture defined in `inspector/tests/conftest.py:117-150` runs implicitly for all tests in `inspector/tests/db/` but is not documented in `inspector/tests/db/conftest.py`. However, the two cited test files that rely on this fixture already document it explicitly: test_boot_health.py (line 19 inline comment) and test_durability.py (lines 1-8 module docstring explaining the autouse behavior and sync inversion). The finding correctly identifies a documentation gap in conftest.py, but the practical navigation burden is low since the affected tests self-document. Severity "low" is appropriate. The proposed action (adding a cross-reference to tests/db/conftest.py docstring) would improve discoverability but is not critical since readers of the actual test files find the explanation there.

findings.title: _actor() / _step() / _seed_user() pattern duplicated across db tests
findings.explanation: Every db test file redefines its own `_actor()` (and several redefine `_seed_user()`) — the public-state test adds a `_step()` shim on top. `_helpers.py` already hosts `seed_user`/`seed_delivery`, but the actor factory is copy-pasted with subtly different defaults (OWNER here vs CONTRIBUTOR elsewhere). This is exactly the BE conftest-promotion smell the audit calls out (`_hf_user()`, `_replace_state()` peers).
findings.proposed_action: Promote `_actor(hf, login, role)` into `tests/db/_helpers.py` (or conftest) as a parametrized factory with role-defaulted variants (e.g. `actor_owner()`, `actor_contributor()`), and consider promoting a generic `step(slug, frm, to)` that wraps `repo_transitions.append` for the timeline tests.
findings.verifier_notes:
All 4 `_actor()` definitions are copy-pasted across db test files with subtly different role defaults (CONTRIBUTOR in test_repo_requests_activity.py, OWNER elsewhere), creating maintenance duplication. _seed_user() was already promoted to _helpers.py but _actor() was not, showing incomplete fixture consolidation. The parametrized form is duplicated in 3 files identically. This matches the conftest-promotion pattern (similar to _hf_user(), _replace_state() cited elsewhere). The semantic differences in role defaults (CONTRIBUTOR vs. OWNER) are real but don't block consolidation — they just require explicit parameters in test calls rather than relying on implicit defaults.

Files: inspector/tests/db/test_public_state_bucket_dates.py:18; test_repo_transitions.py:12; test_repo_requests_activity.py:16; test_review_followups.py:29 all redefine _actor() independently; _helpers.py:8 already has seed_user promoted.

findings.title: `afr == sorted(afr)` is a tautology when timestamps tie
findings.explanation: The docstring promises chronological order, but the test asserts `afr == sorted(afr)`. Two back-to-back inserts can share the same microsecond on coarser clocks (notably Windows where `datetime.now()` resolution is ~15ms), in which case the list is trivially sorted regardless of bug. The assertion would pass even if the function returned timestamps in arbitrary order, as long as they happened within the same tick.
findings.proposed_action: Either (a) inject monotonically advancing timestamps via a freezegun-style fixture or by patching `_serde.now`, or (b) assert strict monotonicity over the insert order recorded by `seq` rather than wall-clock — e.g. compare against the `transitions.seq` column the test indirectly sets.
findings.verifier_notes: The test assertion `afr == sorted(afr)` at inspector/tests/db/test_public_state_bucket_dates.py:69 is indeed weak. Verified through testing that Windows datetime.now() has ~15ms resolution, causing multiple rapid calls to return identical timestamps (demonstrated: 55 duplicates in 100 rapid calls). When timestamps are identical, the assertion passes trivially regardless of insertion order, since sorted() is stable. The function's docstring (public_state.py:84) explicitly promises "chronological order", but the test cannot detect if this guarantee is violated when timestamps tie. The underlying code IS correct (it orders by seq), but the test would miss bugs if the iteration order of repo_transitions.for_slug() were reversed or scrambled for transitions sharing the same timestamp. Proposed action is sound: inject monotonically advancing timestamps (e.g., via freezegun) or assert strict monotonicity using the seq column recorded in transitions table.

findings.title: Test uses synthetic `reciter.test_step` event name instead of real events
findings.explanation: Other transition tests use real domain events (`reciter.requested`, `reciter.alignment_completed`, `reciter.released`). This test hardcodes `event="reciter.test_step"` for every step. While the replay only consults `to_state`, the synthetic event name makes the timeline less representative and would silently miss a future replay change that started filtering on event kind.
findings.proposed_action: Use realistic event names that mirror the actual transition events for each step. Even mapping (state → event) is fine; the goal is keeping the seeded log parallel to what the state machine actually emits.
findings.verifier_notes: Downgrade severity from "low" to "minimal" or "cosmetic". Reframe as: "Test uses synthetic event name—realistic events would improve code clarity and maintainability, not correctness. The replay function only consults to_state; filtering on event kind would require explicit code changes that would surface during review."

findings.title: No coverage for `to_state IS NULL` rows in the replay
findings.explanation: `_bucket_dates_for_slug` has an explicit `if not raw: continue` guard for transitions with no `to_state` (e.g. non-state-change rows that may still carry a slug — claims, access grants on a slug, future event kinds). The current tests only feed rows where every step has a non-null `to_state`, so the guard is untested. A regression that removes the guard would silently raise KeyError on any non-state-mutating slug-scoped transition row in production.
findings.proposed_action: Add a case that seeds at least one slug-scoped transition with `to_state=None` (e.g. `repo_transitions.append(event='reciter.claimed', actor=_actor(), slug='dX')`) and asserts the bucket replay simply skips it.
findings.verifier_notes: The guard at inspector/services/reference/public_state.py:204 (`if not raw: continue`) is genuinely untested. In production, multiple slug-scoped transitions are written with `to_state=None`: (1) `reciter.auto_claim_skipped` (inspector/services/state/state.py:527, no to_state parameter), (2) `catalog.edited` (inspector/services/state/catalog.py:254-259, via audit.append with no to_state), and (3) `catalog.added` (inspector/services/state/catalog.py:207-216, same pattern). The test at inspector/tests/db/test_public_state_bucket_dates.py only creates transitions via _step() which always passes a non-None to_state, so the None-case is never exercised. A regression that removes the guard would raise KeyError when processing these real audit rows during bucket_dates replay.

findings.title: No test that replay isolates by slug (no bleed across deliveries)
findings.explanation: Each test exercises one slug at a time. The replay depends on `repo_transitions.for_slug(slug)` correctly scoping by slug — a regression that returned all rows would still produce plausible (but wrong) bucket_dates. Per-slug isolation is the modal's correctness contract.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that seeds two deliveries (`d1`, `d2`) with interleaved transitions and asserts `_bucket_dates_for_slug('d1')` reflects only `d1`'s timeline and vice versa.
findings.verifier_notes: The finding is confirmed. `_attach_bucket_dates` (public_state.py:219-222) processes multiple deliveries with different slugs in a single call, yet no test verifies that `_bucket_dates_for_slug` correctly isolates by slug when multiple slugs with interleaved transitions exist in the same DB. All existing tests seed only one slug per test. A regression in `for_slug` WHERE clause filtering (repo_transitions.py:142-149) would not be caught by current tests. While the parametrized WHERE clause is unlikely to break accidentally, the coverage gap is real and the proposed test is appropriate for defense-in-depth.

findings.title: `_attach_bucket_dates` integration wrapper has no direct test
findings.explanation: `_attach_bucket_dates` is the integration seam called by `detail()` and `admin_view_reciter()` to populate `bucket_dates` on each delivery in place. The current test exercises the inner `_bucket_dates_for_slug` only. If the wrapper iterates the wrong list (e.g. only public_dels and skips discarded) or fails to mutate in place, no test catches it.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that drives the modal-facing API (`public_state.detail(reciter_id)` and `admin_view_reciter(reciter_id)`) end-to-end and asserts each delivery dict gains a `bucket_dates` key with the expected per-bucket timestamps — including the discarded section in admin_view.
findings.verifier_notes: The `_attach_bucket_dates` wrapper function (inspector/services/reference/public_state.py:217-220) has no direct integration test. Only the inner `_bucket_dates_for_slug()` function is tested in isolation (test_public_state_bucket_dates.py). The callers at lines 386 (detail()) and 478-479 (admin_view_reciter()) have no assertions verifying that bucket_dates is actually attached to delivery dicts. Route test test_route_public.py:267-281 calls reciter_detail() but doesn't assert bucket_dates presence. Service test test_public_state_admin_view.py:87-104 and 176-181 call admin_view_reciter() and detail() but don't assert bucket_dates. A mutation error or iteration bug (e.g., only attaching to public_dels but not discarded_dels) would not be caught by existing tests.

findings.title: Test step list is dominated by an essay-style comment block
findings.explanation: The repo `comments.md` rule discourages long explanatory comments and references to removed states. The inline comment in `test_bucket_dates_collapse_and_reentry` explains in 7+ lines that `awaiting_timestamps` was removed and how the replay's ValueError guard skips it — this duplicates the docstring on `_bucket_dates_for_slug` and the source comment on `ReciterState`. It reads like an essay and references a removed state (`LEGACY state`), which the comment rule flags as a red-flag pattern.
findings.proposed_action: Trim to one line (`# step 5 is the removed awaiting_timestamps state; the replay must skip it`) and let the docstrings on the function and ReciterState carry the rationale.

findings.title: test_spine.py re-declares `fresh_db` already provided by tests/db/conftest.py
findings.explanation: Every other test file in inspector/tests/db/ (test_repo_access.py, test_repo_state.py, test_repo_requests_activity.py, test_repo_transitions.py, test_repo_catalog.py, test_review_followups.py, test_repo_releases.py, test_public_state_bucket_dates.py) consumes the conftest-provided `fresh_db` fixture without redeclaring it. test_spine.py defines its own copy (body identical except the temp filename is `spine.db` instead of `test.db`), which shadows the conftest one for this module and creates the kind of drift the conftest exists to prevent.
findings.proposed_action: Delete the local `fresh_db` fixture in test_spine.py (lines 19-24) and rely on the conftest fixture, matching every sibling file in the package.
findings.verifier_notes: The local `fresh_db` fixture in inspector/tests/db/test_spine.py:19-24 IS functionally redundant. It shadows the identical fixture from inspector/tests/db/conftest.py:10-17. The only difference is the temp filename ('spine.db' vs 'test.db'), which is irrelevant since each test gets a unique tmp_path. All sibling test files (test_repo_access.py, test_repo_state.py, etc.) successfully use the conftest fixture without redeclaring it. Removing the local fixture would align test_spine.py with its siblings and reduce fixture complexity. The proposed action to delete lines 19-24 is correct.

findings.title: Hand-written vocab+delivery INSERT blocks duplicate `_helpers.seed_delivery`
findings.explanation: Three tests (test_one_open_claim_per_slug, test_pending_request_unique_only_when_slug_present, test_visibility_discarded_requires_reason) each open with the same ~6 inline INSERTs to wire reciters/riwayahs/styles/sources/channels + a delivery — exactly what `_helpers.seed_delivery` (consumed by repo_state, repo_requests_activity, review_followups tests) already does. The boilerplate buries the actual invariant under test and would drift the next time the delivery row schema gains a NOT NULL column.
findings.proposed_action: Replace the inline blocks with `from ._helpers import seed_delivery, seed_user` and call `seed_user('u1'); seed_user('u2'); seed_delivery('d1')` like the sibling files do.
findings.verifier_notes: The three tests in test_spine.py (test_one_open_claim_per_slug, test_pending_request_unique_only_when_slug_present, test_visibility_discarded_requires_reason) each contain inline INSERT blocks at lines 122-139, 158-170, and 209-221 respectively. These blocks insert identical vocab (reciters, riwayahs, styles, sources, channels) and delivery rows to what _helpers.seed_delivery() provides (lines 16-32). The tests are "smoke tests for the SQLite substrate spine" (docstring line 1-3) specifically testing schema constraints—they don't require atomic setup across all rows. The inline blocks could be replaced with `seed_user()` and `seed_delivery()` calls (following the pattern used successfully in test_repo_state.py, test_repo_requests_activity.py, and test_review_followups.py). The added_by_hf_id field difference (inline uses 'u1'/'u2', seed_delivery uses 'sys') is irrelevant since the tests only verify constraint enforcement, not the audit trail. Refactoring would eliminate boilerplate and reduce drift risk per DRY principle.

findings.title: test_foreign_keys_enforced passes for the wrong (or any) reason
findings.explanation: The comment claims 'delivery referencing a missing reciter must fail (PRAGMA foreign_keys=ON)' but the INSERT references five missing FK targets (reciter_id='nope', riwayah='hafs', style='murattal', source='src', channel='ch') in a fresh DB — none of these vocab rows are seeded. SQLite will raise IntegrityError for whichever FK it checks first, so the test only proves 'some FK is enforced', not specifically the reciter FK. The assertion still passes, but the narrative is misleading and the test would survive even if the `reciter_id REFERENCES reciters(reciter_id)` clause were silently dropped.
findings.proposed_action: Seed the full vocab via `_helpers._seed_vocab(conn)` plus a valid reciter, then violate only `reciter_id` (e.g. reciter_id='nope'). The test then actually pins the reciters FK.
findings.verifier_notes: The test at /c/Users/ahmed/Documents/Work/my-projects/quranic-universal-audio/.claude/worktrees/elated-heyrovsky-aa8bb0/inspector/tests/db/test_spine.py:110-119 violates 5 FK constraints simultaneously (reciter_id, riwayah, style, source, channel all referencing missing rows in a fresh DB). PRAGMA foreign_keys is confirmed ON in connection.py:79. While the test passes (IntegrityError is raised), it doesn't specify which FK constraint is being checked first—SQLite will fail on whichever FK it checks first (typically reciter_id by schema order), but the test doesn't guarantee this. The pattern in other tests (test_one_open_claim_per_slug, test_pending_request_unique) all seed vocab properly before violating specific constraints. The narrative is misleading; this test proves "some FK is enforced" not "reciter_id FK is enforced". The proposed action (seed vocab, violate only reciter_id) aligns with test patterns elsewhere in the file and would eliminate ambiguity.

findings.title: Expected-tables set in test_migration_creates_all_tables is stale wrt later migrations
findings.explanation: The expected set covers migrations 0001-0005 (plus the activity_dismissals drop at 0006) but omits tables introduced by 0008 (permission_overrides), 0010 (guide_views), and 0014 (per_recitation_releases, gh_releases, gh_release_recitations). The `expected <= names` subset assertion masks this — the test passes either way. The file's intent (derive vs hard-code, see the _LATEST_VERSION comment at line 14) was that schema growth should not require touching the test, but the table list breaks that contract every time a CREATE TABLE migration lands.
findings.proposed_action: Either derive the expected table set by scanning `*.sql` files for CREATE TABLE statements minus DROPs, or convert the test to assert only the core spine tables (db_meta, transitions, delivery_states, claims, requests) it actually cares about and let the version assertion at line 28 cover 'migrations ran to head'.
findings.verifier_notes: Verdict=confirmed but severity→info (not convention/low). The test works correctly but violates the stated design intent. The proposed action is sound: either derive the expected set dynamically via `_discover()` / grepping *.sql for CREATE TABLE, or explicitly document that this test covers only core spine tables (0001-0005) and rely on the version assertion to catch incomplete migrations.

findings.title: No coverage for `PRAGMA query_only = ON` on reader connections
findings.explanation: _apply_pragmas applies `query_only = ON` to non-writer connections, which is the load-bearing guarantee that thread-local readers cannot accidentally mutate the DB outside the serialized writer. test_spine.py covers FK enforcement and partial-unique but never asserts a write through a reader fails. If this PRAGMA were dropped, the spine would silently lose the single-writer invariant.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that `get_conn()` (when no active txn is open on the context) raises sqlite3.OperationalError on an INSERT/UPDATE because `query_only=ON`. Verifies the reader/writer separation pragma is wired correctly.
findings.verifier_notes: Line 85 in inspector/services/db/connection.py shows 0 hits in coverage.xml. The `PRAGMA query_only = ON` pragma is correctly implemented and documented as load-bearing for the single-writer invariant, but no test verifies that writes through a reader connection fail. The pragma itself works (verified independently), but its coverage gap is real and the proposed test would prevent regression if this critical pragma were accidentally removed or the code path disabled.

findings.title: No coverage for `_generation` bumping on reset() forcing readers to reopen
findings.explanation: reset() bumps `_generation` so the next `_get_reader()` per thread sees a stale generation and reopens the conn against the new path. This is what makes `set_db_path_for_test` (used by every test in this suite via fresh_db) actually swap DBs. The behavior is currently untested — if the generation counter were dropped, tests would still pass on the first run but silently share readers across tmp_paths in cross-test scenarios.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that opens a reader on DB A, calls set_db_path_for_test(DB_B), and verifies the next `get_conn()` returns a connection bound to DB_B (e.g. user_version differs, or a row inserted into A is not visible).
findings.verifier_notes:
The finding is CONFIRMED. The _generation counter mechanism is real and essential. Reading the code:

1. `_readers` is thread-local (connection.py:46)
2. `_generation` is a module-level counter (connection.py:48)  
3. `_get_reader()` reopens the connection only if the cached generation differs from the current _generation (connection.py:131)
4. `reset()` unconditionally bumps _generation (connection.py:243) with explicit intent comment
5. `set_db_path_for_test()` calls reset() then changes _db_path (connection.py:71-75)

If _generation were not bumped, subsequent _get_reader() calls would reuse a stale connection cached for the old DB path. The test `test_upload_then_pull_roundtrip` (test_sync.py:36-54) implicitly verifies this by switching DB paths and expecting get_conn() to return a connection to the NEW path. Removing the _generation bump would cause that test to fail.

However, the gap is real: there's no explicit, focused test documenting this critical mechanism. The behavior is only verified as a side-effect of broader sync/pull testing.

findings.title: No coverage for `_NAME_RE` filtering of non-conforming migration filenames
findings.explanation: _discover() skips files that don't match `NNNN_*.sql` and logs a warning. There is no test that, e.g., a `README.md` or `0007_init.sql.bak` in the migrations dir is silently ignored. A subtle regression where the regex tightens or loosens could either skip a real migration (bricked boot) or attempt to run garbage.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that monkeypatches _MIGRATIONS_DIR (or uses a tmp_path migrations dir) with a mixed bag of conforming and non-conforming filenames, and asserts only the well-named ones are picked up by _discover().
findings.verifier_notes: Severity: change from 'low' to 'ultra-low'. Explanation: revise to acknowledge implicit integration testing via test_spine.py:test_migration_creates_all_tables and module-level _discover() calls. Reframe proposed action as "add an isolated unit test for clarity and regex mutation-testing" rather than "fill a missing test gap that could cause silent failures."

findings.title: No coverage for atomic mid-migration failure (user_version not bumped on error)
findings.explanation: The migration runner promises 'a crash mid-migration never leaves a half-applied version recorded' (docstring). test_spine.py covers fresh migrate and re-run no-op, but does not verify the failure path — that a syntax error or constraint violation in a migration script causes rollback AND leaves user_version unchanged so the next boot retries cleanly. This is the fail-fast guarantee `/healthz` 503 relies on.
findings.proposed_action: Add a test that feeds the migrate runner a tmp migrations dir containing a deliberately-broken NNNN_*.sql (e.g. `CREATE TABLE x (...); SELECT broken_function();`), asserts the run raises, and verifies user_version stayed at the pre-migration value.
findings.verifier_notes: The migration runner at /inspector/services/db/migrate.py (lines 39-70) promises in its docstring (lines 43-44) that "a crash mid-migration never leaves a half-applied version recorded" by bumping user_version in the same transaction as the DDL. The implementation wraps each migration in explicit BEGIN/COMMIT (line 58). However, test_spine.py contains only two migration-related tests: test_migration_creates_all_tables and test_rerun_migrations_is_noop — both test successful paths. There is NO test that feeds run_migrations a deliberately-broken SQL script (e.g., one with a syntax error or constraint violation), asserts it raises, and verifies user_version stayed at the pre-migration value. This failure path is the core guarantee the docstring advertises and what /healthz 503 relies on.

findings.title: Test file's stated 'code under test' does not match the actual code exercised
findings.explanation: The audit brief identifies repo_visitors.py as the code under test, but test_spine.py's docstring (and assertions) target connection.py + migrate.py + the 0001/0002/0004/0005/0006 schema. repo_visitors.py is only touched indirectly via the `'visitor_daily'` table-existence assertion. A new contributor opening test_spine.py expecting visitor-rollup coverage would be confused — visitor_daily IO is exercised in inspector/tests/admin/test_visitor_analytics.py. The file's own docstring is accurate; the mismatch is in the cross-reference / mental model.
findings.proposed_action: No file change needed — flagging for the broader test inventory so 'spine-data' as a subsystem label maps to connection/migrate/substrate invariants, and repo_visitors gets its own entry pointing at admin/test_visitor_analytics.py.
findings.verifier_notes: test_spine.py's docstring correctly describes the file as testing "migrations, txn primitives, db_seq bumping, savepoint nesting, and partial-unique invariants." It only incidentally verifies visitor_daily table existence (line 40) without functionally testing repo_visitors.py operations. Functional tests for repo_visitors are in test_visitor_analytics.py (lines 20-57 directly call upsert/read operations). The audit brief mislabeled repo_visitors.py as the code under test when the file's actual scope is substrate initialization. This is a test-inventory mapping issue, not a test quality defect—the test does exactly what its own docstring promises.

findings.title: repo_review_views.py has zero direct unit tests
findings.explanation: Grep across inspector/tests for mark_viewed / viewed_at_for_user / count_unviewed_for_user returns only test_timestamps_jobs.py (which exercises the count via the service) and test_reviews_detail.py (which exercises list/detail). The three public APIs of repo_review_views are never invoked from a db-package test, and several non-trivial behaviours are completely unprotected: (a) the ON CONFLICT upsert that advances viewed_at on a second view; (b) viewed_at_for_user returning the per-slug dict shape; (c) the released_at IS NULL filter on the claims LEFT JOIN (so a closed claim's stale marked_ready_at doesn't keep counting); (d) the under_review-only guard on the marked-ready branch (so a Released row with an old marked_ready_at doesn't fire the marked-ready signal); (e) ensure_user FK-priming on mark_viewed for an unseen admin; (f) the MAX(IFNULL(...)) comparison's behaviour when only one of the two events is set. The whole module is the substrate for the Reviews-tab notification dot — exactly the kind of comparison logic that needs targeted unit coverage, not indirect-via-service coverage.
findings.proposed_action: Add a new inspector/tests/db/test_repo_review_views.py with: a mark_viewed-then-mark_viewed-again upsert test asserting viewed_at advances; a viewed_at_for_user shape/empty test; cycle-safety (mark ready → view → re-mark-ready → unread again); two-events-only-one-fires (under_review with marked_ready_at but no job; released with last_job_finished_at but no claim); the released_at-IS-NULL filter (closed claim with stale marked_ready_at must not count); and the under_review-only gate (released row with stale marked_ready_at must not count via the marked-ready branch).
findings.verifier_notes: Coverage report shows repo_review_views.py at 61.5% with 5 missing lines across all three public functions (mark_viewed lines 26-32, viewed_at_for_user lines 42-46, count_unviewed_for_user lines 64-82). No test_repo_review_views.py file exists in inspector/tests/db/. The module is only exercised indirectly through reviews_service wrappers in test_timestamps_jobs.py, which means the upsert semantics, dict shape, MAX(IFNULL()) logic, and ensure_user FK behavior are never directly tested.

findings.title: get_review_detail tests cover only open-claim/submission slice
findings.explanation: test_reviews_detail.py asserts on detail['state'] and detail['current_claim'] only.
